Spread Love & Acceptance: The whole book, the short version.
By Christian. Published by Spread Love & Acceptance.

This edition: October 2026. Made from the chapters at spreadloveandacceptance.com/book, where they are kept up to date.

Free to read and share. You may print, copy and share this book for personal use and for non-commercial teaching, as long as you credit “Spread Love & Acceptance, spreadloveandacceptance.com” and don’t change it or sell it.

Not therapy. This book is general education about people and relationships. It is not a diagnosis, treatment or a replacement for help from a doctor, counsellor or other trained professional, and it can’t know your situation.

If you are not safe. If you feel afraid of someone you live with, or someone controls your money, phone or movements, that is not a problem to fix with a worksheet. spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety lists free, private help. If you are in danger now, call your local emergency number.

The examples are made up. The people in the scenes and examples are invented, built from common patterns. None of them is a real person or a testimonial.

Research mentioned in the chapters is listed, with links, in the research notes at the back and at spreadloveandacceptance.com/research.

Set in Lora, Fraunces and IBM Plex Mono.

If you need help now

If you might act on thoughts of ending your life, or someone is in danger right now, call your local emergency number: 999 in the UK, 112 or 999 in Ireland, 911 in the US and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand.

If you are struggling, or worried about someone else, you can talk to a trained person now. These lines are free, private and open day and night. You don’t have to be sure it is a crisis to call or text.

Where you areCall or text
United StatesCall or text 988 (the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline), or chat at 988lifeline.org. You can also text HOME to 741741 (Crisis Text Line).
United KingdomCall Samaritans free on 116 123. Or text SHOUT to 85258 (Shout, a free text line).
IrelandCall Samaritans free on 116 123.
CanadaCall or text 9-8-8 (the Suicide Crisis Helpline), in English or French.
AustraliaCall Lifeline on 13 11 14, or text 0477 13 11 14.
New ZealandCall or text 1737 (Need to talk?).
Anywhere elsefindahelpline.com lists free helplines in many countries, by phone, text and chat.

For children and young people

UKChildline, 0800 1111 (free, for anyone under 19)
IrelandChildline, 1800 66 66 66 (free, for anyone up to 18)
CanadaKids Help Phone, 1-800-668-6868, or text CONNECT to 686868
AustraliaKids Helpline, 1800 55 1800 (ages 5 to 25)
New ZealandYouthline, 0800 376 633, or text 234
US988 is for every age.

If you’re worried about someone

Ask them plainly: “Are you thinking about ending your life?” Studies have found that asking does not put the idea in someone’s head, and talking about it may even ease it. Listen, stay with them if you can, and call or text one of the lines above together. Part Three, Chapter 12, page 312 says more about helping someone in a crisis, and Chapter 16, page 384 about worry, low mood and when to get help.

This book is general education, not a crisis service. The website’s tools keep what you type on your own device, so nobody there can see it or reply to it. The numbers were checked in October 2026. Numbers can change; findahelpline.com keeps an up-to-date list.

zqhowqz

How to use this book

This is a book about seeing what is really going on, in yourself and between people, without blaming anyone, and then changing one small thing. This copy holds 26 chapters in three parts, in the short version. There is no wrong way in.

The parts

  • Part One: Self-discovery. Where you came from, who you are now and who you are becoming. You can read all of it on your own.
  • Part Two: Between us. One idea per chapter about sharing a life, a home or work with someone, each with a worksheet that puts it to use.
  • Part Three: Understanding people. How feelings, stress, trust, change, grief, groups and love work, for anyone, in any kind of relationship.

Two sizes of every chapter

Every chapter comes in a short version (about 10 to 15 minutes) and a full version with the research, more examples and more to try. This is the short version. The full version is free at spreadloveandacceptance.com/book.

Read in order, or by need

Read it front to back like any book, or start with the chapter that fits what is going on. Each chapter ends with What to remember, This connects to (the chapters that explain it or put it to use, with page numbers) and Put it to use, with codes you can scan for the matching tool.

In every chapter

  • A short scene: a made-up moment from everyday life.
  • Words you could use: sentences to say out loud.
  • Try this: one small thing to do this week.
  • Common mix-ups: easy mistakes, and what is closer to true.

The site, the program and Professor Puddles

The book has a free website with the workpapers (pages you fill in) and tools (helpers you use) that the chapters mention; the next page explains both. Nothing you type there leaves your device, and there is no account. The six-week program (spreadloveandacceptance.com/prog-01) puts Part Two to work a week at a time, and the self path does the same for Part One. Professor Puddles, the site’s friendly guide, answers questions about the book’s ideas.

Go gently

Some chapters touch hard things: grief, shame, anger, worry, trauma. Skip anything that isn’t right for today. Nothing here is a test, and nothing needs to be done all at once.

Workpapers, tools and three friends

Workpaper WP-03 Workpapers: pages you fill in

A workpaper is a page you fill in, on your own or together: a one-week log, a list of who owns which job, a short check. Each one has a number, like WP-03, and it is always called a workpaper, for example “Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job”. The blank workpapers are also at the back of this book, one page each, to copy.

Tool Tools: helpers you use on the site

A tool is an interactive helper on the website: a quiz, a calm-down timer, a card maker, or the Chat analyzer that reads a message with you. You use it and it gives you something back. It is always called a tool, for example “Tool: Chat analyzer”.

The book keeps the two apart: a workpaper and a tool never share a list. Both are free, need no account, and what you type stays on your device.

Three friends who give hints

  • Professor Puddles, the site’s cheerful raindrop professor, gives most of the hints: a thought to take with you, and the workpaper or tool that fits.
  • Tidbit, the quick, curious pup with the big smile and the collar, bounds in now and then with a playful tip.
  • Sugarfoot, the steady, gentle pup with the long soft ears and the best hugs, turns up with a calm, slow tip.

They keep to the lighter pages. Where a chapter talks about crisis, deep grief or being hurt, the pages stay quiet and plain.

zqhandedqz

If someone handed you this book

Maybe it was left on your side of the bed with a page turned down. Maybe someone said, “Could you just read this bit?” Either way, you didn’t choose it. Fair enough. Here is the short version, written for you.

This isn’t a case against you

The book starts from something researchers have found again and again: when two people each estimate their share of the housework, the two answers usually add up to more than 100%. Nobody is lying. You see every minute of your own effort and only some of theirs, and so do they (Chapter II, page 91). So the book never asks who the bad guy is. Its numbers score the setup, never a person.

What’s in it for you

  • Fewer repeat arguments about the same jobs.
  • Jobs that are clearly yours, so nobody needs to remind you about them.
  • Credit for what you already do. Your jobs go on the list too: the car, the bins, the late-night lifts, the things you fix.
  • A say in what “fair” means in your house. It isn’t always 50/50 (Chapter IV, page 122).

It doesn’t ask for therapy talk, and you never fill anything in about the other person. You can say no.

A first week: three small things

  1. Log your own week. Rough minutes on “Who did what”, including the thinking part: booking, remembering, planning. Ten minutes in all. Only yours, never theirs.
  2. Ask one question, and just listen. “What’s the one job you’d most like to stop thinking about?” Don’t defend or count. Write the answer down.
  3. Take over that job, the whole of it, including the noticing (below).

Words to open the talk

“I read the bit you gave me. I don’t agree with all of it, but I get the point about the stuff nobody sees.”
“I’d rather own a couple of things properly than ‘help’ with everything. Which one would you most like off your mind?”
“Give me a week to see what I actually do. Then let’s look together.”

Best left out, for now: “Just tell me what to do” (it hands the thinking straight back), “You should have asked” and, in the first five minutes, “I do loads too.” That may be true. Save it for when you both have your logs.

Taking over a whole job, noticing included

Every job has a part you can see (doing it) and parts you can’t: noticing it needs doing, remembering, planning and checking it got done (the Preface, page 64). Taking a job over means all of it.

  1. Pick one job that repeats: the children’s clothes and shoes, the bins, the car, school forms, the dentist.
  2. Get the handover once. What it involves, when it’s due, where things are, who to call. Ask your questions now, not every week.
  3. Move the remembering out of their head. A phone reminder, the calendar, a list on the fridge: anywhere but the other person.
  4. Do it start to finish for a month without being reminded. If you need reminding, fix your reminder, not the relationship.
  5. Do it your way. If the result is fine, the method is yours. Their part is to let it be done differently.
  6. Ask for a backstop if you like: someone who notices a slip and says so once, kindly. A backstop isn’t a supervisor (Chapter II, page 91).

A made-up example. Hester has always looked after the children’s clothes: spotting toes at the end of shoes, school sizes, swimming kit, passing on what’s outgrown. Wilf takes it over. Hester writes the handover note: sizes, the shop, which drawer holds the next size up. Wilf sets a reminder for the first Sunday of each month: “Shoes, uniform, kit.” In week two he misses the PE kit for a school trip. Hester says once, “The trip kit is Thursday,” and he adds “school letters” to his Sunday check. A month in, Hester says the biggest change is that she no longer thinks about shoes at eleven at night.

If you think it’s already fair

Log your week anyway. If it comes out even, that is useful to know, and the book will say so: a fair score doesn’t silence anyone, and a low one doesn’t blame anyone. And if this book feels like the wrong place to start, Find it fast, page 9 lists other ways in.

Then

Part One · Then

Know yourself: then, where your lens came from

Why you expect what you expect, and how the rules you picked up growing up still make small decisions for you today.

In this chapter

  1. You’re not one thing
  2. Your lens came from somewhere
  3. Each stage of growing up asks its own question
  4. When something happened matters
  5. Some old answers were learned without all the facts
  6. An old rule can read other people for you
  7. Write down the rulebook from home
  8. You get to choose which rules to keep
  9. What you carry forward is yours
  10. You, in all your relationships
  11. Common mix-ups

This is where the book begins. Part One (Then, Now and Next) is about you. Part Two (a Preface and Chapters I to V) is about the people you share a life with. Part Three (Chapters 1 to 17) is about how people work. Some printed copies hold only one or two of the parts; every chapter is free to read at spreadloveandacceptance.com/book, and the book at a glance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/topic-start-here) there gives a one-minute tour of the whole thing.

Sunday, 10:15am

Your partner is still in bed and the kitchen is a mess. Before you have had a single thought, you feel it. Of course it’s always you. Nobody said that, but in the house you grew up in, whoever noticed the mess cleaned it, and that old rule has just made a decision on your behalf.

Across town, Ray’s house has been quiet since his wife died, and nobody will see the dishes. He still can’t sit down until every one of them is washed and put away, because a rule from the home he grew up in is still keeping watch.

  1. You’re not one thing.

    A reaction usually comes from three places at once. Part of it is how you are built, your wiring, which stays much the same. Part is what life taught you, patterns that can soften over time. And part is the kind of day you are having, which passes. This chapter is about the middle layer, the patterns life taught you, and Now (page 35) looks at the other two.

    A grandmother snaps when her grown-up son is late for Sunday lunch. Some of that is her wiring, because she has always liked things on time. Some is an old rule that lateness means you don’t care, and some is the bad night’s sleep she had. She could tell him, “Some of this is me being tired, and some of it is an old thing. Give me a minute.” The next time you react strongly, it is worth asking whether the reaction is mostly wiring, something you learned or simply today.

    Dig deeper: the three layers

  2. Your lens came from somewhere.

    Family, school, friends, culture, money at home and what you watched all taught you what to expect of yourself, of other people and of how a good partner, parent or friend behaves. By adulthood your lens no longer feels like a lens, because it feels like simply seeing. One friend grew up with big birthday parties and another with quiet ones, so a small dinner out feels hurtful to one of them and perfect to the other. Neither is being unreasonable, and “In my family this was a big deal. What was it like in yours?” usually clears the air.

    Pick one thing you think everyone does and ask someone how their family did it. Where your lens came from (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up) walks through the idea gently, and you can read one section and stop.

    Dig deeper: the lens idea

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: the rules from home aren’t good or bad, they’re just yours to have a good sniff at. A fun first look is how you like to talk.

    Tool: How you connect: the 2-minute style quiz spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength

  3. Each stage of growing up asks its own question.

    A small child is asking whether the world is safe and whether they can do things for themselves. Later the questions become whether they are capable, where they belong and whether they can be close to someone without losing themselves. Later still, adults ask what they are building and whether their life has meant something. The ages are rough and people move at their own pace, but the answers you landed on can become understandings you keep using as an adult. Someone who moved schools four times as a teenager may still feel like the outsider at every new job, and may catch themselves thinking that part of them is still asking whether they belong.

    Read the questions again and notice which one still feels loud for you. Noticing is enough for now.

    Dig deeper: the stages

  4. When something happened matters.

    An experience that touches the question you were answering at the time tends to go deeper. A house move at four is mostly about new routines, while a move at fourteen, right in the middle of wondering where you belong, can leave a longer feeling of being the outsider. Two adult siblings remember their parents’ divorce quite differently. One was six and remembers a new bedroom and a new bus route, and the other was fifteen and remembers feeling torn in half. Both memories are true, and they go some way to explaining why the two of them still argue about that year (see Family rifts, spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts).

    Deeper isn’t permanent, though, because people keep learning all their lives. Think of one big change from growing up, and ask how old you were and what you were trying to work out at the time.

    Dig deeper: why timing matters

  5. Some old answers were learned without all the facts.

    Many people carry beliefs like “I’m only okay when I’m useful”, “my needs are a burden” or “mistakes mean I’m bad”. A child often can’t know what was going on for the grown-ups and only knows how it felt. As an adult you are allowed to look again with the full picture, and looking again doesn’t mean deciding it was all fine, because some things really were not okay. A foster carer who learned as a girl that her needs were a burden finds it hard to ask for respite, a planned break while someone else cares for the children, even when she is worn out. An old voice tells her not to ask, while the adult in her knows that asking is fair.

    Write down one old belief about yourself, and under it write what you would tell a friend who believed the same thing.

    Dig deeper: old answers and fairer readings

  6. An old rule can read other people for you.

    If silence at home meant anger, a partner’s quiet evening can feel like trouble on the way. An expectation that nobody ever said out loud can’t be agreed to either, so the other person can only miss it, whether it is “if you loved me, you’d just know” or “whoever notices, does it”. Each of these is somebody’s family rule. When a housemate leaves without saying goodbye, someone raised in a quiet, angry house may assume she is upset, when she may simply be late for a shift.

    This week, when you catch yourself guessing what someone’s silence means, try asking instead, perhaps with “When you went quiet earlier, I wasn’t sure what it meant. Is everything okay?”

    Dig deeper: rules that read others

    Professor Puddles

    When an old rule jumps in before you’ve had a chance to think, you don’t have to argue with it. Write it down, and look at it again on a calm day.

    Tool: Old rules, new choices spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up

  7. zqaxselfx1xthenxxpxrulebookqz

    Write down the rulebook from home.

    Finish these six lines the way your childhood home would have finished them. “In my family, love looked like…” “When someone was upset, we…” “The jobs were split like this…” “Resting was okay when…” “Asking for help meant…” “The unforgivable thing was…” The rulebook page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up#home) has room to write them, and nothing is saved anywhere except on your own device. Two partners from different faiths once did this and both wrote that holidays belonged to their family, which finally explained why every December had been so hard (see Two faiths, one family, spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths).

    Finishing a single line today is plenty, and the others can wait. If you share one, you might say, “Here’s a rule I grew up with. I’m not saying it’s right. I just want you to know it’s there.”

    Dig deeper: the six rulebook lines

  8. You get to choose which rules to keep.

    For each line of your rulebook, ask whether you still want that rule. When a reaction feels bigger than the moment, try a one-minute lens check once you have settled. Where did you learn this, how old does it feel, and is it true here, with this person, now? What would the adult you choose? A team leader notices that her old rule about mistakes makes her hide problems from her manager, so she writes a new one on a sticky note above her desk, saying that mistakes are information and the team fixes them together.

    Pick one rule from your list and write the version you would like to live by, in the form “I used to think ___. Now I’m choosing ___.” Later you can swap rulebooks with someone you trust and choose shared rules on purpose.

    Dig deeper: the lens check, and choosing together

  9. What you carry forward is yours.

    You couldn’t control the home you grew up in, what other people did or what you learned before you had all the facts. What is in your hands now is smaller and stronger. It includes which old rules you keep, how you treat yourself about them and where you spend your energy today, and that includes people. Give your time and care where they are met with care, and let one-sided effort shrink back to what feels fair, so that you still have something left to give.

    Someone living on their own always plans the meetups with one old friend, who never asks back. They stop chasing, send a warm “I’d love to see you. Let me know when works for you,” and find they see more of the friends who reply (see Always the one reaching out? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends)). Is there a relationship where you give far more than comes back? You could give a little less there this month. (If you are afraid of someone, this isn’t about managing them. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has people to talk to.)

    Dig deeper: your part, then and now

Tuesday morning

Two people get the same text, asking whether they can talk tonight. One is pleased, because she likes knowing ahead. The other feels his stomach drop, because in the home he grew up in, “we need to talk” meant trouble, and he spends the whole afternoon rehearsing answers to a conversation that turns out to be about a holiday.

You, in all your relationships

Your old rules go wherever you go, starting with how you treat yourself, since the voice you use after a mistake is often an old one. At home they decide who notices, who plans and what quiet means, and two housemates can find they are living by two rulebooks about mess, noise and guests. In families, old roles like the helper or the peacemaker switch back on at the front door. At work, someone who was praised mainly for being useful may say yes to everything and then quietly resent it, until seeing the old rule lets them pause before the next yes. After a breakup old rules can get louder, which is a good time to look at them gently (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) lists pages for many situations.

Common mix-ups

  • “Looking back means blaming my family.” Looking back is about understanding. Many of the adults who raised us were working with their own lenses too, and if that doesn’t fit your story, you don’t have to make it fit.
  • “If it started in childhood, I’m stuck with it.” Many old patterns soften with awareness, safety and practice, and some leave a lasting sensitivity you learn to carry and explain.
  • “Every big reaction is an old wound.” Often it is just a full tank. Chapter III (page 107) helps you tell leftover stress from this-moment stress.
  • “If they won’t look at their rules, there’s no point looking at mine.” Knowing your own rules changes how you react, even if nobody else ever reads a word of this.

A note on care: This part looks back at growing up. It is general education, not a diagnosis or therapy, and it can’t tell you what anyone has. Not every home felt calm or kind, so take only what is useful. If looking back feels heavy, you can stop and come back another day, or explore it with a qualified professional, if and when you want that. Nothing here is required, and nothing you write needs to be shared.

If you want to go on, think of one “always” or “never” you felt this week and ask whose voice it sounds like and how old you felt. Then write one sentence that the adult you would rather be could live by, and keep it somewhere you will see it. Where your lens came from, Roots & Wings (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up#roots) and Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself) go further.

What to remember

  • You’re not one thing.
  • Each stage of growing up asks its own question.
  • Some old answers were learned without all the facts.
  • Write down the rulebook from home.
  • What you carry forward is yours.

zqselfx2xnowqz

Now

Part One · Now

Know yourself: now, your wiring, your weather and your words

Why the same words can land differently on different days and in different people, and how to understand today’s you well enough to say what helps.

In this chapter

  1. Today is made of two layers you can work with
  2. Know how you like to be spoken to
  3. Check your weather before you speak
  4. Ask where this feeling is coming from
  5. Plan what settles you on a calm day
  6. Your needs and limits are information, not demands
  7. Being wired differently is not being wrong
  8. Explain yourself without over-sharing
  9. Do your part, and only your part
  10. You, in all your relationships
  11. Common mix-ups

In short

  • Today has two layers you can work with. Work with your wiring, which stays, and around today’s conditions, which pass.
  • Check your state before a hard talk. Weather, the three states, the stress tank and the battery are different words for how much room you have today.
  • If a feeling is hard to name, start with the body. That is common, and it even has a name, alexithymia.
  • Your needs and limits are information. Plan what settles you on a calm day, and say what helps in one short sentence.
  • A mix-up between two different minds runs both ways, so both people adjust a little.

Sunday, 7:50pm

A friend asks whether you are okay, and you say you’re fine. The truth is that you can’t tell whether you are fine, tired or quietly bothered by something, and you couldn’t explain it to yourself, let alone to her.

  1. Today is made of two layers you can work with.

    Your wiring is the lasting part, made up of your temperament, your pace, your senses and how you take in words. You work with it by building a setup that suits you. Today’s conditions are the passing part, such as sleep, hunger, how much you are carrying, the room and the time of day, and you work around them by eating first, sleeping on it or talking tomorrow. Mixing the two up is where a lot of frustration comes from. (Then, page 22, covers the third layer, the patterns life taught you.)

    For example, a dad who works nights finds the school-run chatter unbearable at eight in the morning, and for a while he wonders whether he is cut out for parenting at all. When he swaps to the afternoon pick-up, the same chatter is fun again (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).

    You could say “It’s the hour, honestly. Can we talk after I’ve slept?”

    Try this. Write down one thing that always bothers you, which is probably wiring, and one that only bothers you when you are tired.

    Dig deeper: wiring and conditions

    Professor Puddles

    Your wiring stays the same from day to day. Your weather doesn’t. A one-minute check in the morning helps you tell the two apart.

    Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  2. Know how you like to be spoken to.

    Your pace, your tone, how much you need spelled out and what silence means to you all change how words land. How you connect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength) helps you find words for how you think, talk and listen, and gives you a four-letter Wave Code that is meant as a light-hearted description. The “How to talk to me” card (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card) puts how you take in words on one page, which you can share before a hard talk.

    A grandmother loves phone calls and her grandson loves texts, and for a year each thought the other was being distant. Once they said how they like to talk, they settled on a Sunday call with texts in between.

    This week. Finish the sentence “I take things in best when…” and keep it for your card.

    Dig deeper: your wiring and your Wave Code

  3. Check your weather before you speak.

    Every conversation runs through your own state first. Part Two, Chapter III (page 107) looks closely at the stress tank in a shared home, so this chapter only adds the self side, a one-minute reading on your own before you decide what a hard moment means. My weather today (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) is the quick check, and How much are you carrying? is a fuller one on a short worksheet.

    For example, a long-distance couple notice that their difficult calls always fall at the end of one partner’s late shift, so they move serious talks to weekend mornings (see Long distance, spreadloveandacceptance.com/long-distance).

    Words you could use “I’m running on empty tonight. Can we pick this up tomorrow morning?”

    zqaxselfx2xnowxxstatexwordsqz

    One state, many words. The chapters and tools use a few everyday pictures for one thing, how much room you have today. They describe the same state in different ways.

    • The three states (Chapter 2, page 169, calls them the ladder) are calm and connected, revved up, and running on empty.
    • My weather today uses sky words for the same three. Clear is calm and connected, gusty is revved up, and fogged in is running on empty. Its pressure (light, building or heavy) is how much you were already carrying.
    • The stress tank is the score from How much are you carrying?, from 0 to 1, where higher means fuller.
    • The battery is the other side of the tank, the energy you have left, so a full tank means a low battery.

    “Gusty”, “revved up”, “a fairly full tank” and “a low battery” can all describe the same afternoon, so use whichever words suit you.

    Dig deeper: reading your state before you speak

  4. Ask where this feeling is coming from.

    First name the feeling, perhaps as “tight, annoyed, a bit scared”. Then ask whether it is the size of the moment or feels older, which layer it belongs to, and what it needs right now, whether that is food, space, a heads-up, reassurance or a proper conversation later. It takes a minute and works best once the first wave has passed. When a coworker asks “Quick question?” and your heart races, you might name the feeling as jumpy, recognise an old boss in it as well as a busy day, and ask for five minutes before you answer.

    zqaxselfx2xnowxxhardxtoxnameqzWhen feelings are hard to name. For some people, “What are you feeling?” is a hard question most days, and on bad days it is almost impossible. They notice a racing heart or a heavy stomach but can’t tell whether it is worry, anger or hunger. Psychologists call this alexithymia, which means “no words for feelings”. It is a trait that runs from a little to a lot, it is common, especially among autistic people, and it is not an illness. The feelings are there and the words come slowly. It helps to start with the body (“tight chest, skipped lunch”), to choose between two words (“more tired or more annoyed?”), to use the three sky words in place of feeling words, and to give it time. “I’ll tell you tomorrow” is a real answer.

    Dig deeper: a four-step self-check
  5. zqaxselfx2xnowxxpxsettleqz

    Plan what settles you on a calm day.

    The middle of being wound up is a bad time to work out what helps. The Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) is a plan you make while you are calm, covering what tends to set you off, two calming steps and one sentence for stepping away that says when you will be back. It is for you and never for the other person.

    A teenager makes a plan with herself for rows with her mum. When one heats up, she says, “I need ten minutes in my room, then I’ll come back,” and twelve minutes later she comes back down to the kitchen.

    One small step. On a calm day, write your one stepping-away sentence, including when you will be back.

    Dig deeper: deciding ahead

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: make your calm-down plan on a slow, sunny day, maybe with a cup of tea. It’s much easier than making it in the middle of a storm.

    Workpaper WP-11: The Calm-Down Kit spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11

  6. Your needs and limits are information, not demands.

    What helps you, what matters to you and what you have left are facts about you, and said kindly they let other people plan around you. “A heads-up helps me.” “I can take this one, but not that one.” “I’m low today. Can we talk tomorrow?” You don’t need to justify a need, either. A reason is a kindness you can offer when you want to. In a home with three partners, Quinn needs an hour alone after work, and once he has said so, calmly and once, it stops being a mystery and becomes part of the plan.

    Two workpapers from other chapters can help. Who did what, from the Preface (page 64), has ready-made kind ways to say no, and Say it so it lands, from Part Two, Chapter IV (page 122), helps you turn a raw reaction into a plain request.

    Something to try. Write one need you have never said out loud, and practise saying it as a fact without apologising for it.

    Dig deeper: saying your needs kindly
  7. zqaxselfx2xnowxxpxdifferentqz

    Being wired differently is not being wrong.

    Some people take in words, noise, change and feelings differently from the way most social customs were built. That is wiring, which you can understand, plan around and get support for if you choose. A woman with ADHD keeps forgetting plans with a friend and used to call herself hopeless. Now she says what helps, which is a text the day before, and she turns up (see Neurodivergent relationships, spreadloveandacceptance.com/neurodivergent-relationships).

    zqaxselfx2xnowxxdoublexempathyqzA mix-up runs both ways. When an autistic and a non-autistic person misread each other, it is easy to blame the autistic person. The double empathy problem, named by the autistic researcher Damian Milton, is the idea that the gap runs both ways, because each person reads the other through their own way of communicating and each finds the other hard to read. In one study, a story passed along a chain of autistic people kept as much detail as one passed along non-autistic people, while mixed chains lost detail faster. Wired Differently (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wired-differently) shows how two differently wired people can each misread the other. Asking “Where did we lose each other?” lets both of you adjust a little.

    Dig deeper: wiring is not a flaw

  8. Explain yourself without over-sharing.

    Three short sentences cover most moments. “This is how I’m wired. It won’t change, but here’s what helps.” “This is an old alarm. I’m working on it, and here’s what helps in the moment.” “Today’s a low-battery day.” You never owe anyone your history, so share the part that helps them help you. A man with a long-term illness tells a new friend, “Some days I have less energy, and if I cancel, it isn’t about you,” and leaves his medical notes out of it (see When one of you is ill, spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill).

    Dig deeper: scripts, and how much to share

  9. Do your part, and only your part.

    Today you control your words, your effort, your rest, your limits and what you ask for. You don’t control someone else’s mood, reply, pace or choices, and trying to manage them drains you fast. Do your side well and let go of theirs. It also helps to match energy with energy, meeting warmth with warmth and effort with effort, and giving a little less when you keep giving far more than comes back, because a protected battery is what keeps you kind.

    For example, a grown-up daughter has spent years trying to stop her father worrying about her. She can’t do that, but she can send a short “Home safe” text after long drives and then let his worry be his (see For grown-up children, spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children).

    Try this. Write one thing you keep trying to control that isn’t yours, and next to it one thing that is. (If you are afraid of someone, this isn’t about managing them. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has people to talk to.)

    Dig deeper: your circle of control, and matching energy

Friday, 6:40pm

“Surprise! I’ve booked us dinner with my cousins tonight.” They meant it as a gift. You felt your chest tighten and heard yourself say “Great” in a flat voice. Later, washing up, you wonder whether that was just you, something from years ago or simply the end of a long week, and you suspect it was a bit of all three.

You, in all your relationships

Your wiring and your weather come with you everywhere, starting with how you treat yourself on a hard day, when noticing that you are low comes before deciding that you are failing. Partners can give each other a heads-up, a quiet hour or a better time to talk, and every partner has wiring of their own. With friends and family the question is often how you like to keep in touch and how much you can give this month. At work it may be an agenda ahead or a minute before you answer, and housemates tend to negotiate noise, light and quiet time. If you live on your own, you can build a week that suits how you are built (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Common mix-ups

  • “Knowing myself means finding the right label.” It is mostly about what helps. The three layers and a Wave Code are everyday words, and neither is a diagnosis.
  • “‘That’s just how I am’ ends the talk.” It may be true, especially for wiring, and it works better as an opening, as in “This is how I’m wired, and here’s what helps.”
  • “If I tell people how I’m wired, they have to manage me.” Telling them helps their words land. You still do your part, and they still have their own needs.
  • “I’m fine” means I’m fine. Sometimes it does. It can also mean you have been tired for so long that you stopped noticing, and a quick reading each week shows the baseline you have got used to.

A note on care: This part is general education. It isn’t a diagnosis, a test or treatment, and it can’t tell you whether you’re autistic, have ADHD or anything else, or what anyone else has. If you’d like to understand yourself more deeply, a qualified professional can help, if and when you want that. Nothing here is required, and nothing you try needs to be shared. If talking about any of this with someone ever feels unsafe, or you feel you can’t say no, stop and talk with a trained counselor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counseling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? lists free, private hotlines.

To put the chapter to use, pick one reaction you had this week and write one line for each layer, the wiring part, the older part and today’s part. Take a one-minute reading of your weather, then write one sentence about what helps you, in your own words, and keep it to yourself for a few days before you share it with one person on a calm day. Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself), the “How to talk to me” card and How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying) are free on the site.

  • Part Three · Chapter 2 · Stress and the nervous systemWhy your weather changes how you hear thingspage 169

zqselfx3xnextqz

Next

Part One · Next

Know yourself: next, shaping who you are becoming

You aren’t finished, and some of who you become is up to you. This chapter is about choosing a direction and building small steps that still work on a tired day.

In this chapter

  1. Start with what matters to you
  2. Pick one small goal, in plain words
  3. Name what gets in the way
  4. Make the step tiny, and repeatable
  5. Decide ahead with a simple if-then
  6. Ask for support, as information
  7. Look back kindly once a month
  8. Kindness to yourself is part of the plan
  9. Set goals inside your circle, and spend energy where it comes back
  10. You, in all your relationships
  11. Common mix-ups

In short

  • Start with what matters to you in two or three plain words, then pick one small goal you can actually do.
  • Make the step tiny and decide ahead, as in “If it’s after dinner, then I put my shoes on.”
  • Ask for support as information, and look back kindly once a month.
  • A missed day tells you about the plan, so change the plan and keep going.
  • Set goals inside your circle, and spend your energy where it comes back.

Wednesday, 9:10pm

You meant to start walking after dinner, and you meant to last week too. Tonight you are tired, the shoes are by the door where you left them on Sunday, and you tell yourself you will begin on Monday.

  1. zqaxselfx3xnextxxpxmattersqz

    Start with what matters to you.

    A goal built on someone else’s idea of success is hard to keep up. Before you pick anything, ask what you want your days to be like, and write two or three plain words, such as calm, close to my family, steady or creative. They give you a direction to face rather than a score to reach. How you connect (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength) can help you notice what fills you up and what drains you.

    For example, after their youngest leaves home, a couple each write two words. Hers are “useful, outdoors” and his are “calm, curious”, which suddenly explains why she wants to volunteer at the nature reserve while he wants to dig over the vegetable patch (see Kids grown and gone, spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest).

    Try this. Write two plain words for what matters to you right now, in pencil if you like, since you can change them.

    Dig deeper: values first

  2. Pick one small goal, in plain words.

    Choose just one, and say it as something you will do. “Walk for ten minutes after dinner” is a goal you can keep, while “get healthier” is a hope. Your own actions are up to you, and how other people respond and how things turn out are not. A student sharing a room in halls wants to be less messy, and as an action it becomes putting her clothes in the basket before bed (see Sharing a room, spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room).

    This week. Rewrite one wish as something you will do, starting with “I will…”

    Dig deeper: one goal, in plain words

  3. Name what gets in the way.

    Use what you learned in Then (page 22) and Now (page 35). The obstacle may be your wiring, since a plan that ignores how you are built was made for someone else. It may be an old rule, such as “rest has to be earned”, or simply today’s conditions, like a tired evening. Then change the arrangement and leave yourself alone, for example by moving the step to the morning. A shift worker kept missing his evening run, which had nothing to do with laziness, because his rota changed every week. Once he tied the run to his first day off, he stopped missing it (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).

    Dig deeper: what gets in the way
  4. zqaxselfx3xnextxxpxtinyqz

    Make the step tiny, and repeatable.

    Make it small enough to survive your worst week, so that “put my shoes on” counts. Tie it to something you already do, and do it often. The 90-second daily check-in in Part Two, Chapter I (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/chapter-1-in-depth) works on the same idea, that something small and frequent lasts longer than something big and rare, and Ten-minute start (spreadloveandacceptance.com/start-in-10-minutes) shows how small a whole path can be. Someone on their own after a breakup wants to get back out there, and the tiny step they choose is one message to one friend every Sunday (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

    One small step. Shrink your step until it takes less than two minutes.

    Dig deeper: tiny, repeatable steps

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: tiny steps count, even the wobbly ones! If you like a game, there’s one where each small kind act moves the ball up the field.

    Tool: Gentle games: the Re-check Drive (calm football) spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive

  5. Decide ahead with a simple if-then.

    “If it’s after dinner, then I put my shoes on.” Deciding ahead means one decision fewer on a tired day, which is the same idea as the Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11), made while you are calm. A separated parent who wants calmer handovers decides that when she pulls up outside, she will take three slow breaths before she gets out of the car (see Co-parenting, spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting). If a plan isn’t working, change the plan.

    Something to try. Write one if-then, using a cue that happens every day, such as the kettle, the front door or brushing your teeth.

    Dig deeper: if-then plans
  6. zqaxselfx3xnextxxpxsupportqz

    Ask for support, as information.

    Tell one person what you are trying and what would help, as in “I’m trying to walk after dinner. Could you ask me about it on Sunday?” They can say no, and you don’t need their agreement to start. A woman caring for her husband after a stroke asks her brother whether he could sit with him on Thursday afternoons so she can swim, and because the request is so specific, it is easy for him to answer. Some goals are better shared with a qualified professional, and asking for one is a sensible step whenever you want it.

    Try this. Name one person and one small, specific thing they could do. (If someone uses your goals to check up on you or control you, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has people to talk to.)

    Dig deeper: asking for support

  7. Look back kindly once a month.

    This is the monthly look-back from Part Two, Chapter V (page 138), pointed at yourself. Once a month, take ten minutes to ask what went well and what kept slipping, and whether the gap was in the plan, in how much you had to give that month or in one unusual week. Old misses don’t get added up, and the only question is what to try next month. A grandmother raising her two grandchildren looks back and sees that bedtime is working and homework isn’t, so next month she tries homework at the kitchen table straight after a snack.

    This week. Put ten minutes in your calendar for the first of next month.

    Dig deeper: a monthly look at yourself

    Professor Puddles

    Your monthly look is the solo version of the monthly look-back for people who share a home. Borrow its two questions if you like: what kept slipping, and what would have made it easier?

    Workpaper WP-04: What keeps coming back? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-04

  8. Kindness to yourself is part of the plan.

    A plan that needs you to be harsh with yourself rests on what is sometimes called the second arrow. The first arrow is the slip itself, and the second is the telling-off you give yourself afterwards, which hurts more and helps less. Rest belongs inside the plan, and you can shrink a goal, change it or drop it at any time. A sixteen-year-old who planned to revise every night misses three nights and calls himself useless. His grandmother asks what he would tell his best friend, and he shrinks the goal to twenty minutes before tea.

    One small step. Next time you miss a step, say one sentence to yourself that you would say to a friend.

    Dig deeper: kindness as part of the plan

  9. Set goals inside your circle, and spend energy where it comes back.

    A goal that depends on someone else changing is really a wish. Shape each goal around what you can do, such as asking once, kindly, by Friday. You might wish your adult sister called more often, which sits outside your circle, while calling her on the first Sunday of each month and telling her you would love her to call too sits inside it. Then budget your energy like the limited thing it is, putting more into the people and plans that give back and less into the ones that only take, so that you keep going long enough to reach the goal.

    Something to try. Rewrite one goal that depends on someone else, so that the next step is yours.

    Dig deeper: planning inside your circle

The first of the month

You open your notes. Of the four small things you tried, two have stuck and two quietly stopped somewhere around the second week. You still don’t know why the Saturday swim fell away, and you write a question mark next to it for next month.

You, in all your relationships

A goal for yourself often touches the people around you, and small steps work everywhere. With a partner, offer one small habit rather than demanding one, and with friends, one message a week can be enough. In a family it might be a regular call, a visit you can keep up or a first step after years apart (see Reaching out, spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts). At work it could be one comment per meeting, and with money, one small saving habit you control.

Common mix-ups

  • “A goal has to be big to count.” Small and repeatable is what survives a bad week, and big goals are often just many small ones.
  • “If I know myself, I should be able to change anything.” Wiring stays, so the aim is a goal that fits how you are built.
  • “Asking for support means I couldn’t manage alone.” Asking gives other people the information they need to help.
  • “I’ll start on Monday.” A fresh start can help, but today’s tiny version counts too.

A note on care: This part is general education. It isn’t therapy, coaching or medical advice, and it can’t promise any result. Goals about your health, money, work or a hard stretch in life may deserve a qualified professional, and there’s no shame in asking for one. Nothing here is required, and nothing you write needs to be shared. If a goal ever starts to feel like a weight, you can shrink it or put it down.

To start, write two plain words for what matters to you, one small goal as something you will do, the tiniest first step and one if-then. Then put a ten-minute look-back on the calendar for a month from now. Your self-discovery path (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) and Ten-minute start are free on the site.

zqprefaceqz

Preface

Preface to Part Two

The work nobody sees: invisible labour at home

Part Two of the book is about the people you share a life, a home or a job with, and it opens here. Running a life takes a lot of work that nobody sees. This preface helps you make that work visible, to yourself and to anyone you share it with, so you can talk about it fairly and kindly.

In this chapter

  1. Unseen work quietly adds up
  2. A lot of it is thinking, not doing
  3. The other person usually just hasn’t seen it
  4. Writing it down isn’t keeping score
  5. Each of you writes only your own side
  6. The borrowed words are there to take the blame away
  7. One small step at a time
  8. It can help in many kinds of shared life
  9. The mental load: what the research says
  10. On your own: your own unseen work
  11. One household, followed for a month
  12. Your situation, chapter by chapter
  13. Common mix-ups
  14. Limits and cautions

In short

  • Running a home takes unseen work, the noticing, remembering and planning that many people call the mental load.
  • The other person usually just hasn’t seen it. This work hides by nature, and missing it says little about how much someone cares.
  • Each of you writes only your own side of one ordinary week, and you read the two lists together.
  • The list is for seeing. Thank each other for the past, and plan next week.

Sunday, 9pm

Someone notices that the laundry is still in the washer, the school forms are due on Tuesday and the birthday card never got posted. They also notice that nobody else has noticed. From the hallway the house looks fine, and that is exactly the trouble.

Across town, a widower is finding out how many jobs his wife quietly carried, from the birthday cards and the boiler service to knowing who to ring when someone was ill. He never saw them until they stopped getting done.

  1. Unseen work quietly adds up.

    Remembering appointments, noticing that the milk is low and calming a tense moment never show up on a calendar, so they rarely get a thank-you, and over months they pile up. This book calls the pile unbilled debt, because nobody ever sends a bill for it. You can thank someone for what they carried before, and you leave the past unbilled. Marcus remembers every school form, dentist visit and bit of lunch money for their two children. His husband, Theo, sees two children who always seem to have what they need, because the work is out of his sight.

    Tonight you could write down three things you did today that nobody saw, and leave the list alone for now. If you show it to someone later, something like “I’m not asking you to pay anything back. I just want you to see them” sets the right tone.

    Dig deeper: the work that goes unseen

    Professor Puddles

    The easiest way to see unseen work is to write it down for one ordinary week. Each of you logs only your own jobs, and the thinking counts too.

    Workpaper WP-01: Who did what spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-01

  2. A lot of it is thinking, not doing.

    Before a job gets done, someone has to notice it, remember it, plan it and check that it happened. That thinking takes real time and energy even though nobody can see it. In a shared flat, Yasmin notices that the internet deal is ending, compares plans, picks one and checks it went through. Paying took two minutes, and the thinking took her most of an evening.

    Pick one job at home and split it into its steps, noticing, planning, doing and checking, and then ask who usually does each step.

    Dig deeper: the kinds of unseen work

  3. The other person usually just hasn’t seen it.

    When this work is done well, nothing seems to happen, so the other person is rarely ignoring it. From where they stand, things appear to take care of themselves. Edna minds her grandchildren three afternoons a week and quietly moves her own doctor’s appointments to fit, while her daughter believes it all fits in easily. A gentle question often opens it up, such as “What’s something you do that you think I don’t see?”, followed by listening without explaining.

    Dig deeper: why it stays hidden

  4. Writing it down isn’t keeping score.

    The point is for both of you to see the same picture, in the same words, at the same time, so that the talk starts from facts you share. This book calls that shared record a ledger, a plain list of who did what, kept for seeing. Two coworkers who share one job each list a week of tasks and find that every client call has landed on one of them. They leave last year alone and agree to swap the Friday calls.

    Before you show anyone a list, ask yourself whether it is to plan next week or to prove a point, and share it only if the answer is planning.

    Dig deeper: why a ledger isn’t a grudge

  5. Each of you writes only your own side.

    Nobody fills in anything for the other person. You each note what you did and then read the two lists together, which keeps it fair and keeps it kind. Each of you also adds the context only you have, such as a long week at work or children off school with colds, so that you both understand what you read. Arran, Dani and Sol are three partners sharing a home, and each writes only their own list. Reading them together, Sol learns for the first time that Arran has been ringing the landlord every month.

    Dig deeper: your side, their side

  6. The borrowed words are there to take the blame away.

    The book uses a few terms from accounting and science because they describe what is happening without saying whose fault it is. Each one is explained in plain words, and you never need them to use anything here. Two brothers share their mum’s care, and one of them swaps “You never help” for “There’s some unseen work here we haven’t looked at,” which his brother finds much easier to hear. If words like “ledger” or “debt” feel heavy, use your own, since “our list” and “the stuff nobody sees” do the same job.

    Dig deeper: why the book borrows these words

  7. One small step at a time.

    Each chapter adds one idea and one tool, and one week of notes is enough to start. Later come a 90-second daily check-in about how much you were carrying that day, a weekly catch-up and a monthly look-back, which needs only a few lines a week. A nurse on nights and a partner on days hardly see each other awake, so they start with one week of notes on the fridge and change nothing yet. Your first step can be as small as picking a start day this week and setting one reminder on your phone.

    Dig deeper: how the book fits together

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: counting jobs isn’t keeping score. It’s more like a treasure hunt for the work nobody noticed! The quick split check is a good first sniff.

    Tool: Who does what? Quick look spreadloveandacceptance.com/lemonade-stand

  8. It can help in many kinds of shared life.

    Partners, families, housemates, co-parents and coworkers all share unseen work. The examples often use a couple at home, and the ideas fit anyone who shares a load. In a foster home, the carer tracks family visits, social worker calls and school meetings, while a teenager in the home quietly cooks for the younger ones twice a week, and both kinds of work deserve to be counted.

    Dig deeper: who this book is for

Your part, and only your part. You can’t make anyone see the unseen work, and you can’t write their side of the ledger. You can write your own side honestly, say it once, kindly, and then match what you take on to what comes back. If you keep carrying more than your share with nothing in return, stepping back towards your share isn’t a punishment. It protects the energy you need to stay kind. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Friday, after work

“You didn’t have to do all that,” they say, and they mean it kindly. You think that someone did have to. The list only ever lived in your head, so to them it looked as if it took care of itself.

zqaxprefacexxmentalxloadqzThe mental load: what the research says

Many people call the thinking side of home life the mental load, meaning the noticing and planning that come before a job gets done and the checking after. It includes knowing the baby needs the next size of clothes, and remembering the form, the jab and the party present. It is real work, even when it doesn’t look like any.

Studies of couples find some patterns, on average. In couples of a man and a woman, women tend to do more of the noticing and checking (Allison Daminger, 2019). After a first baby a gap often opens, and in one study of working couples, mothers took on most of the new childcare while keeping their paid hours (Jill Yavorsky and colleagues, 2015). Arlie Hochschild called the home work that starts after paid work ends “the second shift.”

There is a fair point on the other side too. Sometimes the parent who knows how things are done holds on to that, without meaning to, which researchers call gatekeeping. When a parent openly invites the other in and lets them do it their own way, the other parent tends to do more of the care (Sarah Allen and Alan Hawkins, 1999; Sarah Schoppe-Sullivan and colleagues, 2008).

These are averages across many homes, and they say nothing certain about yours. In your home it may be the other way round, or already even, or shared between two men or two women, which is why the book asks you to look at your own week on paper instead of guessing.

Hollie and Gareth have a toddler and a baby, and Gareth works shifts. Their week’s minutes come out nearly even, yet Hollie did almost three-quarters of the jobs nobody asked anyone to do. Their week is in Chapter II (page 102).

You could say “You do lots of the doing. It’s the remembering I’d love you to take some of, whole jobs, start to finish.” Or the other way round, “Show me once how you like it done, then let me do it my way.”

Dig deeper: the mental load, fairly

On your own: your own unseen work

You don’t need anyone else to start seeing the unseen. For one week, notice the jobs only you remember, such as the appointments, the restocking and the smoothing-over, and write them down for yourself. Count it without charging for it, since the point is to see your real load so that you can plan your energy. Notice which jobs are yours by choice and which simply landed on you, and pick one you could hand back, drop or do less often. Nicola, divorced, has the children every other week, and on paper she sees that she still buys the presents for both sides of the family. She hands his side back in one friendly message. More for people living alone or after a breakup is on On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

One household, followed for a month

Three adult siblings share the care of their father, who lives alone in the house they grew up in. On paper the visits are split evenly, two days each. When each of them writes a week of their own side, the picture changes. The eldest, Ffion, also holds the prescriptions, the hospital letters and the calls to the GP, none of which counts as a visit. Their brother is surprised and a little defensive, and the first conversation ends early. A month later they try again, and he takes over the prescriptions completely, with the reminders on his own phone. Their sister still finds the hospital letters too much to face, so Ffion keeps them for now, and they agree to look again in the spring. The ideas in this chapter fit friendships, teams and shared houses in the same way, and Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) has a page for many kinds of shared life.

Your situation, chapter by chapter

Some situations get their own section:

  • Faith, culture, elders and in-laws. Chapter I (page 88)
  • Small children or a new baby. Chapter II (page 102)
  • Two homes after a split, and step-parents. Chapter III (page 119)
  • Money between you, and a couple with a housemate. Chapter IV (page 134)
  • New together, or grandparents raising a grandchild. Chapter V (page 148)

Common mix-ups

  • “If it mattered, they would have asked for help.” Unseen work is often hidden from the person doing it too, until it is written down.
  • “It has to be exactly 50/50.” The goal is a split you can both see and both agree to.
  • “We should start by going over the last ten years.” Start with one ordinary week. You can thank someone for the past without trying to settle it.
  • “The one doing less doesn’t care.” Usually they just can’t see it yet. Once you have both seen it, what you do next is a choice you make together.

To start, each of you can list the things you did this week that nobody saw, then swap lists, read the other one slowly and say one thing on it you hadn’t noticed before. Pick one item from their list and say thank you for it in a specific way. If writing things down isn’t your style, a ten-minute talk over a cup of coffee with the same questions works too. Fixing comes later, once you have both seen the same picture. Who did what (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-01) turns this into a gentle week-long log, and How to say a specific thank-you (spreadloveandacceptance.com/turning-toward) has more ideas.

Limits and cautions

These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If talking about the split ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

A list should never be demanded, checked over your shoulder, or used to keep track of where you go or what you spend. If that is happening, it isn’t a ledger. It’s control, and it’s not your fault. Signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#signs). If you are a counsellor or group leader using this book with others, see For counsellors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors).

I

Part Two · Chapter I

Why we get out of tune: communication at home

Why two kind, reasonable people can end up in a tangle neither of them started, and how to get back in step.

In this chapter

  1. The tangle often isn’t about the words
  2. Nearly in step is the noisy part
  3. Three things knock you out of tune
  4. Stress changes your station
  5. Nobody has to be wrong
  6. Get back in tune before you carry on
  7. Go back in with a clear sentence
  8. Small daily check-ins keep you in tune
  9. Faith, culture and family voices
  10. On your own: your side of the tuning
  11. One example, followed through
  12. Common mix-ups

In short

  • A clash is often about how things were said. Pace, tone and urgency can be out of step even when both of you mean well.
  • Nobody has to be wrong. Say that you are out of tune, pause with a time to come back, and slow down.
  • Go back in with one clear sentence that says what happened, how you feel and what you would like.
  • A 90-second daily check-in keeps small drifts small.

Tuesday, 6:40pm

“I said I’d do it.” “I know, I’m just asking when.” Four sentences later nobody is talking about the bins any more, and neither of you could point to the moment it turned.

  1. The tangle often isn’t about the words.

    Two people can each say something reasonable and still clash, because the tone underneath doesn’t match. It is like two radios slightly out of tune, which together make a crackle that neither was making alone.

    For example, one housemate asks whether anyone is using the oven tonight, and the other asks back whether she left a mess. A plain question has been heard as a complaint.

    You could say “I think the words were fine. Something in how we said them got crossed.”

    Try this. After your next small clash, ask yourself whether it was the words or the way they came out.

    Dig deeper: the radio static

  2. Nearly in step is the noisy part.

    Radios on very different stations don’t whistle at each other. The whistle comes when they are close but not quite matched, which is why people who know each other well can still clash. Research suggests we check our meaning less with people we are close to, because we assume they already understand us.

    Two sisters who talk every day argue about holiday plans far more often than either does with the cousins they see once a year.

    Words you could use “I think I assumed you knew what I meant. Let me say it more clearly.”

    This week. With someone close to you, check one meaning today, with “Just so I’ve got it right, you mean…?”

    Dig deeper: why close can be noisy

    Tidbit

    Ooh, Tidbit loves this one: compare your daily rhythms and see whose engine runs fast in the morning and whose at night. Different speeds aren’t wrong, just different!

    Tool: Rhythms side by side spreadloveandacceptance.com/tools/frequency-calibration

  3. Three things knock you out of tune.

    The first is how fast you are talking. The second is tone, as when a simple update is heard as a complaint. The third is how urgent something feels, since “when you get a chance” can mean tonight to one person and next week to another. Texts lose most of their tone, which makes urgency especially easy to misread.

    For example, a business partner texts “Need to talk” between two meetings. The other partner reads it as a crisis and lies awake until two in the morning, and in the end it turns out to be about the printer.

    Ways to say it “By when would be good?” “Is this an update, or a worry?”

    One small step. Add a time to your next request, so that “at some point” becomes “by Friday”.

    Dig deeper: pace, tone and urgency

  4. Stress changes your station.

    When you are tense, you may talk faster and be more likely to hear a pause as a snub. When you are tired and flat, your replies get slower and shorter. The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks), a thirty-second self-check, gives you a best guess at which state you are in.

    A dad gets home from a night shift and answers his teenage son in single words. His son decides that he doesn’t care, when he is simply running on empty.

    Words to try “I’m running low right now, and it isn’t about you. Can we talk after I’ve slept?”

    Something to try. Before a tricky talk, name your state to yourself as calm, revved up or running on empty.

    Dig deeper: how stress shifts your tune

  5. Nobody has to be wrong.

    Two radios that both work perfectly will still crackle if they are slightly off, and arguing about whose fault the static is won’t clear it. Retuning, which means getting back in step, will.

    For example, a grandmother tells her grown-up son that he looks tired. She means it as care, and he hears that he isn’t coping, so both of them are right about what they meant and what they heard.

    You could say “I don’t think either of us meant it that way. Can we try that again?”

    Try this. In your next clash, try “we” in place of “you”, as in “We got crossed there.”

    Dig deeper: taking the blame out

  6. Get back in tune before you carry on.

    Say out loud that you think you are out of sync, and check how tense you feel. Either of you can call a pause, and whoever pauses names a time to come back. Slow down gently, with shorter turns and more pauses, and only then go back to the actual topic.

    Two roommates in halls agree on a pause word, “static”, on a calm day. In the middle of an argument about noise one of them says it, and they stop and come back at nine as agreed.

    Words you could use “I need ten minutes. I’ll come back at half past.”

    This week. Agree a pause word with someone today, while you are both calm.

    Dig deeper: the four steps to retune

  7. Go back in with a clear sentence.

    When you return to the topic, say what happened, how you feel and what you would like. “The bins go out early on Wednesday morning. I get anxious when they’re late. Could you put them out tonight?”

    For example, a co-parent texts, “The swim kit wasn’t in the bag and I felt stressed at drop-off. Could you pack it on Sunday nights?”

    One small step. Write one sentence like that about something small, before you need it.

    Dig deeper: going back in

    Professor Puddles

    When you go back in, one clear sentence beats a speech. This workpaper helps you shape it before you say it.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

  8. Small daily check-ins keep you in tune.

    A short chat each day, like the 90-second daily check-in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-13-daily-check-in), makes tiny corrections before small things drift into a big argument. Habit research suggests small routines at a regular time are easier to keep than big ones done rarely. The quiet, easy stretches are the ones that drift most, so keep it going even when nothing seems wrong (see Complacency, spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency).

    A long-distance couple in two time zones send each other one 90-second voice note every morning, and on the weeks they forget, they notice the difference by Thursday.

    Ways to say it “Today I was carrying quite a lot. One thing I liked today was…”

    Something to try. Pick a time and a cue, such as straight after dinner, and try the check-in for three days.

    Dig deeper: staying in tune

Your part, and only your part. You control what you send, whether you check how it landed, and whether you step out to retune. You don’t control how it’s heard or how fast the other person settles. Matching energy here means matching care and effort, never volume: if someone gets louder, you don’t have to follow. Stay at your level, and give the conversation the energy it gives back. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Saturday, 10am

One of you says the spare room needs clearing out at some point. She meant this month, and he heard today and has already cancelled his plans in his head. By lunchtime you are both upset about a room nobody has touched, and when you stop to ask what “at some point” meant, you find you are still not sure you agree.

zqaxchapterx1xxfaithxcultureqzFaith, culture and family voices

For many couples, faith is where they turn first, and a shared faith can be one of the strongest tools for staying in tune. Praying together, or a quiet moment after worship, can serve as a daily check-in. Some couples each pray on their own before they come back to a hard talk, with the pause still ending at a named time. A pastor, imam, rabbi, priest or trusted elder can be a good first person to talk to, and many can suggest a trained counsellor who shares your faith.

Emeka and Ngozi, married for twenty-six years, do their monthly look-back on a Sunday after church, over lunch. When a talk gets heated, either of them can say, “Let’s pray on it and come back at eight,” and they do.

Culture shapes how you talk too. In many families, respect for elders decides who can speak plainly to whom, and one habit helps a great deal, which is that each of you speaks to your own parents and relatives once you have agreed the message together.

Words to try “Can we pray about this and talk again tonight?” “Mum, we love you, and we’ve thought about it carefully. This year we’ll visit in August instead of at Easter.”

From two faiths or cultures? See Two faiths or cultures, one family (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths). Dig deeper: faith, elders and family far away

On your own: your side of the tuning

Getting out of tune takes two, but retuning can start with one. You can learn your own pace, tone and sense of urgency, so you notice when you are the one running fast or slow. Learn your early signs of drifting, such as a tight chest, a clipped reply or the wish to win. Learn how you take words in best and say it once, as in “I hear things better in writing.” When you drift, step out, settle and come back, which you can do without anyone’s permission. Hamid lives alone and has noticed that his texts to friends come out short when he is tired, so now he waits until morning to answer anything that matters (more in On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

One example, followed through

Cerys, Marisol and Dougie share a house and a car, and two of them talk fast while the third, Dougie, talks slowly. At house meetings Dougie kept getting talked over, and for a while the other two read his silence as agreement. It came out in March, when he said he had never actually agreed to the new car rota. They tried a simple change, a round in which each person speaks once before anyone answers. It felt stilted at first, and Cerys kept wanting to jump in. By the third meeting Dougie was saying more, and the rota he suggested is the one they now use. They still have the occasional evening when the meeting turns into two fast talkers and one quiet one, and someone usually says “round” to reset it. Help by relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) has pages for many other kinds of shared life.

Common mix-ups

  • “Retuning means giving in.” You still come back to the topic, at a time when you can hear each other.
  • “If we’re out of sync, one of us must be wrong.” Two fair points in two different tones can still clash.
  • “A pause means the topic is dropped.” A pause always comes with a time to come back.

To try it, agree on a shared phrase while things are calm, such as “I think we’re out of tune”, so that it works as a signal when you need it. For one week, each of you can note one moment you felt out of step, and at the end you can compare whether it was mostly pace, tone or urgency. Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder), Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) and the 90-second daily check-in are free on the site.

A limit to keep in mind: These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If talking things through ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

A pause is for both of you. If one person is never allowed to pause, or a “pause” is used to punish with days of silence, that isn’t retuning. Signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#signs).
