II

Part Two · Chapter II

Is the split working? A fair look at chores at home

One gentle question: can the way you share the work keep going, or is one of you quietly running on empty?

In this chapter

  1. Look at the month, not last night
  2. Three things go in
  3. Balance: how the hours split
  4. Ownership: does each job have a name?
  5. Stress: how full each stress tank is
  6. One number comes out, from 0 to 1
  7. Start with the biggest shortfall
  8. It judges the setup, never a person
  9. Words this chapter uses
  10. On your own: is your own load working?
  11. One setup, looked at twice
  12. Common mix-ups
  13. Small children and a new baby
  14. If only one of you wants to try this
  15. More for your situation

In short

  • Look at the month, not last night, using what you both wrote down.
  • Three things go in, which are how the hours split, whether each job has a name, and how full each person’s stress tank is.
  • One number comes out, from 0 to 1. Start with whichever part pulled it down most.
  • It judges the setup, never a person, and it is where a talk starts.

Any given week

One of you is quietly doing eleven small things a day that the other has never had to think about. When the other says it feels even, they mean it, because from inside their own week it does.

  1. Look at the month, not last night.

    When people ask whether the split is working, the answer usually comes from whatever happened most recently. This chapter asks a calmer question, using what you both wrote down. Ask it again every few months, even when things seem fine, because a split that worked once can quietly go stale.

    For example, two housemates had one awful week of dishes in May. The whole month, written down, showed three ordinary weeks and one exam week.

    Try this. Put a short check in your calendar for about a month from now.

    Dig deeper: what the check is for

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: one bad evening isn’t the whole story. Give it a month, then run the check together, slowly, with a snack.

    Tool: Fair split check: this week spreadloveandacceptance.com/is-the-setup-working

  2. Three things go in.

    The first is how evenly the hours are shared. The second is whether every regular job has a clear owner, from the job list in One owner per job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job). The third is how stressed each of you already is from everything else going on. A workpaper is one of the site’s free fill-in worksheets, and you don’t need any of them to start, since rough notes on paper work too.

    You could say “Let’s each bring our own numbers, so neither of us has to guess.”

    Dig deeper: where each number comes from

  3. Balance: how the hours split.

    From your week-long logs, work out each person’s share of the hours. An even split scores 1 and one person doing everything scores 0, whichever person it is. If you have agreed an uneven split that suits you, perhaps because one of you works longer hours outside the home, compare against that split instead. With three or more of you, compare each person’s share with an even share (100 divided by the number of people) or with the split you agreed. Three partners who log 30 hours of home jobs between them, at 15, 9 and 6, would each have 10 as an even share. The “Who does what?” page (spreadloveandacceptance.com/lemonade-stand), where each person lists their hours, does the arithmetic.

    This week. Log one week each, and include the small jobs that take under ten minutes.

    Dig deeper: the balance score

  4. Ownership: does each job have a name?

    Each job gets two names. The owner does the job from start to finish, and the backstop notices if it slipped and checks in gently, which is very different from supervising. It can be the same person, though a second name gives the job a gentle check. Count the jobs that have an owner and divide by all the jobs on the list, and leave the jobs nobody owns on the list, because they matter most. A decision you make together, such as which school, can be marked “Both (decide together)” and counts as owned, while a job that needs doing gets one name.

    Two sisters care for their dad, and nobody owned his prescription, so for a fortnight each thought the other had ordered it.

    Words you could use “Can we put a name next to this one, so it doesn’t fall between us?”

    Dig deeper: the ownership score

    Professor Puddles

    A job without a name tends to land on whoever notices first. Write one owner next to each job, and the guessing stops.

    Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-03

  5. Stress: how full each stress tank is.

    Each of you rates how full your own stress tank is with How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying), where a higher score means more stress. Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 up to 0.60 is medium, and 0.60 or more is high. The score uses the average of your two scores, but if either of you is at 0.60 or more, talk about that first, even when the overall result looks fine. A setup that only works when you are both well rested can’t last, so more stress lowers the result. A grandmother raising two grandchildren scores 0.70 while her son, who helps at weekends, scores 0.35, and her 0.70 is the headline.

    One small step. Each of you scores your own tank on the same day, before looking at the other’s.

    Dig deeper: the stress score

  6. One number comes out, from 0 to 1.

    A result of 0.70 or above reads as working well, meaning the setup is holding. From 0.40 up to 0.70 it reads as needs a look, because something is drifting, often who owns what, and below 0.40 it reads as needs a rethink, together. The result is called the setup score. It is a simple weighted sum, in which the hours count most, then the owners, then stress, and although it looks like a probability it isn’t one. Two friends who run a café together score 0.55, which tells them nothing is broken and something is drifting.

    Something to try. Write the date next to your number, so you can compare next month.

    Dig deeper: the formula and what each range means

  7. Start with the biggest shortfall.

    The single number matters less than which of the three parts pulled it down most. The shortfall is how far one part fell below the most it could add, and in the middle band it is often ownership, which is why the calculator suggests One owner per job first. Separated parents score 0.62 and find that their biggest gap is that nobody owns the school forms, so that is the only thing they change this month.

    Ways to say it “Which part pulled the number down most? Let’s start there.”

    Dig deeper: reading your result

  8. It judges the setup, never a person.

    The number isn’t a verdict on who’s better or whether the relationship works. It’s where a conversation starts, never how one ends. These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If talking about the split ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

    For example, one partner sees 0.35 and says, “So I’m the problem.” The other says that the bathroom has no owner and that he works nights, and they start there.

    Try this. Before you start, agree that either of you can say “pause” and come back later.

    Dig deeper: what the number is not

Your part, and only your part. The score describes the setup you share, but your levers are your own: your jobs, your hours and what you agree to take on. You can propose a fix; you can’t make the other person accept it. If the balance stays one-sided, step your load back towards your share on purpose, and say so kindly. Matching effort with effort protects your stress tank, and your tank is part of the score too. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Sunday evening

Two week-long logs and two cups of tea sit on the table. One list has 31 rows and the other has 18, and for a moment nobody says anything. Then one of you says, “I honestly didn’t know about half of these.”

Words this chapter uses

A log is a simple list of the jobs you did this week and roughly how long each took. The owner does a job from start to finish, including remembering it, and the backstop notices if a job slipped and checks in gently. Your stress tank is how much stress you are already carrying from the rest of life. The setup is the way you share the work right now, which can always be changed, and the setup score is the one number from 0 to 1 that sums up the three readings. Invisible jobs count too. Planning meals, remembering birthdays, booking the vet and noticing that the soap is running low all belong in your log.

On your own: is your own load working?

You can ask the same question about your own week, which is whether you are spending more energy than comes back. Add up what you carry, the jobs, the people and the worries, and set it beside what refills you, such as rest, help and people who give back. If it runs in the red, change your side by dropping, delaying, asking or saying no kindly. A limit describes your supply, and it says nothing about your worth. After a breakup, Leanne has her children every other week and fills the quiet weeks with favours for friends, and writing it down shows her that she never rests (more in On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Words to try “I’d love to help, and I can’t this week. Can I let you know next week?”

One setup, looked at twice

Three people share a flat above a bakery, and everyone agrees that cleaning matters while nobody owns the bathroom. Their first check scores 0.67, and the biggest shortfall is ownership: eight of the twelve jobs have a name, and the bathroom, the bins, the recycling and the hallway don’t. They give each of those four jobs an owner and a backstop. A month later, with the hours and their stress tanks about the same as before, the score is 0.79. Ownership went from 0.67 to 1.00, and that part counts for 0.35 of the score, so it adds 0.12. The bathroom is better and the recycling is still a sore point, because the one who owns it works late on collection night, and that is the job they talk about next. Shift work, illness and caring can all make hours look even while sleep or energy is not, and an uneven split agreed on purpose can be the fair one (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours, and When one of you is ill, spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill).

Common mix-ups

  • “A low number means the relationship is failing.” It means the current setup needs changing, and setups change all the time.
  • “We can just guess the numbers.” A guessed number is a feeling with a decimal point, so use your written logs.
  • “One of us can fill it in for both.” Each person writes their own log and scores their own stress tank.
  • “Fair means exactly 50/50.” Fair is what you both agree to, with your eyes open, and an uneven split you chose together can be fair. Two kinds of fair (page 122) looks at this.

zqaxchapterx2xxsmallxchildrenqzSmall children and a new baby

Small children bring a flood of new jobs, and most of them are thinking jobs, such as the nursery bag, the jabs, the party invitations, the next size of clothes and the night wakings. That is why the mental load (see the work nobody sees, page 73) often grows after a baby arrives, usually without anyone deciding it. Log the children’s jobs too, with the thinking time, and count the nights. Hand over whole jobs, such as the clothes and sizes or the GP and the jabs, so that the new owner does the noticing too, in their own way. If a baby is on the way, write your first job list together before the birth, plan the nights and agree to look again at six weeks, at three months and before either of you goes back to work. In the first weeks, share by energy more than by hours, so that whoever was up in the night gets the rest.

Hollie and Gareth have Alfie, who is three, and Poppy, who is eight months old, and Gareth is a paramedic on shifts. Their logged minutes come out nearly even, yet Hollie did almost three-quarters of the jobs nobody asked for. They leave the minutes alone and move one whole job, the children’s clothes, to Gareth.

You could say “Could you own the nursery bag from now on, including noticing when we’re low on nappies? I won’t check it.”

Dig deeper: small children, new babies and shift work

zqaxchapterx2xxonexpersonqzIf only one of you wants to try this

That is common, and you can still start. Log your own week, score your own tank and then share one small thing you noticed, without asking the other person to agree with your numbers. A dad noticed he spent five hours a week driving his teenage son around, said so without any accusation, and they agreed on a bus pass for two days a week. Share one finding at a time and then let it rest for a few days.

If the other person refuses to talk about the split at all, ever, or makes you feel afraid for raising it, that isn’t a setup problem. Please read Not safe at home?

More for your situation

Money together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together) · Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together) · Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Grandparents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grandparents) · Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting) · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · Empty nest (spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest) · At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work) · For counsellors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors)

To run the check, each of you first logs one week in Who did what (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-01), because the number only means something if you each wrote your own. Next, fill in the job list in One owner per job together, including any jobs nobody owns yet, and each score your own stress tank on the same day. Put the three numbers into the calculator (spreadloveandacceptance.com/is-the-setup-working), look first at the biggest shortfall, pick one small change together and check again in a month.

III

Part Two · Chapter III

Full tanks and different angles: stress and perspective

Why some reactions are bigger than what caused them, and why two people can see the same moment so differently.

In this chapter

  1. A full tank overflows
  2. Some stress is left over from earlier
  3. Check your stress tank in a minute
  4. Three everyday states
  5. There are seven angles on the same moment
  6. Both views can be true
  7. Say it instead of making each other guess
  8. A full tank means “later,” not “never.”
  9. Words this chapter uses
  10. On your own: reading your own tank
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. Two homes: co-parenting after a split
  13. If only one of you wants to try this
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • A full tank overflows, so stress left over from earlier makes small things feel big.
  • Check your tank in a minute, and say the band out loud so nobody has to guess.
  • Two people can see one moment from different angles, and both views can be true.
  • A full tank means later, so pause, name a time and come back.

Thursday, 5:15pm

They ask, perfectly pleasantly, whether you remembered to call the dentist. Your answer comes out much bigger than the question deserved, and you can hear it happening while it happens.

  1. A full tank overflows.

    If you are already tired, stretched or stressed from somewhere else, a small question can get a big reaction, which is simply human. Anything decided in that moment is worth coming back to once you have both calmed down. A nurse gets home after a night shift and her housemate asks whether she saw his message, and she snaps at him. Twelve hours on her feet did the snapping, and the message just happened to come at the end of them.

    You could say “Sorry. That was bigger than the question. I’m running on empty.”

    Dig deeper: how full your tank is

  2. Some stress is left over from earlier.

    Ask yourself how much of this feeling is about the thing in front of you and how much you brought in with you. Being upset about the dishes and being exhausted, with the dishes as the thing you noticed, are different problems. Some of what we bring in is much older, such as an understanding from growing up that whoever notices the mess has to clean it, and if a feeling seems a lot older than the moment, Where your lens came from (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up) helps you find where it started.

    For example, a teenager has a hard day at school, comes home and explodes because his brother took the phone charger, which was the last drop in a tank that was already full.

    Words you could use “I think I brought this in with me. Give me ten minutes.”

    Dig deeper: leftover stress

    Professor Puddles

    Before a hard talk, check how full your own tank is. Five quick questions, about two minutes, and you’ll know whether now is the time.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  3. Check your stress tank in a minute.

    How much are you carrying? measures how full your stress tank is, and a higher score means more stress in the tank. Score five things from 0 to 4, which are sleep, work elsewhere, any unsettled argument, how your body feels and time pressure today, then add them up and divide by 20. Under 0.30 is light, 0.30 up to 0.60 is medium and 0.60 or more is high. If it has been high for a long time it can start to feel normal, so a quick reading each week is worth it. A man caring for his wife after surgery scores 0.65 three days in a row, which tells him he needs help more than he needs to try harder.

    Try this. Score yourself tomorrow morning, before you look at your phone.

    Dig deeper: the stress-tank score

  4. Three everyday states.

    Knowing whether you are calm and connected, revved up or running on empty tells you whether now is a good time to talk. The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks), a thirty-second self-check, helps you make a best guess. The labels come from polyvagal theory, whose main claims are still debated by scientists, and here they are used only as everyday words. In one long-distance couple, he takes the video call at midnight his time and is often running on empty, so they move the hard talks to weekend mornings.

    This week. Find one body clue for each state, such as a tight jaw for revved up.

    Dig deeper: the three states

  5. There are seven angles on the same moment.

    The seven angles are tiredness, time pressure, history, what home was like growing up, your sense of fairness, how you communicate and stress from outside. Many arguments are two people looking from different angles, each sure that the other sees what they see. The “See their side” step of Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder) is built on these seven angles and helps you picture how the same moment might look from the other side, with questions to ask in place of guesses. Planning the holidays, one parent sees it from family habit, since they always go to her mum’s, and the other sees it from fairness, since they went there last year too.

    Ways to say it “Which angle are you seeing this from?”

    Dig deeper: the seven angles

  6. Both views can be true.

    You can each be right about what you see and still be looking at different parts of the same thing, so the useful question is which angle each of you is seeing it from. Two adult brothers argue about their late mother’s house, because one sees thirty years of memories and the other sees a roof that needs £9,000 of work, and both are looking at the real house.

    Words to try “You’re right about what you see. Can I tell you what I see?”

    Dig deeper: two true views

  7. Say it instead of making each other guess.

    Before a hard conversation, each of you says how full your stress tank is and which angle you are seeing things from. It works best at the start. Two coworkers begin a tense meeting with one sentence each about their tank and their angle, and the meeting is shorter and calmer than the last one.

    You could say “Before we start, I’m about half full today, and I’m seeing this from the time angle.”

    Dig deeper: using both together

    Tidbit

    Tidbit’s tip: say your number out loud, like “I’m a seven today.” It’s quick, and nobody has to guess!

    Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  8. A full tank means “later,” not “never.”

    A high score is a reason to pause and never a way out of the talk. Say when you will come back, and let the Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) help in the meantime. After your calming steps, check your tank again. Under 0.50, go back at the time you said. From 0.50 to 0.59, take another round if you still feel hot, and if you are still at 0.60 or more after two rounds, pick a new time and say when. A dad and his fourteen-year-old get heated about phone time. He tells her he is too wound up and will talk at seven, and at seven he knocks on her door.

    Words you could use “I need a break. I’ll come back at seven. I promise.”

    Dig deeper: pausing without avoiding

Your part, and only your part. Your stress tank is the only one you can empty. You can’t calm someone else’s tank for them, and pouring yours into theirs leaves two empty tanks. Protect yours: rest, say “later,” and give energy where it’s met. When both tanks are full, the kindest thing you control is the timing. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Monday morning

You both look at the same pile of post on the kitchen table. One of you sees a to-do list, and the other sees proof that nobody else ever opens the post. You try saying your angles out loud, and it helps for about a minute before the old argument about the gas bill comes back. The pile is still there at lunchtime, and neither of you has decided whose it is.

Words this chapter uses

Your stress tank is how much stress you are already carrying before this moment even starts. Leftover stress is the part of a feeling you brought in from somewhere else, like poor sleep or a hard day, while this-moment stress is caused by what is in front of you right now. An angle is the point of view you are seeing a moment from, such as tiredness or fairness.

On your own: reading your own tank

On your own, the most useful habit is a one-minute reading of your tank before you react. Check it for a few mornings in a row and look for a pattern, ask yourself before a hard moment how much of it is left over from earlier, and decide on a calm day what settles you so that it is ready when you need it. Living alone after a breakup, Bryony noticed that she snapped at her sister every Monday, and her morning readings showed why, since Sunday nights were her worst sleep of the week. Now she asks for Tuesday instead (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own).

Common mix-ups

  • “A big reaction means it was a big deal.” Sometimes it does, and often it means the tank was already full.
  • “A high score is an excuse.” It is a note to come back later and never a pass to skip the talk.
  • “I can tell how full their tank is.” Only they can say, since each person scores only themselves.
  • “Pausing is the same as the silent treatment.” A pause has a time to come back, which is why you always say when.

zqaxchapterx3xxtwoxhomesqzTwo homes: co-parenting after a split

Children carry two homes, and changeover day fills their tank, so being quiet, clingy or cross for a few hours after a handover is common and usually says nothing bad about the other home. It helps to give them landing time, with a snack, something familiar and no questions about the other home for the first hour. The child is never the messenger, because adult news goes adult to adult. For money, follow any formal arrangement, split the extras by a ratio you agree, keep one list and settle up once a month. With an ex, share the band and keep the story, as in “I’m in a heavy week. Could we swap Wednesday?”, and your private life stays yours. If an ex won’t cooperate but isn’t dangerous, parallel parenting can work, with written messages only, short and business-like, handovers at school and your own list for your own home. When there are new partners, the parent stays the owner of anything involving the other home, and a step-parent starts as a friendly adult rather than the one who tells the children off.

Harriet gives Freya, who is eight, and Arlo, who is five, an hour of toast and blankets when they come back from their dad’s, and she has stopped asking what happened at Dad’s at the front door. Sunday evenings are calmer, though Arlo still cries at bedtime on changeover days, and she is waiting to see whether that eases.

Words you could use (a business-like message) “Hi Dylan. Freya’s school trip is on 6 November and costs £24. I’ve paid it and put it on the extras list. Thanks, Harriet.”

If you are afraid of your ex, a shared plan isn’t the right tool: see Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) Dig deeper: two homes, money and step-parents

If only one of you wants to try this

You can do all of this on your own side, by checking your own tank, naming your own angle and pausing and coming back on time. The other person doesn’t have to use the words for it to help, and when one person starts saying it out loud, the other often starts to as well. A daughter visits her dad every Sunday, and every week they clash over his health. She starts each visit by saying she is a bit tired today, so if she goes quiet it isn’t about him. He never scores anything himself, and the visits still get calmer.

A note on safety: A full tank explains a reaction. It never excuses shouting, threats or hurting anyone. If someone’s “stress” often turns into fear for you, that isn’t a tank problem. These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If sharing how you feel ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? lists free, private hotlines.

More for your situation

Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) · Co-parenting (spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting) · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · When one of you is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) · Long distance (spreadloveandacceptance.com/long-distance) · Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room) · Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together) · For counsellors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors)

Before your next hard conversation, score the five things in How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying), add them up and divide by 20, then say one sentence out loud about your tank and your angle. If either of you scores 0.60 or more, put off anything that doesn’t need deciding in the next hour, and agree on a time to come back.

IV

Part Two · Chapter IV

Two kinds of fair: equal vs fair at home

Agree on what “fair” means before you argue about it, and give a comment a moment to land before you answer it.

In this chapter

  1. There are two kinds of fair
  2. Fair by results
  3. Fair by promises
  4. Once a job has an owner, look to the owner
  5. Covering is kind. Say it out loud
  6. Let a comment land before you react
  7. Notice, name, decide
  8. Keep the two questions apart
  9. On your own: your own kind of fair
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. Money between you
  12. A couple and a housemate
  13. More for your situation
  14. A note on safety

In short

  • There are two kinds of fair, by results (did it all get done?) and by promises (did each of us do what we agreed?), so agree which one you are using.
  • Once a job has an owner, look to the owner, and when you cover for someone, say so out loud.
  • Let a comment land before you react by noticing it, naming it and then deciding what to say.
  • Keep the two questions apart, because whether the job was done is a fact and whether the comment hurt is a feeling.

The same argument, twice a month

One of you counts hours, and the other counts who noticed that the job needed doing. You are both counting honestly, in two different currencies, and then arguing about the exchange rate.

  1. zqaxchapterx4xxextwoxkindsqz

    There are two kinds of fair.

    One kind asks whether everything got done, and the other asks whether each person did what they said they would. Both are reasonable, and friction starts when each of you is using a different one without realising. Nisha and Kezia share a room in halls. Nisha thinks a week is fair if the room is tidy by Friday, whoever tidies it, while Kezia thinks it is fair if each of them keeps their own half clean.

    You could say “When you say fair, do you mean it all gets done, or that we each do our bit?”

    Dig deeper: the two kinds of fair

  2. Fair by results.

    This kind of fair judges by outcomes, by whether the right things got done by whoever had the time or energy. It is flexible and easy-going. Done carefully it counts the cost to whoever covered, and done carelessly it can hide who is always stepping in. A grandmother raising her grandchildren has a grown-up son who helps wherever it is needed when he is home. The house runs, and she is always the one who notices what is needed.

    Try this. For one week, mark every job you picked up that wasn’t planned.

    Dig deeper: judging by results

  3. Fair by promises.

    This kind asks whether each person did the jobs they agreed to own. It is clear and steady, and it can feel rigid in a week when life gets in the way. Two business partners run a café, and one owns the ordering while the other owns the staff rota. When the rota is late, they ask the rota owner about it, rather than “the team”.

    Words you could use “It’s my job, and I can’t do it this week. Could you take it, and I’ll take the bins?”

    Dig deeper: judging by promises

  4. Once a job has an owner, look to the owner.

    The owner is the person who does the job from start to finish. A second name on the list is a backstop, who notices if it slipped and checks in gently without supervising, and it can be the same person. If the job is yours, the question is whether you did it, and somebody quietly covering for you doesn’t answer it. That protects the person who keeps filling the gaps. In one stepfamily the thirteen-year-old owns feeding the dog and his stepmum is the second name. When the bowl is empty at seven, she says “Dog’s dinner?” once, without doing it for him and without a lecture.

    Dig deeper: agreeing which kind you’ll use

  5. Covering is kind. Say it out loud.

    Helping out when the owner can’t is lovely, and it helps to mention it, so that the help is seen, as in “I put the bins out this week, since you were away.” Help that stays silent turns into unseen work, and unseen help slowly becomes expected (see Complacency, spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency). Two grown-up sisters take turns driving their dad to appointments, and when one covers, she texts the other the same day to say she took Dad on Thursday because of the late shift.

    Dig deeper: covering without resentment

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: covering for someone is kind. Say it out loud, gently, and ask for what you’d like next time, so it doesn’t turn into quiet resentment.

    Tool: Small wins: Flip it spreadloveandacceptance.com/small-wins

  6. zqaxchapterx4xxexlandqz

    Let a comment land before you react.

    When a remark hits harder than it should, say “Give me a second.” The idea is borrowed loosely from brain science, where the brain turns down sounds and sensations automatically in a fraction of a second, while this pause is a few seconds you choose to take on purpose. Let the spike pass, then decide whether the remark needs an answer now, later or not at all. A nurse comes home from a night shift and her husband says, “Oh, you’re up.” She hears “at last” and says she needs a second because she is very tired, and it turns out he meant he was glad to see her (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours).

    This week. Agree your “give me a second” phrase today, while things are calm.

    Dig deeper: giving a comment time to land

    Professor Puddles

    When a comment stings, give it a minute to land before you answer. This workpaper is a short check for your reply.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

  7. Notice, name, decide.

    First notice that a comment landed hard, then name it kindly, as in “That hit harder than you probably meant,” and once you have settled, decide how to reply. Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) helps with the words. A teenager tells her dad that he never listens. He feels his chest tighten, says that it stings and that he wants to hear her properly, and decides it needs a real talk the next evening, after her swimming.

    Ways to say it “I want to answer that, just not this minute. Can we talk at eight?”

    Dig deeper: the three steps

  8. Keep the two questions apart.

    Whether the job was done is a question about a fact, and whether the comment hurt is a question about a feeling. Both matter, and each goes better in its own conversation. Separated parents share their children across two homes, and the bag comes back without the school shoes, along with a text about it that felt cold. They sort out the shoes first and talk about the text on Sunday (see Co-parenting, spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting).

    One small step. When a talk tangles, ask “Fact or feeling?” and finish one first.

    Dig deeper: facts and feelings, separately

Your part, and only your part. You control whether, when and how you bring something up, and whether you cover a job out loud. How the other person responds is theirs. If you cover again and again with no thanks and no change, match the energy: cover less, and say so kindly. Fair by promises only works when both people keep theirs. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

The weekly catch-up

Sam and Alex share a home. Alex owns the bins but works late on Tuesdays, and Sam has quietly taken them out three weeks running. At the catch-up Sam mentions it, and Alex admits that Tuesday nights aren’t realistic with the late shifts. They agree to try a swap for the rest of the month, with Sam taking the bins and Alex taking the recycling and the weekly grocery order, and to settle it at the monthly look-back in Chapter V (page 138).

Wednesday, 7pm

“Thanks for doing the dishes,” one of you says, a little flatly. It was meant as a thank-you and it sounded like a criticism, and before you know it you have replied to the criticism.

On your own: your own kind of fair

Fair starts with knowing what it means to you and which jobs are truly yours. Write down what fair means to you in one sentence, and list the jobs you own alongside the ones you picked up without ever agreeing to. Olu lives alone and has his children every other weekend, and his sentence is that fair means not doing their jobs just because he misses them (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). Pick one job you took on without agreeing, and either keep it on purpose or raise it on a calm day.

Common mix-ups

  • “If it got done, there’s no problem.” Someone may be paying for it in time and energy.
  • “Holding the owner to it is being strict.” It is keeping the agreement you both made, which is kinder than quiet resentment.
  • “Letting a comment land means ignoring it.” It is about timing, and you still get to answer.
  • “I covered for months, so now I can bring it all up.” A long list lands like a bill, so mention covering as it happens.

zqaxchapterx4xxmoneyqzMoney between you

Money is where the two kinds of fair meet most often. Some couples put everything into one pot. Some keep their money separate and pay agreed bills, often half each, which is fair by promises, the same rule for both. Others each pay into a shared pot in line with what they earn and keep the rest, which is fair by results, since each is left with a similar share. Many couples mix them, with a joint account for bills and food and some money each that nobody has to explain. The right way is the one you both chose with your eyes open. To talk about it, start with your money stories, how money worked at home when you were growing up, then move on to the numbers and to a “talk first” amount for big purchases that applies to both of you. A limit you both chose and both keep is care, not control.

Niamh takes home £2,600 a month and Tariq £1,900, and their rent and bills will be £1,500. They split it 58/42, in line with their pay, so she pays £870 and he pays £630.

Words to try “Can we each say how money worked in our families growing up?” “Would half each, or in line with our pay, feel fairer to you?”

Dig deeper: money, step by step

zqaxchapterx4xxhousemateqzA couple and a housemate

A couple sharing a home with a housemate who isn’t a partner is a different shape from three equals. It helps to keep two lists, house jobs for all three of you, such as the bins, the bathroom, the bills and the landlord, and couple jobs for the two of you. Decide house questions with all three of you there, rather than in bed the night before, hear the housemate first on anything that affects them, keep couple arguments out of shared rooms and never ask them to referee. Ollie and Hamza share a flat with their friend Bex. They split the rent by room, since the couple has the bigger one, and the bills by person, and all three hold a short house meeting on the first Sunday of the month.

You could say “That’s a house question. Let’s decide it when Bex is here.”

Dig deeper: two lists, and money with three

More for your situation

Each of these pages takes the ideas in this chapter into one kind of relationship. Start from your relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) lists them all.

  • Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends) · More than two partners (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two) · Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room) · Money together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together)
  • Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship) · When a child has ADHD (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts)
  • Different hours · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · When one is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) · Two faiths (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths) · On my own

On a calm, easy day, each of you can say which kind of fair comes more naturally, results or promises. Then pick three regular jobs and write an owner for each in the job list in One owner per job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job), with a second name for someone who notices if it slips. Finally, agree a short phrase for when something lands hard, such as “Give me a second”, along with the promise that the person who asked for a second will come back to it.

A note on safety

These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If talking about what’s fair ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

A promise is something both people chose and either can ask to change. Rules one person sets for the other, with checking, punishment or money held back, are control, and that is not your fault. See normal limits and control (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together#control).

Words you could use, with someone you trust “Things at home don’t feel fair, and I’m scared to bring it up. Can I talk it through with you?”

V

Part Two · Chapter V

The monthly look-back: a calm relationship check-in

Once a month, look back for the problems that keep coming back, and fix the setup instead of having the same argument again.

In this chapter

  1. Weekly check-ins miss patterns
  2. You need four weeks of notes and one list
  3. Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped
  4. A problem that keeps coming back usually has no real owner
  5. Sort each repeat into one of three kinds
  6. Count the gaps each month
  7. Look back even when nothing is slipping
  8. It’s not a review of either person
  9. Keep it short and kind
  10. A look-back, three months in
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. Starting out: before you move in
  13. Raising a grandchild (kinship care)
  14. More for your situation
  15. On your own: a monthly look at yourself

The third Tuesday in a row

The bins again. You could have the same ten-minute back-and-forth about Tuesday, or you could notice that this has now happened three Tuesdays running and wonder what it is about Tuesdays.

  1. Weekly check-ins miss patterns.

    One missed job looks like bad luck. The same job missed week after week is a pattern, and patterns are easiest to see when you look at the whole month. The look-back is a careful, friendly glance over that month, closer to a self-check than an inspection. Four flatmates had an overflowing bathroom bin every week, and every week it seemed like bad luck, until they looked at the month together and saw that it had happened every single week since September. Choosing a monthly date now, such as the last Sunday, and putting it in everyone’s calendar is the first step.

    Dig deeper: why once a month

  2. You need four weeks of notes and one list.

    Bring the month’s four weekly notes from Who did what (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-01), where a few lines a week is enough, and your job list from One owner per job (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-03-one-owner-per-job). Twenty minutes is usually enough. If either of your stress tanks is high that day, at 0.60 or more on How much are you carrying? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-02-how-much-are-you-carrying), move it a day or two. A couple on different shifts keep their weekly notes in one shared note on their phones and do the look-back on the one evening a month they are both off.

    Dig deeper: getting ready

  3. Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped.

    A job slipped if it was noticed and not done, only done after being raised more than once, or quietly covered by someone who isn’t its owner. Look closely at every job with two or more ✗, because three or four in a month is a real pattern. Two foster carers find that the reading log was missed three weeks out of four. They mark the ✗ in pencil, together, before either of them explains anything.

    Dig deeper: gathering the month’s notes

  4. A problem that keeps coming back usually has no real owner.

    Such a problem gets patched every week and never fixed. The owner is the person who does the job from start to finish, so the fix is to give the job one owner whose name sticks, or to talk honestly about whether anyone has the time and energy for it. In a home with three partners, “whoever’s free” does the grocery order, and it was late three times this month, because with nobody owning it, everybody assumed someone else had it.

    Dig deeper: spotting the gaps that keep reopening

  5. Sort each repeat into one of three kinds.

    If a job has no clear owner, update the job list. If its owner can’t keep up, have a kind, honest talk. If there was a short-term cause, like illness or travel, note it and move on. Separated parents looking at the missed homework folder ask whether nobody was sure which home signs it, whether one of them is swamped, or whether it was simply the week she had flu (see Co-parenting, spreadloveandacceptance.com/co-parenting).

    Dig deeper: sorting each gap

  6. Count the gaps each month.

    Write down how many gaps of each kind you found. If the number of jobs with no clear owner falls over several months, the setup is working, and a single month can be a normal swing. If it keeps rising, something bigger has changed and it is worth a talk. Two business partners write their monthly count on a whiteboard in the back office. In March four jobs had no clear owner, and by June one did.

    Dig deeper: keeping count

    Professor Puddles

    The look-back has its own workpaper: a month of notes, one list, and an ✗ for each week a job slipped. It makes a pattern easy to see.

    Workpaper WP-04: What keeps coming back? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-04

  7. Look back even when nothing is slipping.

    A month with no gaps is good news, and it is also the month most likely to go unchecked. When something has worked for a while, people stop looking, and nothing breaks on the day that happens. Keep the look-back going in quiet months and add one question, “What’s something we’ve stopped noticing or mentioning?”, which is how a look-back guards against complacency (spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency). The children have left home and nothing is slipping, and at the look-back one of them says that they don’t really talk at dinner any more.

    Dig deeper: the quiet months

  8. It’s not a review of either person.

    You don’t add up old hours or punish old mistakes. You can thank someone for what they carried before, and you leave the past unbilled. The only question is where the setup isn’t working yet and what you will try next month. After a month in hospital, one partner comes home to a long list of what slipped, and they thank each other for what each carried and set up only the month ahead.

    Dig deeper: what the look-back is for, and what it isn’t

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: a look-back can start with a high five. Name one thing that went well first! The weekly card has a nice way to begin.

    Tool: Kitchen-table check-in spreadloveandacceptance.com/check-ins

  9. Keep it short and kind.

    Start with something that went well and talk about the job instead of the person. If a gap needs a proper talk, set it for another day using Check-ins (spreadloveandacceptance.com/check-ins). If a talk starts going badly, either of you can call a pause, and whoever paused names a time to come back. A mum and two teenagers hold their look-back over pizza. Each says one good thing first, one gap gets a new owner, and it is over in fifteen minutes.

    Dig deeper: how to talk about a pattern

Your part, and only your part. In the look-back you can only fix the gaps you own, and offer help with the rest. You can’t make someone keep a rhythm. Keep the rhythms you can keep, notice which ones are kept in return, and let your effort follow: more where it’s shared, less where it isn’t, so the rhythm doesn’t run on one person’s energy. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

The last Sunday of the month

Two mugs of tea, four weeks of notes and twenty minutes. You go down the list together. Most weeks went fine, and two jobs keep coming up, the recycling and the call to the landlord, so you give each of them a name and finish your tea.

A look-back, three months in

Sam and Alex’s bins slipped three weeks in a row because Alex works late on Tuesdays. After the trial swap they make it official, so Sam owns the bins and Alex takes the recycling and the weekly grocery order, which keeps the hours even. The second month is clean. In the third, the grocery order slips twice, both times in a week when Alex’s mother was in hospital, and they mark it as a one-off and leave the list alone. What changes in month three is that Alex mentions, almost in passing, that he has stopped enjoying their Saturday mornings, which no list had shown, and they agree to talk about it properly on Thursday.

You could say “I don’t think anyone dropped this. I think nobody ever picked it up.”

Common mix-ups

  • “This is where we settle who owes what.” Past hours are never billed to anyone, though you can still say thank you for them, and you only fix the setup going forward.
  • “If a job slipped, the owner failed.” The gap might be in the list, in the owner’s capacity or in one unusual week.
  • “We can skip the weekly checks and just do this.” The monthly look-back only works if the weekly notes feed it.

A note on safety: These tools only work when each person feels free to say no, to ask for a pause, or to keep their own notes private. If looking back together ever feels unsafe, or one of you feels you can’t say no, stop using the tools and talk with a trained counsellor on your own. When someone is afraid of their partner, counselling together isn’t advised. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private hotlines.

A look-back is something you both choose. If one person demands logs of the other’s every hour, checks their phone without agreement, or uses the ✗ marks to punish, that is control, not a look-back, and it is not your fault. See Not safe at home? and normal limits and control (spreadloveandacceptance.com/money-together).

zqaxchapterx5xxmovingxinqzStarting out: before you move in

If you are new together and about to share a home, the tools work best now, before habits set, at about one step a week. In the first week, each of you writes down the rulebook from the home you grew up in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/growing-up) and then you swap, with curiosity. In the second, talk about money, starting with your money stories and moving on to the split (Chapter IV, page 134). In the third, write your first job list, with one owner per job and the thinking jobs included (One owner per job, spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/fill/wp-03), and in the fourth, make a pause plan (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw) on a calm day. In the fifth, each name three things that matter most to you about a home (Part Three, Chapter 10, page 286). After the move, log one ordinary week once two weeks have passed, and do your first short look-back after four. None of it is a test, and the point is that neither of you has to guess.

Niamh and Tariq, eight months together, find that their families meant different things by “tidy”, and they agree on the kitchen every night and the rest on Sunday.

Dig deeper: the plan, week by week

zqaxchapterx5xxkinshipqzRaising a grandchild (kinship care)

Many grandparents and other relatives raise a child whose parents can’t, and much of it involves things that keep coming back, such as cancelled calls, hard evenings after contact and forms. A monthly look-back helps. Some repeats you can own, and some, like a parent who misses calls, you can’t, and for those you can own the plan for the evening after. The child may love both the parent who can’t look after them and you, so tell them they don’t have to choose, and don’t run the parent down in front of them. Explain an absent parent in short, true and kind words for their age, always with the message that it isn’t their fault. When the parent is your own adult child and things are hard between you, keep messages about the child short and civil for the child’s sake, and leave the door open. Look after yourself too, by asking for respite and joining other kinship carers. In England and Wales, the charity Kinship (kinship.org.uk) can help.

Maureen, who is sixty-three, is raising her grandson Tyler, who is nine. Her look-back shows that his mum’s Sunday call fell through three times this month, so she plans those evenings with hot chocolate and his football annual, and asks her brother to take Tyler swimming on Sunday afternoons.

Words you could use, with the child “Mum loves you. She isn’t well enough to look after you right now, and that’s not your fault.”

Dig deeper: loyalty, explaining by age, and rifts with your adult child

More for your situation

A look-back works in every kind of relationship, with small changes. Start from your relationship (spreadloveandacceptance.com/by-relationship) lists pages for each one.

  • More than two partners (spreadloveandacceptance.com/more-than-two) · Money together · Gaming and time together (spreadloveandacceptance.com/gaming-and-time-together) · Sharing a room (spreadloveandacceptance.com/sharing-a-room)
  • Foster and kinship families (spreadloveandacceptance.com/foster-and-kinship) · When a child has ADHD (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids) · Grown-up children (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grown-up-children) · Family rifts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/family-rifts) · Kids grown and gone (spreadloveandacceptance.com/empty-nest)
  • Different hours (spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours) · Coming home (spreadloveandacceptance.com/coming-home) · When one is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill) · Two faiths (spreadloveandacceptance.com/two-faiths) · On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own) · For counsellors (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors)

On your own: a monthly look at yourself

Once a month, look back at your own month kindly, more like a weather report than a scorecard. Ask what filled your battery and what drained it, which of your limits held and which slipped, and choose one small thing to keep and one to change. Gillian lives on her own after a divorce, and her look-back shows the same ✗ three weeks running, because she skipped her Thursday swim to answer work emails, so she moves the emails and keeps the swim (see On my own).

To begin, put a relaxed twenty-minute date in the calendar once a month and keep your weekly notes somewhere you can both find them. At the look-back, start by naming one thing that went well, and end by writing down how many gaps of each kind you found, so that over the next few months you can see whether the number is falling. What keeps coming back? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-04-what-keeps-coming-back) is the workpaper for that conversation.

That’s the end of Part Two. The book goes on in Part Three: Understanding people (page 154), chapters on how people work, for anyone. To put Parts One and Two into practice first, try the six-week program (spreadloveandacceptance.com/prog-01): six gentle weeks, with one chapter and one small tool each week.

What to remember

  • Weekly check-ins miss patterns.
  • Mark an ✗ for each week a job slipped.
  • Sort each repeat into one of three kinds.
  • Look back even when nothing is slipping.
  • Keep it short and kind.

Part Three · Chapter 1

How feelings work: signals, the body, and naming what you feel

What feelings are for, where they start, and why putting a name to one can make it easier to carry, whether you are on your own, at home, with friends or at work.

In this chapter

  1. A feeling is a signal, not a verdict
  2. Feelings start in the body
  3. Naming a feeling helps you hold it
  4. More words, better tools
  5. Feelings come in layers
  6. Feelings rise and pass like waves
  7. Feelings spread between people
  8. If you weren’t brought up to talk about feelings
  9. Feeling it isn’t the same as doing it
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In short

  • A feeling is a signal that something matters to you. It doesn’t tell you what to do about it.
  • Feelings start in the body. A tight chest or a hot face often comes before the word for it.
  • Naming helps. “I feel let down” is easier to hold than a big, nameless rush.
  • You can let a feeling be there and still choose what you do next.

Why the tools work. Two tools in other chapters rest on what this one explains.

  • My weather today and the daily check-in (Part One, Now, page 35; Part Two, Chapter I, page 78) ask for one word about how you are. Naming a feeling turns its volume down a little, and a daily word catches feelings while they are still small.
  • Say it so it lands (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 122) asks you to describe a feeling, because “I felt let down” is easier to hear than “you never care.”

Thursday, 4:50pm

A message from your manager asks whether you have a minute tomorrow, and your stomach drops. By the time you get home you have snapped at the cat, skipped dinner and replayed every mistake of the last month, although nobody has said anything bad at all.

Feelings sit underneath almost everything else, from how we talk and how we see each other to how we handle stress. This chapter looks first at how feelings work and then at what to do with them.

  1. A feeling is a signal, not a verdict.

    Feelings are fast messages about what matters to you. Fear warns that something might be dangerous, anger that something seems unfair or in your way, and sadness that you have lost something that mattered. A signal is worth listening to, though it can be wrong about the details, the way a smoke alarm can go off for burnt toast.

    For example, you feel jealous when a friend makes a new close friend. The jealousy proves nothing about you, and nothing about whether your friend is leaving. What it does show is how much the friendship matters to you.

    Things to tell yourself “This feeling is telling me something matters. What is it?” “Is this the fire, or the toast?”

    Try this. Next time a strong feeling arrives, finish this sentence: “This feeling is trying to protect…”

    Dig deeper: what feelings are for

  2. Feelings start in the body.

    Often your body reacts before your mind has a word for it, with a racing heart, a hot face, a heavy chest or a knot in the stomach, and your brain then tries to make sense of the signal. That is why being hungry, tired or in pain can feel so like being upset, because the mind is guessing at what a strong signal means.

    A teenager comes home furious with his mum over very little. After a cheese sandwich and twenty minutes on the sofa, most of the fury has gone, and he admits he skipped lunch.

    Things to tell yourself “Where is this in my body?” “Am I hungry, tired, cold or sore right now?”

    This week. Three times today, pause and ask yourself what your body feels like right now, and leave it at noticing.

    Dig deeper: the body and the brain’s best guess

  3. Naming a feeling helps you hold it.

    Putting a feeling into words can turn its volume down a little. In brain-scan research by Lieberman and colleagues (2007), simply putting a name to a feeling (“I feel scared”) turned down the brain’s alarm response. A name gives a big, cloudy rush some edges, so that you can see it, talk about it and decide what to do.

    For example, two housemates are tense all evening. Eventually one says, “I think I’m embarrassed about the noise complaint, and I’ve been acting cross,” and the other, who had been wondering what she had done wrong, puts the kettle on.

    You could say “I think what I’m feeling is…” “I’m not sure what this is yet. Maybe worried?”

    One small step. Once a day, name one feeling out loud or on paper. A guess like “something like sad” still counts.

    Dig deeper: why naming works

    Professor Puddles

    If the words won’t come, weather words often will. Pick “foggy” or “stormy” and start from there.

    Tool: My weather today spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks

  4. More words, better tools.

    “Bad” is a very blunt word. “Disappointed,” “left out,” “overwhelmed” and “ashamed” each point to something different, and each needs something different. A review by Kashdan, Barrett and McKnight (2015) found that people who can tell their feelings apart more finely tend to cope with them in healthier ways. You don’t need fancy words, and numbers, colours or body words work too.

    A dad tells his partner that he feels bad about his mum, and they talk in circles for half an hour. Then he says, “Actually, I feel guilty that I haven’t visited, and scared she’s getting worse,” and they start looking at train times.

    Words you could use “On a scale of one to ten, I’m about a six.” “It’s less angry and more… let down.” “It feels heavy, like a grey day.”

    Something to try. When you notice “bad,” try for one more exact word. When you notice “fine,” try for one more honest one.

    Dig deeper: finer words, finer tools

  5. Feelings come in layers.

    The feeling you show first isn’t always the first one you felt. Anger is often a cover for hurt or fear, because anger feels stronger and safer. We also have feelings about our feelings, such as being ashamed of being sad or scared of being angry, and that second layer can hurt more than the first.

    For example, a grandmother is short with her daughter on the phone after the grandchildren’s visit is cancelled. Under the shortness is hurt, and under the hurt is a quieter fear that she is no longer needed.

    Thoughts you could try “What might be under this one?” “It’s okay to feel this. I don’t also have to feel bad for feeling it.”

    Try this. Next time you feel angry, ask yourself gently whether there is hurt or worry underneath. You don’t have to say it to anyone.

    Dig deeper: first feelings and feelings about feelings

  6. Feelings rise and pass like waves.

    Most feelings, even big ones, rise, peak and settle if you don’t keep feeding them. Moods are different. A mood is more like weather, a background feeling that lasts hours or days and colours everything, often without you noticing. A grey mood can make a small thing feel huge, and a good mood can make the same thing feel like nothing.

    A woman living alone has a bad morning and decides her whole life is going nowhere. By evening, after a walk and a long call with her sister, the same life looks ordinary and fairly okay, with a dentist’s appointment on Tuesday and a book she wants to finish.

    Things to tell yourself “This is a wave. It will peak and pass.” “Is this a feeling about now, or a mood colouring everything?”

    This week. Leave big decisions until the wave has passed. Write the decision down and look at it again tomorrow.

    Dig deeper: waves and weather

  7. Feelings spread between people.

    We pick up each other’s feelings from a tense voice, a sigh or a slammed door, often without noticing. That is part of how people bond, and it also means stress can move round a home or a team like a cold. You can care about someone’s feeling without catching all of it.

    For example, a team leader comes into a meeting rushed and anxious, and within ten minutes the whole team feels behind. The next week she stops at the door for two slow breaths before she goes in, and the meeting runs to time.

    Things to tell yourself “Is this feeling mine, or did I pick it up?” “I can stay beside their storm without standing in the middle of it.”

    One small step. Notice who you tend to “catch” feelings from. Before your next talk with them, settle yourself for one minute first.

    Dig deeper: how feelings spread

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: good moods are catching too! Tail wags definitely are. Want a small way to share one?

    Tool: Stay close: one small idea spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding

  8. If you weren’t brought up to talk about feelings.

    Many people grew up in homes, generations or cultures where feelings were kept private, with sayings like “Don’t make a fuss”, “Big boys don’t cry” and “We don’t talk about that.” This is common for men and for older people, and in some cultures it is a sign of respect and strength.

    Keeping feelings private is no flaw, and it doesn’t mean you don’t feel. Many people who rarely put a feeling into words show it every day by doing, whether that is fixing the tap, driving someone to hospital or simply turning up. Caring by doing is real caring, and words can be added slowly, a few at a time.

    A retired builder whose wife has died has never talked about his feelings. On the touchline at his grandson’s football match, he says to his son, “I wasn’t brought up to say this, but I miss her. Every morning.” His son puts a hand on his shoulder, and they watch the second half together.

    Ways to say it “I wasn’t brought up to say this, but I miss her.” “I’m not good with words for this. It’s been a hard week.” “I don’t know what to call it. I just feel heavy.” “I’m not one for talking, but I wanted you to know I’m proud of you.”

    Something to try. Pick one sentence above and say it once this week, to one person or just out loud on your own. A text counts, and so does writing it down.

    Dig deeper: when feelings weren’t talked about

  9. Feeling it isn’t the same as doing it.

    A feeling usually comes with an urge to shout, run, hide, check, fix or text. You don’t choose the feeling, but you have more choice over what you do with the urge. Pushing a feeling down tends to make it come back stronger, and acting on every urge can hurt people, so the middle path is to let the feeling be there and choose the action.

    For example, a father feels a hot rush of anger when his son breaks a window with a football. He says, “I’m too cross to talk right now. Let’s sort this out in ten minutes,” and goes to fetch the dustpan.

    Words to try “I’m feeling a lot right now. I’m going to take a minute before I answer.” “I want to reply when I’m calmer.”

    Try this. Pick one urge you often act on too fast, like sending a sharp text, and make a rule to wait ten minutes first.

    Dig deeper: feelings, urges and choices

Friday, 9:05am

You notice the knot in your stomach again, and this time you name it. You are scared you are in trouble. So you ask your manager straight away whether today’s chat is something you should worry about, and she looks surprised and says it is about the summer rota. You go back to your desk and eat the breakfast you skipped.

In everyday life

If you live on your own, nobody else is there to notice how you are, so a daily one-word check-in with yourself matters more (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). With a partner, “What are you feeling?” can sound like a test, while “Do you want to tell me, or shall I just sit with you?” is easier to answer. Children learn feeling words from the adults around them, and saying “I’m frustrated, so I’m taking a breath” teaches more than any lesson. At work, a short “I’m a bit flat today, and I’m not upset with anyone” can stop a whole team guessing. If someone close to you shows care by doing, by clearing the drive or cooking on a bad day, you can thank them for it in words.

Common mix-ups

  • “Some feelings are bad.” Some feelings are painful and some actions are harmful, but the feeling itself is information.
  • “If I feel it, it must be true.” Feeling stupid doesn’t make you stupid. A feeling is a signal to check.
  • “I should be able to name it straight away.” Many people find feelings hard to name, and some find it very hard. Body words, numbers and colours all count.
  • “Their face tells me what they feel.” Faces are a poor guide, because people show the same feeling in different ways, and asking is kinder and more accurate than guessing.

If you want to help someone else with this

  • Ask before you name it for them. “You’re angry” can feel like a label, while “You seem upset. Am I reading that right?” leaves room for them to correct you.
  • Make the feeling make sense. “Of course you’re upset, that was a lot” helps more than advice, and you can make sense of a feeling without agreeing with every action.
  • Offer choices. “Do you want ideas, or just someone to listen?” Many people only want the second.
  • Accept other ways of saying it. A number, a text, a drawing or “I’m at a seven” is a real answer.
  • Settle yourself first. If their sadness makes you anxious, calm down before you go to them, so they don’t have to look after your feelings too.

You could say “That sounds really hard.” “Do you want to talk, or would company help more?” “You don’t have to find the right word. A number is fine.”

When to get more help

Everyone has hard days and big feelings. It may be time to talk to a doctor, a counsellor or another trained professional if:

  • a low, numb, anxious or angry feeling stays most days for two weeks or more;
  • feelings are stopping you from sleeping, eating, working or seeing people;
  • you are using alcohol, drugs or other things to stop feeling;
  • you feel you can’t cope, or have thoughts of harming yourself. If that’s happening now, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line straight away. You deserve help today.

If you feel afraid of someone you live with or are close to, that fear is an important signal. It is not something to “manage” on your own. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.

This chapter is general education, not a diagnosis or therapy. It can’t know your situation.
