Part Three · Chapter 2

Stress and the nervous system: the ladder, flooding, rest and recovery

What stress does to your body and your mind, why kind people say things they don’t mean when they are flooded, and the kinds of rest that actually help you recover.

In this chapter

  1. Stress is your body getting ready
  2. Stress depends on what you have to meet it
  3. The ladder: three everyday states
  4. When you’re flooded, thinking goes offline
  5. Stress adds up, like a tank filling
  6. Settle the body first
  7. Rest isn’t one thing
  8. Sleep and stress feed each other
  9. Stress is easier to carry when it’s shared
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In short

  • Stress is your body getting ready for a demand. A little helps you rise to it, but too much for too long wears you down.
  • You move between three everyday states through the day, calm and connected, revved up and running on empty, and each one changes how you think and hear.
  • When you are flooded, careful thinking goes offline, so pause, let your body settle and come back at a set time.
  • Rest is a skill. Different kinds of tired need different kinds of rest, and sleep matters more than most people think.

Why the tools work. Several tools in other chapters lean on what this one explains.

  • How much are you carrying? and the stress tank (Part Two, Chapter III, page 107) work because stress adds up from many small loads. A full tank makes small things feel big, so you check the tank before you judge the moment.
  • The Calm-Down Kit (Part One, Now, page 35) settles the body before any words, because a flooded body can’t think or listen. Its rule about coming back at a set time keeps a pause from looking like walking out.
  • The setup score (Part Two, Chapter II, page 91) counts stress as well as hours, because a split that looks fair on paper can still leave one person running on empty.

Monday, 7:52am

The bus is late, the kids can’t find a shoe, and your phone buzzes with a work message. Your partner says, “Have you seen my keys?” and you hear yourself snap, “I’m not your secretary!” A second later you wonder where that came from, because the keys were never the problem and you were already running late before anyone spoke.

Feelings are the subject of Chapter 1 (page 154). This chapter looks at the system underneath them, your nervous system, and what happens to it under pressure. Understanding stress won’t make a busy life any quieter, but it can make your own reactions, and other people’s, a lot less mysterious.

  1. Stress is your body getting ready.

    When something needs dealing with, your body gears up. The heart speeds up, breathing quickens, muscles tense and stress hormones rise. That is useful when you need to catch a falling glass, meet a deadline or speak up in a meeting. The trouble starts when the body stays geared up for too long and never gets the chance to come back down.

    For example, a nurse handles an emergency calmly and well. Two hours later, at home, she can’t sit still and finds herself crying at an advert for car insurance, because her body is still running the emergency.

    Thoughts you could try “My body is getting ready for something, and that’s its job.” “The emergency is over. I can let my body catch up.”

    Try this. After something stressful, give your body a clear signal that it’s over, such as a walk round the block, a shower, a stretch or one song played loud.

    Dig deeper: the stress response

  2. Stress depends on what you have to meet it.

    The same event can be easy for one person and huge for another. Stress grows when a demand looks bigger than what you have to meet it, whether that is time, energy, money, help, skill or sleep. That is why a small thing can tip you over on a bad day, and why giving someone more support can shrink their stress without changing the task at all.

    Two coworkers get the same tight deadline on a Thursday. One has a quiet evening ahead, and the other has a child at home with a temperature and a partner away for work. On paper it is one task, yet one of them will lie awake over it.

    You could say “It’s less the task than how little I have left today.” “What would make this feel more doable?”

    This week. When something feels huge, write two lists side by side, one for what it asks of you and one for what you have. Then ask what could make the second list a little longer.

    Dig deeper: demands and resources

  3. The ladder: three everyday states.

    The ladder is a picture for three states your body moves between during the day. When you are calm and connected, breathing is easy and you can hear hard things. When you are revved up, you feel fast and tense, and small things seem urgent or personal. When you are running on empty, you feel flat and slow and short of words.

    Most people move up and down the ladder many times a day. The Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) is a thirty-second self-check that gives you a best guess at where you are right now.

    For example, a grandfather minding his toddler granddaughter all afternoon is calm at two o’clock, revved up by four and running on empty by six. Neither of them has changed, only the hour and how much of the day is left in him.

    You could say “I’m revved up right now.” “I’m running on empty. Can this wait till morning?”

    One small step. Set three reminders on your phone for today. Each time one goes off, notice which rung you are on, and leave it at noticing.

    Dig deeper: the ladder

  4. When you’re flooded, thinking goes offline.

    At the top of the stress curve the body is in full alarm, and careful thinking, listening and seeing the other side all get much harder. Many people call this being flooded. You might say things you don’t mean, freeze, or only want to get out of the room. A flooded person is still a decent person whose body needs to come down before the talk can go anywhere useful.

    Two adult siblings start sorting their late father’s things. Within minutes they are shouting about a lamp that neither of them wants, while the real subject, that he is gone, sits unspoken in the boxes around them.

    You could say “I’m too flooded to listen well. Can we stop for twenty minutes and come back at four?”

    Something to try. Learn your own flood signs, such as heat in your face, a racing heart, narrowed vision or a loud inner voice. When you notice two of them at once, pause.

    Dig deeper: flooding

  5. Stress adds up, like a tank filling.

    Think of a tank that holds all the stress you are already carrying today. Stress from one place spills into the next, so traffic, a hard meeting, a noisy shop and a worrying text all fill the same tank. By evening a tiny thing makes it overflow. The last drop gets the blame even though the tank was nearly full already, and small daily hassles count as much as big events.

    For example, a teenager explodes when asked to empty the dishwasher. His mum later finds out that his closest friendship fell apart at lunchtime, and the dishwasher simply happened to be the next thing anyone asked of him.

    You could say “My tank was already full when I got home, and that wasn’t really about you.” “Rough day? You don’t have to explain.”

    Try this. Before you react to a small thing in the evening, ask yourself how full you were before it happened. Part Two, Chapter III (page 107) has a simple way to tell.

    Dig deeper: why stress adds up

    Professor Puddles

    Stress fills up a little at a time, like a puddle in a long shower of rain. I would know. Five quick questions tell you how full yours is today.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  6. Settle the body first.

    You can’t think your way out of a body in alarm, but you can help the body come down, and the thinking usually follows. Slow breathing with long out-breaths helps many people. So does moving, humming a familiar song, steady pressure such as a heavy blanket, or simply leaving a noisy room. What works differs from person to person, so it is worth finding your own short list on a calm day.

    A manager feels her heart race before she has to give some hard feedback. She walks once round the block, breathing out slowly, and goes into the room a little steadier than she would have been.

    Things to tell yourself “Body first, words second.” “What has helped me settle before?”

    This week. On a calm day, list three things that settle you and keep the list on your phone. The Calm-Down Kit (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11) helps you build it.

    Dig deeper: settling the body

  7. Rest isn’t one thing.

    An hour on the sofa scrolling your phone may leave you more tired than before. Recovery comes in different kinds. There is sleep, there is switching off from work in your head, there is real relaxation, there is doing something absorbing that you enjoy, and there is the feeling of being in charge of your own time. Being with people restores some people and drains others, so the right rest depends on the kind of tired you are.

    For example, two housemates plan a relaxing Saturday with friends round. One of them wakes up on Sunday refreshed, and the other needs the whole of Sunday alone with a book before she feels like herself again.

    You could say “I need quiet rest tonight rather than people rest. It isn’t about you.” “What kind of tired are you?”

    One small step. Ask yourself whether you are body-tired, people-tired, brain-tired or feelings-tired, and pick a rest that matches.

    Dig deeper: kinds of rest

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: rest can be a nap, a walk or ten minutes of soft music. Find the kind that suits you, and keep it close.

    Tool: Cool-down corner: calm sounds and music spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes

  8. Sleep and stress feed each other.

    Stress makes sleep harder, and poor sleep makes stress hit harder. After a short or broken night, small things feel bigger, tempers are shorter and people pull away from each other. In a brain-scan study by Yoo and colleagues (2007), one night without sleep made the brain’s alarm centre react more strongly to upsetting pictures.

    In a daily study by Gordon and Chen (2014), people reported more conflict with their partner after nights of poor sleep. And in experiments by Ben Simon and Walker (2018), people who had missed a night’s sleep kept others at a greater distance and felt lonelier. You can’t always fix sleep, but you can notice when it is part of the story.

    A nurse coming off three night shifts finds herself in tears over a parking ticket. Her sister says, “You’ve barely slept. Let’s sort it out on Thursday.” By Thursday it is a parking ticket again, annoying and payable.

    You could say “I slept badly, so if I’m short with you today, that’s why.” “Can we talk about this after we’ve both slept?”

    Something to try. Before a hard conversation, ask whether you have both slept, and if not, pick another time. At night, try the same few calm steps before bed in the same order, so your body learns the signal. If poor sleep goes on for weeks, talk to a doctor, because sleep problems are common and often treatable.

    Dig deeper: sleep and stress

  9. Stress is easier to carry when it’s shared.

    People calm each other. A steady voice, a hand on the shoulder or just a quiet person nearby can help a nervous system settle. Saying your state out loud also helps others read you right, because “I’m stressed about work” stops a partner or friend from wondering whether it is about them. Sharing stress in this way lets someone stand beside you without asking them to carry it for you.

    For example, a father tells his ten-year-old, “I’m a bit stressed about money this month. Sorting it is my grown-up job, and you’re not in trouble.” Over the next few days his son stops tiptoeing round him and starts asking for help with his homework again.

    You could say “I’m stressed, and it isn’t about you.” “Would a hug help, or some space?”

    Try this. Tonight, tell one person your state in one sentence, and ask how they are.

    Dig deeper: stress between people

Monday, 7:58am

Six minutes after the snap, you find your partner by the door, still patting their pockets. “Sorry. My tank was full before you said a word, and your keys are on the bathroom shelf.” They laugh and ask whether it has been a rough start. The bus is still late and the shoe is still missing, but the two of you are on the same side of the morning again.

In everyday life

If you live on your own, nobody is there to notice when you are running on empty, so it helps to build rest into the week before you need it. With a partner, agree a pause word on a calm day, along with the rule that whoever pauses names a time to come back (One of you wants to talk now, the other needs space, spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw, has more on this). A child can’t settle until the nearest grown-up does, which means your calm is something they borrow long before they learn it for themselves. At work, a flooded colleague can’t take in feedback, and waiting an hour often works better than pushing on.

Some people run on empty for reasons built into their lives, such as shift work, long-term illness or caring for someone. That calls for a different setup rather than more effort (see Different hours, spreadloveandacceptance.com/different-hours, and Caregivers, spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers). If you have ADHD, keeping track of everything can quietly fill the tank before the day has started. It helps to move the remembering out of your head with a shared list, labelled alarms and one place for keys, and to plan hard talks for your better time of day. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-2-stress-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

  • “All stress is bad.” Short bursts of stress help you rise to a challenge. The harm comes from stress that never gets a recovery.
  • “If I’m calm, I can’t be upset.” Calm means steady. You can be calm and sad, or calm and firm.
  • “Pausing is avoiding.” A pause with a time to come back is a way to finish the talk well. Avoiding is the pause that never comes back.
  • “Rest is lazy.” Recovery is part of the work, and bodies and minds that never recover tend to break down.
  • “Running on empty means they don’t care.” Short replies and a flat face more often mean someone is worn out.

If you want to help someone else with this

A lower voice, slower words and a steady presence help a stressed person more than being told to calm down. Taking one task off someone’s list can do more than any pep talk, so ask what kind of help they want, whether practical help, company, a distraction or some space, rather than guessing. Don’t debate with someone who is flooded. Offer a break and a time to come back, because the facts will still be there in twenty minutes. And if someone has been running on empty for weeks, mention it gently and help them find support.

You could say “You seem really stretched. Is there one thing I could take off your plate?” “We don’t have to sort this now. Shall we pick it up after dinner?”

When to get more help

Stress is normal. Constant stress that never lets up is a warning sign. It may be time to see a doctor, counsellor or other trained professional if:

  • you’ve felt exhausted, dread-filled or numb most days for several weeks, even after rest;
  • you can’t sleep, or sleep but never feel rested;
  • you have physical signs that worry you, such as chest pain, constant headaches or stomach trouble (always get chest pain checked straight away);
  • you’re relying on alcohol, drugs or other habits to get through the day;
  • you feel you can’t cope, or have thoughts of harming yourself. If that is happening now, contact your local emergency number or a crisis line.

If the stress comes from being afraid of someone, such as how they will react, what they will do or whether you are allowed to leave, that is not ordinary stress. Your body may be warning you. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has free, private help.

This chapter is general education, not medical advice or diagnosis.

  • Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now): steps to calm down, alone or together.
  • Drift (spreadloveandacceptance.com/calm-visualizer), Brain Breakers (spreadloveandacceptance.com/soundscapes) and calm games (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pause-and-play): gentle ways to come down.

Part Three · Chapter 3

How we see each other: perception, bias, and the stories we tell

Why two people can watch the same moment and come away with two different stories, and how to see others, and yourself, a little more fairly.

In this chapter

  1. Seeing is a best guess
  2. You see what you’re looking for
  3. We fill the gaps with stories
  4. We judge ourselves by our reasons, and others by their actions
  5. Quick shortcuts can lead us astray
  6. Everyone feels like the one who sees clearly
  7. “Us” and “them” changes what we see
  8. Ask, don’t guess
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Seeing is a best guess. Your brain fills in a lot of what you think you see and hear.
  • We fill gaps with stories, and the story often feels like a fact.
  • We judge ourselves by our reasons and others by their actions, and that gap causes a lot of hurt.
  • Asking is kinder and more accurate than trying to read someone’s mind.

Why the tools work. Three tools in other chapters rest on what this one explains.

  • Who did what (the Preface to Part Two, page 64) works because everyone sees their own effort more clearly than other people’s, so two honest guesses of “I do about 60%” can add up to more than 100%. Writing it down replaces two guesses with one shared page.
  • Rewind the talk (Part Two, Chapter III, page 107) slows down the habit of judging ourselves by our reasons and other people by their actions.
  • The Chat analyzer follows this chapter’s last idea, that asking works better than guessing.

Wednesday, 12:15pm

You wave at a coworker across the canteen, and she looks straight through you and walks off. All afternoon you wonder what you did, until at four o’clock she messages to say sorry for not stopping, because she had just had a call about her dad. She never saw you wave.

How feelings work (page 154) and Stress and the nervous system (page 169) look inward. This chapter looks outward, at how we see other people, why misunderstandings are so common even between kind and clever people, and what helps.

  1. Seeing is a best guess.

    Your eyes and ears take in far less than you think, and your brain fills in the rest from what it expects. Most of the time this works well and fast, but it means that what you see is partly what you expected to see, so two people can watch the same moment and honestly see different things.

    For example, two parents watch their son in a football match. One sees him giving up, and the other sees him being careful with the ankle he twisted last week.

    Things to tell yourself “This is what I see, and there may be more to it.” “What else could this be?”

    Try this. Next time you’re sure what someone meant by a look, think of two other things it could have meant.

    Dig deeper: perception as a best guess

  2. You see what you’re looking for.

    Attention is like a torch in a dark room. You see what it lights up and can miss what it doesn’t, even when it is right in front of you. If you are looking for proof that someone doesn’t care, you will notice every missed call and none of the little kindnesses.

    A woman decides that her new manager doesn’t like her, and for a month she notices every short email he sends. She misses the fact that he gave her the best project on the team.

    Things to tell yourself “What might I be missing?” “If I were looking for the opposite, what would I see?”

    This week. For one week, write down one kind thing that a person you are struggling with does each day.

    Dig deeper: the torch of attention

  3. We fill the gaps with stories.

    When we don’t know why someone did something, the mind makes up a reason fast. A late reply becomes anger and a closed door becomes rejection, and the story arrives feeling like a fact. Memory works this way too, because each time we remember something we rebuild it a little, so two people can honestly remember the same evening differently.

    For example, a friend doesn’t reply for two days and you decide she is fed up with you. She was camping in Snowdonia with no signal.

    You could say “The story I’m telling myself is that you’re upset with me. Is that right?”

    One small step. When something someone did hurts, write down the story you are telling yourself, and then one other possible story.

    Dig deeper: stories and memory

  4. We judge ourselves by our reasons, and others by their actions.

    When you are late, you know why, whether it was the traffic, a phone call or a child who lost a shoe. When someone else is late, you only see the lateness, and it is easy to decide they are careless. We all tend to blame other people’s character for things that are really about their situation.

    A driver cuts in front of you and you call him an idiot under your breath. The next week, rushing to the hospital, you cut someone up yourself, and you know exactly why.

    Thoughts you could try “What might be going on for them that I can’t see?” “If I did this, what would my reason be?”

    Something to try. When someone annoys you today, think of one situation that would explain it without making them a bad person.

    Dig deeper: actions and reasons

    Professor Puddles

    We know our own reasons and only see other people’s actions. Writing out their side, in their words, is a fair way to even that up.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  5. Quick shortcuts can lead us astray.

    The brain uses shortcuts to save time, and many are useful. Some lead to unfair judgements, such as a first impression that colours everything after it, a bad moment that outweighs ten good ones, or a quick guess about someone from their age, accent, looks or group. Everyone has these shortcuts, and the trouble starts when nobody notices them.

    For example, a housemate decides on the first day that the new tenant is messy because of one box left in the hall. Every bit of mess after that counts as proof, while her own goes unseen.

    Things to tell yourself “Am I looking for proof of what I already think?” “Would I judge this the same if someone I like did it?”

    Try this. Pick one person you’ve made your mind up about. Look for one thing that doesn’t fit your view of them.

    Dig deeper: shortcuts and bias

  6. Everyone feels like the one who sees clearly.

    Most of us feel that we see things as they really are and that anyone who disagrees must be missing something, biased or not thinking straight. The other person feels exactly the same about you, and each of you can see the other’s lens more easily than your own.

    Two adult siblings argue about how their parents raised them, and each insists they are just being realistic, which is true of what each of them lived through.

    Words you could use “I think we’re both seeing this from where we stand. Can you tell me how it looks from yours?”

    This week. In your next disagreement, explain the other person’s view back to them until they agree that you have got it, and then give yours.

    Dig deeper: why we each feel like the realist

  7. “Us” and “them” changes what we see.

    People split into groups quickly, even over tiny things. We tend to see our own group as varied and full of individuals and other groups as all the same, and we give our own side the benefit of the doubt. Spending real time with people from the other group, as equals, is one of the best ways to soften this.

    For example, at one depot the night shift calls the day shift lazy and the day shift calls the night shift sloppy. After a joint training day, people start using each other’s names.

    Things to tell yourself “Would I say this about one of ‘us’?” “Who in that group do I actually know?”

    One small step. Have one real conversation this month with someone from a group you tend to see as “other”, and ask about their day before you ask about their views.

    Dig deeper: us and them

  8. Ask, don’t guess.

    Imagining yourself in someone’s shoes is a kind start, though research suggests it doesn’t make us much more accurate about what they think, while asking does. A simple, curious question like “What was that like for you?” works better than the cleverest guess.

    A grandmother thinks her teenage grandson hates visiting because he is always on his phone. When she asks, she finds he is messaging a friend who is having a hard time, and that he likes being at her house because it is calm.

    Ways to say it “Can I check what you meant?” “What was going on for you?” “I might have this wrong. How did it look from your side?”

    Something to try. Once today, swap a guess for a question.

    Dig deeper: seeing more fairly

Thursday, 12:20pm

You see your coworker in the canteen again, and this time you go over and ask how her dad is. She tells you about the hospital and the waiting, and you end up sharing a table until the end of the break.

In everyday life

We tell stories about ourselves too, and “I always mess things up” is usually built from a few bright memories that leave a great deal out. After years together, partners stop checking and start assuming, and “I know what you meant” can do a lot of quiet damage in a long relationship. Children are often labelled early as the difficult one or the easy one, and the label becomes a lens that only sees what fits. With ADHD, attention is pulled by whatever is new or urgent and can lock on hard, so someone may truly not have seen or heard. It helps to get their attention first and to put requests in writing. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-3-seeing-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

  • “I just see things as they are.” Everyone sees through a lens, and knowing that is where fairness starts.
  • “My memory is a recording.” Memory is rebuilt each time, so two honest people can remember the same event differently.
  • “Giving the benefit of the doubt means ignoring what happened.” It means checking the story before deciding, and if something hurtful keeps happening, that matters.
  • “Their face or tone told me what they meant.” Faces and tones vary a lot between people, cultures and neurotypes, so treat them as clues.

If you want to help someone else with this

  • Start with how they feel. Make sense of the feeling first, and only then ask gently whether there is another way to see it.
  • Offer information. “I know she had a hard week” helps more than “You’re being unfair to her.”
  • Check your own guesses out loud, as in “I assumed he was annoyed. I’ll ask.”
  • Be careful with labels. Labels for children, coworkers or family members stick, and then shape what everyone sees.
  • Believe people about their own experience. Seeing other angles never means telling someone their experience didn’t happen.

Words to try “That sounds really hurtful. Do you know what was going on for them?” “It might be worth asking. Want to plan what to say?”

When to get more help

Seeing other people’s side is a strength. It should never mean doubting yourself when you know something is wrong. If someone often tells you that what you saw, heard or remember didn’t happen, that you’re “too sensitive” or “imagining it,” and you find yourself unsure of your own mind, take that seriously. It can be part of controlling behaviour. Signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) and Not safe at home? can help, privately.

It may also help to talk to a counsellor or other trained professional if you notice you often feel others are against you, find it hard to trust anyone, or keep getting stuck in the same painful stories about yourself. Those patterns are common, understandable and often change with support.

This chapter is general education, not diagnosis or therapy.

  • Chat analyzer (spreadloveandacceptance.com/signal-translator): how a sentence might land before you say it.

  • The library: the fundamental attribution error (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/thinking), confirmation bias (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/thinking#confirmation-bias), negativity bias (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/thinking#negativity-bias), naive realism (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/thinking#naive-realism), mind-reading (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/thinking#mind-reading) and how memory is rebuilt (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/thinking#memory-reconstruction).

Part Three · Chapter 4

How communication works: meaning, listening, repair and messages

Talking feels simple because we do it all day, yet every message has to travel from one mind to another, and a lot can change on the way. This chapter follows that journey and looks at what helps a message arrive the way you meant it.

In this chapter

  1. Meaning is made between two people
  2. Every message says two things
  3. Listening is something you do, not something that happens
  4. Check, don’t guess
  5. Hard things land better when they start soft
  6. Mix-ups are normal. Repair is the skill
  7. Messages lose their tone on the way
  8. Different styles aren’t wrong styles
  9. Small talk has a job, and it can be short
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In short

  • Meaning is made between two people. What you say and what they hear can differ without either of you being wrong.
  • Every message says two things, the words themselves and what they seem to say about the two of you.
  • A short question saves a long misunderstanding, so check before you guess.
  • Mix-ups are normal, and repairing them is the skill. Small talk is allowed to be short.

Why the tools work. Three tools in other chapters rest on what this one explains.

  • Say it so it lands (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 122) asks for what happened, how you feel and one clear request, because every message carries its content and a second message about the relationship.
  • The 90-second daily check-in (Part Two, Chapter I, page 78) works because mix-ups are normal, and small, frequent repairs keep people in tune better than rare big talks.
  • The Chat analyzer’s whole-conversation view shows where a written conversation lost its tone.

Thursday, 8:15am

Ana texts her brother to ask him to call when he is free. She means there’s no rush and she has a small question about the weekend. He reads it on the bus and spends the whole ride wondering who is ill.

Small habits help a message arrive, such as listening, checking, starting softly and repairing quickly, and a few ready-made lines make small talk easier for anyone who dreads it.

  1. Meaning is made between two people.

    Words don’t carry meaning on their own. The speaker has a meaning in mind, and the listener builds their own from the words, the tone, the timing and everything they already expect. Most of the time the two match well enough, and sometimes they don’t, without either person being able to see the gap from where they stand.

    For example, a manager writes “Let’s chat tomorrow” to a new coworker, meaning a friendly catch-up, and he spends the evening convinced he is in trouble.

    You could say “I think what I meant and what you heard might be two different things. Can we check?”

    Try this. Today, notice one moment when someone took your words differently from how you meant them, and leave blame out of it.

    Dig deeper: how meaning travels

  2. Every message says two things.

    There is what you say, and there is what it says about the two of you. “You’re late” is a fact about time, and it can also mean “I was worried” or “I don’t matter to you.” People often argue about the fact when the hurt is in the second layer.

    When one housemate asks another whether she used his pan, the question is about a pan and also, underneath, about whether his things are respected, which no amount of talk about the pan will settle.

    Words you could use “I don’t really mind about the pan. I think I wanted to know my stuff matters here.”

    This week. Next time a small thing stings, ask yourself what it seemed to say about us.

    Dig deeper: the two layers of a message

  3. Listening is something you do, not something that happens.

    Hearing happens by itself, while listening is a choice. Most of us listen partly to reply, so that we can fix, defend, advise or tell our own story. Real listening means following what the other person is trying to say and letting them know you got it before you add anything of your own.

    For example, a teenager says school is pointless, her dad starts explaining why it isn’t, and she stops talking. The next time she says it, he asks, “Pointless how? Tell me about today,” and she talks for twenty minutes.

    Ways to say it “So what I’m hearing is... Have I got that right?” “Do you want ideas, or do you want me to just listen?”

    One small step. In one conversation today, wait until the other person has finished, then say back what you heard before you reply.

    Dig deeper: what good listening is

  4. Check, don’t guess.

    Once we know something, it is hard to imagine not knowing it, so we leave out steps, assume the other person can tell what we mean and guess what they meant instead of asking. We do this most with the people we know best. A short check costs a sentence, while a wrong guess can cost a whole evening.

    Two friends plan something low-key for a birthday. One pictures a takeaway on the sofa and the other books a quiet restaurant, and both are disappointed because each thought it was obvious.

    Words to try “Just so I’ve got it right, you mean...?” “When you say soon, do you mean today or this week?”

    Something to try. Pick one person you know well and check one meaning with them today, even if you feel sure.

    Dig deeper: why we guess, and how to check

    Professor Puddles

    Checking takes ten seconds and saves an evening. When you’re ready to reply, this workpaper helps you say it so it lands.

    Workpaper WP-09: Say it so it lands spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-09

  5. Hard things land better when they start soft.

    How a hard talk begins often shapes how it ends. A complaint about one thing (“The bins weren’t taken out”) is easier to hear than a criticism of the person (“You never help”). A simple shape works for most hard things, which is to say what happened, how you feel and what you would like.

    For example, a woman wants her elderly father to stop driving at night. She leaves out “You’re not safe any more” and says, “You had two near-misses last month and I lie awake worrying. Could I drive us in the evenings?”

    You could say “What happened was... I felt... Could we...?”

    Try this. Write one sentence in that shape about something small that has been bothering you. You don’t have to send it yet.

    Dig deeper: saying hard things kindly

  6. Mix-ups are normal. Repair is the skill.

    Even close, kind people misunderstand each other all the time. What keeps a relationship steady is noticing and fixing it with lines like “That came out wrong”, “I think I misread you” or “Can we start again?”, and small repairs made often build trust.

    At the supermarket a stranger snaps “Excuse me!” when you block the aisle, and you snap back. A second later you add, “Sorry, long day,” and she smiles and says the same is true for her.

    Words you could use “Can I try that again?” “I think I took that the wrong way. What did you mean?”

    This week. The next time something comes out wrong, repair it out loud within a minute, and notice how small a repair can be.

    Dig deeper: how repair works

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: a mix-up isn’t the end of anything. Come back, sit close, and go through it step by step.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  7. Messages lose their tone on the way.

    A text or email carries the words without your face, your voice or your timing, so the reader fills in the tone with however they feel right now, and a tired reader hears a tired, cross message. Short replies, missing greetings and late-night timing all get read as meaning something.

    For example, in the group chat for a school fundraiser, one parent replies “Fine.” to a plan, and two others decide she is annoyed, when she was typing one-handed while stirring a pan of soup.

    Ways to say it “Quick reply, not a cross one!” “This isn’t urgent. Any time this week is fine.”

    One small step. Before you send your next tricky message, read it out loud in the grumpiest voice you can. If it sounds harsh, add a warm word or a time frame.

    Dig deeper: texts, email and tone

  8. Different styles aren’t wrong styles.

    Some people say exactly what they mean and others hint and expect you to read between the lines. Some talk fast and overlap while others need a pause to think. Families, cultures and different kinds of minds all shape this, and a clash between two styles is usually a matter of translation.

    Asked whether the report is ready, an autistic employee says, “No, I need two more days.” Her manager hears bluntness until they talk about it, after which he starts to find her clarity a relief.

    Words to try “I’m quite direct, so if I sound blunt, it doesn’t mean I’m cross.” “It helps me if you say exactly what you need.”

    Something to try. Write one sentence about how you like to be spoken to, and share it with one person this week.

    Dig deeper: styles, cultures and minds

  9. Small talk has a job, and it can be short.

    Small talk (“Cold today, isn’t it?” “Busy weekend?”) isn’t really about the weather. Its job is to say that you see the other person and that the two of you are okay. In 1923 the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski called this “phatic communion”, talk whose main purpose is bonding more than information. Small moments like this matter more than people expect. Sandstrom and Dunn (2014) found that people who had a short, friendly exchange with a coffee-shop barista felt more belonging and a better mood than people who kept it purely efficient.

    Small talk is hard work for many people, though, including many autistic people, shy or anxious people and people speaking a second language. The rules are unwritten, it can feel pointless and it uses energy. A few ready-made lines, sometimes called social scripts, take the guesswork out, and keeping it short is allowed.

    For example, a dad who dreads the school gate keeps three lines ready, starting with “Morning! How’s your week going?”, then “Oh, nice,” and finally “Right, I’d better get going. See you Friday.” Some mornings he still hides in the car until the bell, but most days he gets through it.

    You could say “Morning! How’s your week been?” “How do you know Nico?” “Oh, how was that?” “Lovely to see you. I’d better get on.” And to opt out kindly, “I’m not great at chit-chat, but it’s really nice to see you.”

    Try this. Write your own three lines, one to open, one follow-up question and one to close, and use them once this week. If you would rather skip ahead to a real topic, “Can I ask you about something I’m actually curious about?” works too.

    Dig deeper: small talk and social scripts

Thursday, 9:02am

Ana’s brother rings the moment he is off the bus and asks who is ill. She laughs and says nobody, she only wanted to know whether he is free on Saturday, and he laughs too, a little shakily. The following week her text reads, “No rush and nothing’s wrong. Quick question about Saturday, call when you’re free.”

In everyday life

On your own: how you talk to yourself

You also send yourself messages all day, from “Typical, I always mess this up” to “That was hard, and I handled it.” The same ideas apply, so notice the tone, check whether the message is fair and repair it when it is harsh. Catch one harsh sentence you say to yourself today and rewrite it the way you would speak to someone you like.

zqaxunderstandingx4xcommunicationxxwithxothersqzWith other people

Between partners, “We never go out any more” sounds like a complaint about evenings, and underneath it may mean “I miss you,” so answering that layer goes further than defending the calendar. “Stop that!” tells a child what not to do without saying what to do instead, while “Feet on the floor, please” is easier to follow. In meetings, silence is often taken as agreement until a quieter colleague says later that she never agreed, and a round of “Anyone see it differently?” catches this early. “Are you eating properly?” is care in one generation’s language and checking up in another’s.

  • Feedback at work. Talk about the work, not the person, with one recent example and what good looks like. Then ask, “What’s been getting in the way?” When you’re the one receiving it, “Thanks. Can I think about it and come back tomorrow?” is a fine first answer. The full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-4-communication-in-depth) walks through a whole performance conversation.

Common mix-ups

  • “If they loved me, they’d just know.” Closeness makes us check less without making us understand more, so saying it clearly is a kindness.
  • “Listening means agreeing.” You can fully understand someone and still see it differently, and understanding comes first.
  • “Repairing means admitting I’m the bad one.” A repair just says that it didn’t go the way you wanted, and either person can make one.
  • “Texts are safer for hard things.” They feel safer to send and are easier to misread, so for tender things, add warmth or talk.

If you want to help someone else with this

Maybe a friend keeps having the same argument with their partner, or your teenager feels nobody listens. You can’t communicate for them, but you can help.

  • Listen first. The most useful thing is often to be the person who really hears them, without fixing.
  • Help them separate the two layers, by asking what it was about and what it seemed to say about the two of them.
  • Offer the simple shape of what happened, how they feel and what they would like, and let them find their own words.
  • Stay out of judging the other person’s character. You only hear one side, and they may make up next week.
  • Notice if it’s more than a mix-up. If they seem afraid of the other person, gently share Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety)

Words you could use “Do you want me to just listen, or help you think about what to say?”

When to get more help

Most mix-ups can be eased with the ideas here. Some situations need more.

  • When talking makes things worse every time, a couples or family counsellor can slow conversations down and help both people be heard.
  • When you’re afraid of how someone will react, that isn’t a communication problem. Clearer words are not the fix, and you don’t have to keep trying. Not safe at home? lists free, private help, and signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#signs) may help you name what’s happening.
  • When someone is always “misunderstanding” you in ways that make you doubt your memory or your sense of what happened, talk with someone you trust outside the relationship.
  • When speaking or understanding is hard for you every day, because of anxiety, a hearing or language difference, or how your mind works, a doctor, speech and language therapist or counsellor may help. Needing support is not a failing.
  • If you’re overwhelmed right now, start with Upset right now (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now).

Workpapers, tools and reading on the website

Try one of these this week with one real conversation. Say it so it lands (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-09-say-it-so-it-lands) helps you shape a hard sentence, Rewind the talk (spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder) walks you back through a talk that went wrong, and the wiring card (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card) puts how you communicate on one page.

5

Part Three · Chapter 5

Attachment, trust and belonging

Why we need each other, how the bonds we had early on shape what we expect today, and how trust and belonging are built, lost and rebuilt, one small moment at a time.

In this chapter

  1. Belonging is a basic need
  2. Early bonds teach us what to expect
  3. Patterns, not boxes
  4. Trust is built in small moments
  5. Feeling safe with someone calms the body
  6. Fitting in isn’t the same as belonging
  7. When trust breaks, rebuilding takes time
  8. You can start building connection from wherever you are
  9. If you’re a teenager
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In short

  • Belonging is a basic need. Feeling lonely or left out is a signal, like hunger.
  • Early bonds set expectations that can change. What we learned about being cared for can soften over time.
  • Trust grows in small moments. Doing what you said, again and again, matters more than big gestures.
  • You can start small, with one friendly exchange or one kept promise.

Why the tools work. Two tools in other chapters rest on what this one explains.

  • One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, page 91) works because trust is built from small promises kept, and a named owner turns a vague hope that someone will do it into a promise others can rely on.
  • The monthly look-back (Part Two, Chapter V, page 138) looks at the month and leaves both people out of the dock, because feeling safe is what lets people say what went wrong without bracing for blame.

Sunday, 9:30pm

Kai sent a long message to a friend at lunchtime, and it has been read without a reply. By evening Kai has gone from thinking she is busy to thinking she is annoyed to wondering whether anybody really likes him. The friend, meanwhile, is at her nephew’s birthday party with her phone in her coat pocket.

  1. Belonging is a basic need.

    People need to feel connected, the way we need food and sleep. When we feel left out, it can hurt in a way that feels almost physical (Naomi Eisenberger and colleagues, 2003). That hurt works like hunger, telling us to reach for connection.

    For example, Rhea moves to a new city for work. She is busy and doing well, yet by the third month she feels flat and teary on Sundays, when the office is shut and nobody in the city knows her well enough to call.

    Things to tell yourself “Feeling lonely says I need connection, like anyone does.”

    Try this. This week, reach out to one person, even if it is only a short “thinking of you” message.

    Dig deeper: why we need each other

  2. Early bonds teach us what to expect.

    As children, we learn from the people who cared for us whether others will come when we need them. If help usually came, we tend to expect it. If it came sometimes, or rarely, we may learn to cling harder or to stop asking. These lessons are a starting point that later relationships can change. This is the idea of attachment, first described by John Bowlby (1969) and studied by Mary Ainsworth and colleagues (1978).

    A toddler at the park runs off to explore, runs back to check that his grandmother is still on the bench, and runs off again, braver each time because he knows where she is.

    You could say (to a child) “I’m right here. Go and look, and come back whenever you want.”

    This week. Think of one person who was a safe base for you, at any age, and what they did that helped.

    Dig deeper: what attachment is

  3. Patterns, not boxes.

    As adults, some of us worry a lot about being left, and reach out more when we feel unsure. Some of us pull back when things get close, and need more space. Many of us feel mostly secure, and most of us mix all three.

    These are patterns that can soften and change, especially in steady, kind relationships. Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver (1987) first described them in adults, and later work, such as R. Chris Fraley and colleagues (2015), suggests they work as sliding scales.

    For example, when things feel tense, Ronan wants to talk it through straight away while his wife Clara needs to go quiet first. He reads her quiet as a sign she is leaving, and she reads his questions as pressure. Once they see the pattern, they agree that Clara will say “I need an hour, and I’m coming back,” and that Ronan will wait.

    Words you could use “I’m not going anywhere. I just need some quiet. Let’s talk at eight.”

    One small step. Notice whether you reach out more or pull back when you feel unsure of someone, and leave judgement out of it.

    Dig deeper: anxious, avoidant and secure

  4. Trust is built in small moments.

    Trust rarely comes from big gestures. It grows from small, ordinary things done again and again, such as doing what you said, turning towards someone when they reach out, and being the same person on a hard day as on a good one.

    A new team member says she will send the figures by Thursday, and she does. The next week she warns early that something will be late. By the third month her manager trusts her completely, and he would struggle to name a single moment when it happened.

    Ways to say it “I said I’d do it by Friday. I’m running late, so here’s where it’s at.”

    Something to try. Keep one small promise today, and notice how it feels to be someone who does what they said.

    Dig deeper: how trust grows

    Professor Puddles

    Trust grows in small moments that repeat. This workpaper helps you notice the little rituals you already have, and keep them going.

    Workpaper WP-15: Keep your little rituals alive spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-15

  5. Feeling safe with someone calms the body.

    Being with someone we trust can settle our nervous system. In one study, holding a trusted partner’s hand calmed the brain’s response to threat (James Coan and colleagues, 2006). A calm voice, a hand to hold, or just someone nearby can make a hard moment easier to bear. It works both ways, so we can be that safe presence for others too, often without saying much.

    For example, after a panic attack, Kieran’s friend doesn’t try to fix anything. He sits next to him on the step outside the flats and says, “Take your time. I’m here,” and they stay there until Kieran’s breathing slows.

    Words to try “You don’t have to talk. I’ll just sit with you.” “Would company help right now, or quiet?”

    Try this. Notice who helps you feel calmer, and tell them simply that you always feel better after seeing them.

    Dig deeper: a safe haven

  6. Fitting in isn’t the same as belonging.

    Fitting in means changing yourself to be accepted. Belonging means being accepted as you are. Groups like teams, families, clubs and communities can offer both. Being left out of a group hurts even when the group doesn’t matter much to us, and real belonging grows where people feel safe to be themselves and to speak up.

    At a new job, Ola laughs at jokes she doesn’t find funny and hides the fact that she doesn’t drink, and she goes home exhausted every Friday. At her book club she says what she really thinks, and people ask her to say more.

    You could say (in a group) “I see it a bit differently. Is it okay if I say why?” “Has everyone had a chance to say something?”

    This week. Think of one place where you can be fully yourself, and how you might spend a little more time there.

    Dig deeper: groups, work and community

  7. When trust breaks, rebuilding takes time.

    When someone lets us down badly, trust doesn’t come back with one apology. It returns slowly, as words are matched by actions over time. The person who broke trust can own what happened and be patient. The person who was hurt can decide, at their own pace, whether and how much to trust again.

    For example, two adult sisters fall out after one shares a private story at a family dinner. The apology is a start, and what slowly rebuilds trust is the months afterwards, when the story never comes up again and the sister checks before sharing anything.

    Words you could use “I know sorry isn’t enough. I’ll show you, and you can take whatever time you need.”

    One small step. If you’ve broken someone’s trust, name one specific thing you’ll do differently, and do it.

    Dig deeper: rebuilding trust

  8. You can start building connection from wherever you are.

    If you feel alone right now, big friendships can feel out of reach, and belonging can start much smaller, with a chat with a neighbour, a regular class or an online group about something you love. Even small, light contact with people we barely know can lift our mood (Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn, 2014).

    After his divorce, Martin starts saying more than “thanks” to the man at the coffee stall, and a few weeks later they talk football every morning. It is a small friendship, and it makes Mondays easier.

    Ways to say it “I’m new around here. Is there anything you’d recommend?” “I loved what you said in the group. Would you like to get a coffee sometime?”

    Something to try. Have one small, friendly exchange with someone you don’t know well this week.

    Dig deeper: building connection

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: one small hello is a great start! Want an idea? There’s a tool that picks one for you.

    Tool: Stay close: one small idea spreadloveandacceptance.com/bonding

Monday, 8:10am

Kai’s phone buzzes with an apology. Her phone was in her coat all day at her nephew’s party, she loved the message, and is he free for coffee on Thursday? Kai thinks about how far last night’s story ran, and decides that next time a reply is slow he will send a light “No rush, just thinking of you” and leave it there.

If you’re a teenager

Ezra is sixteen when he sees a photo of his three closest friends at the cinema and finds out there is a group chat he isn’t in. It hurts like a punch, because being left out really does register a bit like pain. He drafts something sharp, deletes it and messages one friend instead, saying he’s a bit gutted not to be asked and asking whether he did something. It turns out they thought he would be at football. One of the friendships really is drifting, though, and that is allowed to hurt too.

Words to try “Bit gutted not to be asked. Did something happen?” “I’d like to come next time, even if I can’t always make it.” “I miss how we used to be. Are we okay?”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

In everyday life

When one partner texts a lot while apart and the other forgets, agreeing on one goodnight message can keep both feeling connected. A child who acts up at pick-up may simply be letting go of a long day with the safest person they know. A friend who always cancels may be overwhelmed, and “Is it easier if we do something short?” keeps the door open. At work, a team where mistakes can be admitted without blame builds trust faster than one where everyone hides them, and in a shared house, one simple weekly meal can turn people who share a kitchen into people who look out for each other.

zqaxunderstandingx5xbelongingxxonxyourxownqzOn your own: belonging with yourself

Belonging also includes how you treat yourself. If you are kind to yourself on a bad day, you carry a small safe base wherever you go, and people who learn to comfort themselves often find it easier to let others in, because they are less afraid of being let down. You are allowed to need people, and a lonely day is hard without being a forecast. On my own (spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own) has more for people living alone.

Common mix-ups

  • “Needing people means I’m needy.” Everyone needs connection, including the people who hide it well.
  • “My attachment style is fixed for life.” Patterns can change, especially through steady, kind relationships and reflection.
  • “Jealousy and checking up show how much they love me.” Reaching for reassurance is human, and so is asking for something out of care for the relationship. Controlling who someone sees, or checking their phone without agreement, is not love and is not an attachment style. See signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety).
  • “If I forgive, I have to trust again straight away.” Forgiving and trusting are different. Trust can return slowly, or not at all, and that’s your call.

If you want to help someone else with this

  • Be a steady presence. Reliability matters more than big gestures. Turn up when you said you would.
  • Take loneliness seriously. If someone says they feel alone, listen before you remind them how many friends they have.
  • Invite, and keep inviting. People who feel left out may say no a few times, and a warm invitation with no pressure still matters.
  • Make room in groups by noticing who is on the edge and asking their view.
  • Leave labels out. Telling someone they are “so avoidant” or “so clingy” rarely helps, while asking what would help often does.

You could say “I’m here, and I’m not going anywhere.” “We’re having a few people over on Friday. No pressure, but I’d love you to come.”

When to get more help

  • If loneliness has lasted a long time, or comes with low mood, hopelessness or thoughts of not wanting to be here, please talk to a doctor or a mental health service. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number or see Upset right now (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now).
  • If fear of being left, or of getting close, keeps hurting your relationships, a counsellor or therapist can help you understand where it comes from and how to change it.
  • If someone uses your need for them against you, by cutting you off from friends, checking where you are, or threatening to leave to get their way, that is not about attachment. Not safe at home? lists free, private help.
  • If trust was broken in a way that frightened you, you don’t owe anyone a second chance. Your safety comes first.

Reading on the website

Pick one small way to turn towards someone this week. Turning towards (spreadloveandacceptance.com/turning-toward), When one talks and one goes quiet (spreadloveandacceptance.com/pursue-withdraw) and How to apologise so it counts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/apology-languages) have more ideas.

Reading pages to read on the website

  • Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends): when a friendship drifts, and how to reach out.
  • The languages of connection (spreadloveandacceptance.com/languages-of-connection): the different ways people show care.
  • Complacency (spreadloveandacceptance.com/complacency): why good things fade, and how to keep them alive.
  • From the library: Attachment theory (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships) · Adult attachment (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships#adult-attachment) · Trust (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships#trust) · Bids for connection (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships#bids-for-connection) · Loneliness (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection) · Weak ties (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection#weak-ties) · Psychological safety (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/teams) · Masking (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/wiring)

6

Part Three · Chapter 6

Habits and change: why change is hard and how small steps work

Why it’s so hard to change, even when we really want to, and what actually helps: small steps, a kinder setup, patience with slips, and remembering that other people’s change belongs to them.

In this chapter

  1. Change is hard for good reasons
  2. Habits run on cues
  3. Start smaller than feels useful
  4. Change the setup, not just your willpower
  5. Being in two minds is normal
  6. Slips are part of change
  7. Change sticks when it fits who you want to be
  8. You can support change, but not force it
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Change is hard for good reasons. Habits save effort, so the old way is always the easy way.
  • A small step and a kind setup outlast willpower. Make the first step tiny and change what is around you.
  • Slips are part of change. A missed day tells you something about the plan and nothing about your character.
  • Other people’s change is theirs. You can support it, though you can’t force it.

Why the tools work. Three tools in other chapters rest on what this one explains.

  • One small step a week (the six-week program; Part One, Next, page 50) works because change that lasts starts smaller than feels useful, and an if-then plan does the deciding ahead of time.
  • The setup score and One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, page 91) change the setup instead of asking for more willpower, because habits follow cues and easy paths.
  • What keeps coming back? (Part Two, Chapter V, page 138) treats a repeat as information about the plan, because slips are a normal part of change.

Monday, 7:05am

The plan was a walk before work, and the trainers are by the door. Somehow the phone is in your hand instead, and at 7:40 you are still scrolling beside a cup of cold coffee. By evening a quiet voice is telling you that you never stick to anything, though what you actually ran into this morning was a habit with years of practice behind it.

  1. Change is hard for good reasons.

    Much of what we do each day runs on autopilot, which saves energy and is the reason habits exist at all. The downside is that the old way is always quicker and easier than the new one, so change asks your brain to do something effortful again and again until the new way becomes the easy one.

    For example, Jodie wants to stop snapping at her children in the morning rush, and she means it every night. Every morning the same rush brings the same snap, somewhere between the lost reading book and the cold toast, because the morning has worn a groove deeper than her good intentions.

    Things to tell yourself “This is hard because it’s a habit.” “Old grooves take time to fill in.”

    Try this. Pick one thing you would like to change and write down when it usually happens, where, and what is going on just before.

    Dig deeper: why change is hard

  2. Habits run on cues.

    Most habits have a trigger, such as a time, a place, a feeling, a person or the thing you have just done. The cue starts the routine, and some kind of reward, like relief, comfort or a little buzz, keeps it going. Once you know the cue, you can plan for it.

    A man notices that he reaches for snacks when he opens his laptop after dinner, whether he is hungry or not. Since the laptop is the cue, he starts making a pot of tea before he opens it.

    Things to tell yourself “What happened right before I did that?” “What was I getting from it?”

    This week. For three days, each time the habit happens, jot down the time, the place, the feeling and what you were doing just before.

    Dig deeper: cues and routines

  3. Start smaller than feels useful.

    Big goals are inspiring but easy to drop. Tiny steps feel almost silly, and they work because they are easy enough to do on a bad day. It helps to tie the new step to something you already do, as in “After I put the kettle on, I’ll…”, and to grow it only once it has stuck.

    For example, two housemates want a tidier kitchen. They have been promising each other a big weekly clean for months, so they agree instead that after dinner each of them wipes one surface. It takes two minutes, and by the second week the hob has stopped being a source of tension.

    You could say “Let’s start with something tiny, and see if it sticks.” “After I ..., I will ...”

    One small step. Shrink your change until it takes two minutes or less. Write it as “After I ___, I will ___.”

    Dig deeper: why small steps work

  4. Change the setup, not just your willpower.

    Willpower runs low when we are tired, hungry or stressed, while your surroundings stay the same all day. Make the new habit easier by putting it in sight or getting things ready the night before, and make the old one a little harder by moving it out of reach or adding a step. Small changes to your setup often do more than trying harder.

    A teenager wants to sleep better and has tried for weeks to stop scrolling in bed. Then he starts charging his phone in the kitchen overnight, and within a week he is asleep before midnight most nights.

    Words you could use (to yourself or a partner) “What could we change about the setup so this gets easier?”

    Something to try. Make one small change to your space today that makes the new habit easier or the old one harder.

    Dig deeper: shaping your setup

    Professor Puddles

    Changing the setup is often easier than changing a person. At home, that can be as simple as one owner for each job.

    Workpaper WP-03: One owner per job spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-03

  5. Being in two minds is normal.

    Part of you wants to change and part of you doesn’t, and the reluctant part usually has its reasons. The old habit may give comfort, save effort or protect you from something. Pushing harder against that part rarely works, while listening to it often does.

    For example, Asif wants to drink less, but he also loves Friday evenings in the pub with his team. When he asks himself what Friday gives him, the answer is friends, laughter and a way to unwind, so he keeps the Friday and switches to alcohol-free after the first pint.

    Thoughts you could try “What does the old habit give me?” “What would make the change worth it to me?”

    Try this. Write two lists, one of what you like about how things are and one of what you would like about changing. Both lists are allowed.

    Dig deeper: readiness and mixed feelings

  6. Slips are part of change.

    Nearly everyone who changes something slips back sometimes, and one slip doesn’t undo your progress. What often does the damage is the thought that follows, the “I’ve blown it, so why bother?” Treating yourself kindly after a slip makes it more likely that you will start again.

    After three calm weeks, a dad shouts at his son over homework. That night he sits on the end of the bed and says, “I shouted, and I’m sorry. I’m working on it.” The next evening they do the homework at the kitchen table with the radio on, and nobody raises their voice.

    Things to tell yourself “A slip is one moment out of many.” “What made today harder, and what can I plan for next time?”

    This week. Decide now what you will do after a slip, such as one kind sentence to yourself and one small step to start again.

    Dig deeper: slips and starting again

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: a slip is a stumble, not a fall. Shake it off and try the tiny step again tomorrow. A game for small kind acts makes practising more fun!

    Tool: Gentle games: the Re-check Drive (calm football) spreadloveandacceptance.com/recheck-drive

  7. Change sticks when it fits who you want to be.

    Change made only to please others, or out of shame, is hard to keep. Change that connects to what you care about, to the kind of person, parent, friend or colleague you want to be, has deeper roots, and each small action becomes a vote for that person.

    For example, a woman who keeps meaning to be better at keeping in touch starts thinking of herself as someone who shows up for her friends. Sending one voice note on a Sunday evening becomes part of who she is, and some weeks it turns into an hour on the phone.

    Things to tell yourself “Who am I becoming with this step?” “This matters to me because...”

    One small step. Finish this sentence for your change: “I want to do this because I care about...”

    Dig deeper: values and who you’re becoming

  8. You can support change, but not force it.

    It is natural to want the people we love to change, perhaps to drink less, tidy more or look after themselves better. Their change belongs to them, though, and pressure tends to make people dig in. It helps more to say clearly what you need, to ask what would help and to notice their small steps out loud.

    A coworker keeps missing deadlines. His teammate skips the lecture about being organised and asks what would make the handover easier, and the two of them set up a shared checklist that he now updates every Friday.

    Ways to say it “I can’t change this for you, but I’d love to help if you want me to.” “I noticed you did that this week. That really helped.”

    Something to try. Notice one small positive change someone else made this week, and tell them.

    Dig deeper: change with other people

Two weeks later, 7:05am

The trainers are still by the door, but the phone charges in the kitchen overnight now, and the plan has shrunk to shoes on and out to the end of the road. Some mornings that is all you manage. Most mornings it turns into a walk past the allotments and back. On the Thursday you miss, the voice starts up again, and you tell it that tomorrow you will get as far as the end of the road.

In everyday life

Take one couple who want to spend less time on their phones in the evening. Earlier attempts failed because each of them watched the other, so this time they agree on a basket by the door where both phones go at nine, with one exception for whoever is on call for an elderly parent. The first week is awkward, and on the Wednesday one of them sneaks a look at the football scores. By the third week the basket has become part of the furniture, and the evenings have a shape again, with a film, a crossword or an early night.

Big life changes, such as a move, a new baby or a new job, break old routines, which is disruptive and also a good moment to start new habits. If you have ADHD, make the cue impossible to miss, do the step the moment it appears and make the reward come straight away. Expect the novelty to wear off, and swap the method when it does instead of blaming yourself. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-6-change-in-depth).

On your own: a kind plan for change

If you are working on something alone, the ideas fit into one small plan. Choose one change, the one that would make the most difference or the one that feels most doable. Give it one cue, written as “After I ___, I will ___.” Make one tweak to your setup so it is easier to start, decide on the smallest version you could still do on a tired day, and write down one kind sentence to use after a slip. The self path (spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path) and Know yourself, next (page 50) walk through this step by step.

Common mix-ups

  • “If I really wanted it, I’d just do it.” Wanting is only the start, and habits, setup, tiredness and stress all play a part.
  • “It takes 21 days to form a habit.” There’s no magic number. In one study, led by Phillippa Lally (2010), it took about two months on average, with a very wide range.
  • “Being hard on myself will keep me on track.” Harshness tends to make people give up, while kindness makes it easier to try again.
  • “Routines mean being rigid.” For many people, especially autistic people, routines are what make life manageable. Change can respect that.

If you want to help someone else with this

Ask before you advise, perhaps with “Would ideas help, or would you rather just talk it through?”, and help them find their own reasons by asking what would be different for them if this changed. Practical help with the setup, such as a lift to the gym, a shared calendar or a quieter evening, often does more than encouragement alone. Notice small steps out loud, be kind about slips, and look after yourself as well, because you can care deeply and still set limits on what you will put up with.

Words to try “I’m on your side with this. What would help?” “You’ve done this three days running. That’s not nothing.”

When to get more help

  • If a habit is harming your health or life, such as drinking, drugs, gambling, eating or self-harm, please talk to a doctor or a specialist service. Needing help with this is common and nothing to be ashamed of.
  • If you can’t stop even though you’ve tried many times, professional support can make a real difference. It isn’t a sign of weakness.
  • If change feels impossible because you’re exhausted or low most days, that may be burnout or depression. A doctor or counsellor can help.
  • If someone is demanding you change in ways that frighten you, or punishing you when you don’t, that isn’t support. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.
  • If you’re overwhelmed right now, start with Upset right now (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now).

Workpapers, tools and reading on the website

Pick one tiny change and try it for a week. The 90-second daily check-in (spreadloveandacceptance.com/workpapers/wp-13-daily-check-in), the quick checks (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) and the self path can help you keep track.
