Part Three · Chapter 7

Self-worth, shame and self-compassion

Why your worth isn’t a score you keep earning, how shame differs from guilt, and why being kind to yourself makes it easier to grow.

In this chapter

  1. Your worth isn’t a score
  2. Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.”
  3. Shame makes you want to hide
  4. The inner critic is trying to protect you
  5. Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off
  6. Comparing yourself pulls your worth outside you
  7. You can own a mistake without drowning in it
  8. Worth is learned between people, and we can give it
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

Thursday, 11:20pm

You sent the wrong file to the whole team. Someone noticed, fixed it and said there were no worries. Hours later you are still awake and replaying it, and the voice in your head has moved on from the file. It is telling you that you are useless, and that everyone knows it now.

This chapter looks at how self-worth and shame work and then at what you can do about them, whether you are on your own, at home, with friends or at work. Nothing here is a diagnosis, so take what helps and leave the rest.

  1. Your worth isn’t a score.

    Many of us carry a quiet scoreboard on which we are worth something only when we are useful, liked, slim, busy, top of the class or never a bother. Psychologists call these “conditions of worth”, and the trouble with them is that any score can drop. If your worth rises and falls with each day’s results, every bad day feels like a verdict on you. A retired teacher may feel lost for months after she stops working, even though nothing is wrong, because for forty years being needed was how she knew she mattered.

    It can help to finish the line “I feel okay about myself when I…” three times. The endings you write are your scores, and for now it is enough to notice them. On a bad day, you might remind yourself that you matter on days when you achieve nothing at all.

    Dig deeper: worth that doesn’t have to be earned

  2. Guilt says “I did a bad thing.” Shame says “I am bad.”

    Guilt is about something you did, so it points towards fixing it by saying sorry or making it right. Shame is about who you are, which feels impossible to fix, and so it tends to make people hide, freeze, blame someone else or lash out. Research on the two feelings, such as June Tangney and Ronda Dearing’s (2002), suggests guilt is more likely to lead to repair. When a teenager breaks his mum’s favourite mug, guilt tells him to own up and offer to help pay for a new one. Shame tells him he ruins everything, and he wraps the pieces in newspaper and hides them at the bottom of the bin.

    Next time you feel bad about something, ask whether it is about what you did or about who you are. If it has become about who you are, try to turn it back into one thing you did, and then ask what would make that thing right.

    Dig deeper: guilt, shame and repair

  3. Shame makes you want to hide.

    Shame shows up in the body first, as a hot face, lowered eyes, a sinking stomach and the wish for the floor to swallow you. It can also come out sideways, as sudden anger or a cold, closed face, which is how a small comment can start a big fight. In a meeting a coworker asks, “Didn’t we already cover this?”, and his colleague snaps back at him. Later she realises the snap had nothing to do with the question, because what she felt was stupid in front of everyone.

    Learning your own shame signs helps. Next time you suddenly want to disappear or to snap, you can name it quietly to yourself as shame, and sometimes say out loud, “I think I felt embarrassed just then, and it came out sharp. Can I try again?”

    Dig deeper: how shame works in the body

  4. The inner critic is trying to protect you.

    That harsh inner voice usually started as protection. If you criticise yourself first, perhaps nobody else can hurt you, and if you are hard on yourself, perhaps you will never fail again. It meant well. A voice that only threatens keeps your body on alert, though, and it is tiring to live with. A young dad calls himself an idiot every time he forgets something for the baby, the same word his own father used about him, so the voice he hears is an old one that he borrowed long ago.

    Write down one thing your inner critic says often, and ask whether you would say it to a friend you love, and what you would say instead. Some people find it helps to answer the critic directly, with something like “Thanks for trying to protect me. I can take it from here.”

    Dig deeper: the critic and the soothing system

  5. Self-compassion isn’t letting yourself off.

    Self-compassion means treating yourself the way you would treat a good friend who is struggling. One well-known model has three parts, which are kindness in place of attack, remembering that everyone struggles, and noticing the pain without drowning in it. Studies, such as one by Juliana Breines and Serena Chen (2012), suggest that people who are kind to themselves after a failure are often more likely to try to improve. A woman who fails her driving test for the third time tells herself that this is hard, that lots of people need more goes, and that she will practise reversing round corners before the next one. Then she books another lesson.

    If it feels okay, put a hand on your chest or arm and say three lines slowly to yourself once today. “This is a hard moment.” “Other people feel this too.” “What do I need right now?”

    Dig deeper: what self-compassion is, and isn’t

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: speak to yourself the way you’d speak to a friend having a hard day, slowly and kindly. Writing it down first can help.

    Tool: Write it through spreadloveandacceptance.com/write-it-through

  6. Comparing yourself pulls your worth outside you.

    We all measure ourselves against others, because that is how people work out where they stand. Feeds full of other people’s best moments make that measuring unfair, and self-esteem that depends on being better than others goes up and down a great deal. Two old friends meet for dinner, one with a new house and the other renting a room. The renter spends the evening quietly ranking herself and misses the fact that her friend is lonely and had wanted to talk.

    When you notice a comparison today, try swapping it for a question about the other person, such as “How are you, really?” It also helps to remember that you are comparing your inside with their outside.

    Dig deeper: comparison and steady self-worth

  7. You can own a mistake without drowning in it.

    Owning a mistake is easier when it doesn’t mean you are worthless. A simple shape helps. Say what you did, say what it did to the other person, say what you will do now, and then stop, because beating yourself up proves nothing about how sorry you are. A housemate forgot to pay her share of the bill and the internet was cut off for the weekend. She tells the others, “I forgot to pay, and that left you without internet all weekend. I’ve paid it and set a reminder,” and that is the end of it.

    Think of one small thing you still feel bad about, write the three-part sentence, and decide whether to send it, say it or simply let it rest.

    Dig deeper: owning it, repairing it, letting it rest

    Professor Puddles

    Owning a mistake can be short and plain: what happened, that it was yours, what you’ll do. If it went wrong in a talk, Rewind the talk helps you find the words.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  8. Worth is learned between people, and we can give it.

    Children learn their worth from how they are treated, and adults go on learning it. How we talk to each other matters a great deal, because “you did a careless thing” leaves room to change and “you’re so careless” closes the door. Praise for effort and for who someone is, as well as for results, helps people feel they matter on bad days too. A team lead begins each project review by asking what the team learned instead of who got it wrong, and within a few months people are raising problems in week two instead of week ten.

    Today you could say one thing to someone that has nothing to do with their results, such as “I’m glad you’re here, whatever happened today” or “I’m glad I know you.”

    Dig deeper: how worth is given and learned

Your part, and only your part. You can’t control how other people judge you, or what you were taught about your worth growing up. You can control how you speak to yourself now, whether you repair what you can, and where you spend your time. Give your energy to people who treat you as someone who matters. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Friday, 9:15am

You write one line to the team, saying sorry for the mix-up with yesterday’s file and attaching the right one. When the old voice starts up, you answer it the way you would answer a friend. You made a mistake and you fixed it, which is what a decent colleague does. Nobody mentions the file again, and by lunchtime you have stopped thinking about it too.

In everyday life

Shame turns up in ordinary places. Between partners, “You forgot to call” can land as “You’re a terrible partner”, so the reply comes out as a defence instead of a sorry. A child told “You’re so naughty” hears something about who they are, while “That was a naughty thing to do” leaves them a way back. A friend who says yes to everything may be quietly burning out because saying no feels like risking being dropped. At work, someone may hide a small error for weeks because owning it feels like proof that they don’t belong there.

On your own: a kinder voice to keep

You don’t need anyone else to start this, only to notice how you talk to yourself and to practise one gentler sentence. Catch the critic’s favourite words, such as “always”, “useless”, “pathetic” and “should”, and swap one of them for a plain fact, so that “I’m hopeless” becomes “I was late twice this week.” On hard days, keep a short list of things you did well, or simply did, and let getting up count. You are allowed to be disappointed in what you did and still be on your own side.

Common mix-ups

  • “Self-compassion is self-pity.” Self-pity says “only me, poor me.” Self-compassion says “this is hard, and other people go through it too,” which connects you to others.
  • “If I’m kind to myself, I’ll get lazy.” Research suggests the opposite is more common, because fear of your own attack makes people avoid trying and hide mistakes.
  • “Self-worth means thinking I’m great.” It means you matter even on the days you are not great.

If you want to help someone else with this

Talk about what happened, never about what kind of person they are. Arguing with someone’s shame (“You’re not useless!”) can feel like being told they are wrong to feel it, so you might try “It sounds like you feel really low about it. I don’t see you that way.” Helping them find one small thing they can do gives the feeling somewhere to go. Kindness on ordinary days, when nothing has gone wrong, teaches worth best of all.

You could say “That sounds like it’s weighing on you. Want to work out one thing that would help?” “You don’t have to earn being cared about.”

When to get more help

Everyone feels shame and self-doubt sometimes. It’s worth talking to a doctor, counsellor or therapist if harsh thoughts about yourself are there most days, if they stop you working, eating, sleeping or seeing people, or if you feel you deserve to be hurt. Therapies such as compassion-focused therapy and cognitive behavioural therapy are built to help with exactly this.

If you are having thoughts of hurting yourself or not wanting to be here, please tell someone today. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.

If someone close to you keeps telling you you’re worthless, stupid or lucky to have them, that isn’t a self-esteem problem. It can be a way of controlling someone. Signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) and Not safe at home? have free, private help.

Part Three · Chapter 8

Loss, grief and big life changes

What grief is, why it comes in waves, how it shows up in the body, and how to carry a loss, or a big change, without having to “get over it.”

In this chapter

  1. Grief is love with nowhere to go
  2. Grief comes in waves, not neat stages
  3. Grief lives in the body, too
  4. Some losses nobody sees
  5. People grieve in different ways
  6. You don’t have to let go
  7. Big changes are losses too, even the good ones
  8. Most people find a way through, and support helps
  9. Losing a partner in later life
  10. In everyday life
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Grief is love with nowhere to go. It hurts because the person, place or life mattered.
  • It comes in waves. A good week followed by a bad day is part of grieving, and it doesn’t send you back to the start.
  • You don’t have to let go. Many people keep a bond with the person they lost, and that is healthy.
  • Most people find a way through. Support helps, and some losses need more help than friends can give.

Saturday, 9:05am

Six months on, you are doing fine, or so you tell people. Then in the supermarket you see the cereal your dad always bought, the one with the faded blue box, and you have to leave your trolley in the aisle and go and sit in the car. Nobody around you knows why.

This chapter is for anyone who has lost someone or something, whether a person, a pet, a marriage, a friendship, their health, a home, a job, a country or a future they had pictured. It looks at how grief works and then at what can help. There is no right way to grieve, and nothing here is a timetable.

  1. Grief is love with nowhere to go.

    Grief is what we feel when something we were attached to is gone, and it isn’t only for deaths. A divorce, a miscarriage, a diagnosis, a move, a friend who drifted away or children leaving home can all bring real grief. Its size usually matches the size of the bond, whatever other people think the loss ought to mean. A man may be surprised by how hard he takes his dog’s death while his friends tell him it was only a dog, yet that dog walked beside him every morning for twelve years, through two jobs and a divorce.

    It can help to say a loss out loud to yourself, especially one you have never called grief. “I’m grieving the friendship” or “I’m grieving the life we planned” is a small sentence that often brings some relief, because it gives the feeling a name and a reason.

    Dig deeper: what grief is, and what counts

  2. Grief comes in waves, not neat stages.

    You may have heard of five stages of grief, running from denial through anger, bargaining and depression to acceptance. They came from listening to people who were dying, and they were never meant as steps that everyone follows in order. Most people swing back and forth, spending some hours deep in the loss and some hours getting on with life, and that swing is healthy. A widow may feel guilty for enjoying lunch with her sister and then cry all evening, and both the lunch and the tears are part of grieving.

    Letting yourself have a small break from grief, such as a walk, a programme you like or a meal with a friend, takes nothing away from the person you lost. When a wave comes, it usually passes, even if it knocks you over first.

    Dig deeper: waves, and the swing between loss and life

  3. Grief lives in the body, too.

    Grief can bring tiredness, poor sleep, no appetite or extra appetite, aches, a tight chest, forgetfulness and a foggy head. Your brain is slowly learning that someone or something it expected to be there has gone, and that learning takes time and uses energy. A teacher whose mother has died keeps losing her keys and forgetting meetings, and she starts to worry that something is wrong with her memory. It is grief fog, and it eases as the months pass, though nobody can tell her exactly when.

    While it lasts, protect a few basics, such as one regular meal, a set bedtime and a short walk outside. It is fine to tell people at work or at home, “I’m grieving, so I’m slower than usual. Could you send me a reminder?”

    Dig deeper: the grieving body and brain

  4. Some losses nobody sees.

    Some losses are hard to explain to anyone else. Someone may still be alive but changed, through dementia, addiction or illness, or gone without having died, like an estranged parent or a missing relative. Other losses go unrecognised, such as the death of an ex-partner, a pregnancy loss or a friend you only ever knew online. A woman whose father has dementia still visits him every Sunday, but the dad who knew her is fading, and she is grieving someone who hasn’t died. Grief without a ceremony, or without anyone noticing, can feel very lonely.

    If a loss of yours had no ceremony, you can make a small one of your own by lighting a candle, writing a letter, planting something or visiting a place that mattered. You might also tell one person, “I’m grieving something people might not see as a loss. It is one for me.”

    Dig deeper: ambiguous and unrecognised grief

  5. People grieve in different ways.

    Some people grieve by talking and crying, and others by doing, whether that means fixing things, organising, working or building something. Neither way is more loving. Families often clash because one person thinks another isn’t grieving when they are grieving differently, and culture, faith, age and how your mind works all shape the way it comes out. After their son’s death, one parent wants to talk about him every evening while the other spends every weekend in the garage restoring his old bike. Each feels the other is getting it wrong, and each is grieving the same boy.

    A question can bridge the gap. “What has helped you most, even a little?” asked of someone who shares your loss, and listened to without correcting, often shows that the two of you want the same thing by different roads.

    Dig deeper: grieving styles and families

  6. You don’t have to let go.

    An older idea said that healthy grief meant moving on and cutting ties. Many grief researchers now see it differently. People often keep a bond with the person they lost, in memories, rituals, conversations in their head and values they carry forward, so the relationship changes shape without having to end. A teenager wears her grandfather’s watch to every exam. She doesn’t believe in luck, and she would find it hard to explain why the watch matters, except that it feels as if he is in the room.

    You might choose one way of keeping a bond, such as cooking their recipe, telling a story about them at a family meal or keeping one of their habits. Some people find it helps to ask, in a hard moment, what the person they lost would have said.

    Dig deeper: continuing bonds

  7. Big changes are losses too, even the good ones.

    A new baby, a promotion, retirement, moving country, a child starting school, coming out or getting well after a long illness can all bring grief for the old life. Change often has three parts, an ending, a confusing time in between and a new beginning, and the middle part is both the hardest and the easiest to rush. A couple moves to a new city for a job they both wanted. Six months in, one of them feels low and then guilty for feeling low, because this was the plan. What they also lost, though, was a circle of friends, a favourite café and a whole way of life.

    You can be glad about a change and still miss what came before. For one change you are going through, it may help to write down what ended, what still feels unclear and one small thing that is new and good.

    Dig deeper: endings, the in-between, beginnings

    Professor Puddles

    When a change is hard to talk about, writing can come first. This is a quiet place to put the words down, at your own pace, and to send them only if you want to.

    Tool: Write it through spreadloveandacceptance.com/write-it-through

  8. Most people find a way through, and support helps.

    Research suggests that, over time, many people find they can live with a loss and still feel joy, even though they never forget. Being with people who let you talk, or let you stay quiet, helps. For some people, though, grief stays at full strength for a long time and makes daily life very hard.

    Doctors call this prolonged grief. It means a strong longing for the person, or being taken over by the loss, most days, still going many months after the death (6 to 12 months or more, depending on the guideline) and getting in the way of life. It has nothing to do with weakness, and there is specific help for it. A year after his wife died, a man still can’t go into their bedroom or see his friends, and his doctor refers him to a grief counsellor. Things begin to move slowly, starting with one evening a week at his brother’s.

    On a good day, write down two people you could text on a hard one, and one place you could call if those people aren’t enough. If it has been a long time and nothing is easing, it is reasonable to say, “I think I need more help.”

    Dig deeper: resilience, support and stuck grief

Your part, and only your part. You can’t control the loss, how long grief lasts, or how other people react to it. You can control small things: eating something, resting, telling one person how you are, and saying no to what you can’t manage right now. That is enough for a hard season. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Saturday, 9:40am

You sit in the car for ten minutes and let the wave come. Then you go back in, find your trolley where you left it and put the cereal in. At home you text your sister that you saw Dad’s cereal and cried in the car park. She replies straight away that the same thing happened to her with his aftershave in a chemist’s, and asks whether you can call tonight.

zqaxunderstandingx8xlossxxlaterxlifeqzLosing a partner in later life

After a long marriage the loss is in everything, from the empty chair to the jobs that were always theirs, the paperwork done alone and the first birthday and anniversary without them. Do one small thing at a time, and let one drawer count as a day’s work. It is fine to ask someone to sit with you while you fill in the forms.

Your grown-up children have lost a parent while you have lost a partner, and you may grieve on different timetables. If they start checking on you every day, that comes from love and worry, not control. You can still say what helps: “I love that you ring. Could we make it two evenings a week, and I’ll ring you if I need you?”

Dig deeper: the first year, and grown-up children

In everyday life

After a miscarriage, one partner may want to talk while the other goes quiet, and each can end up worrying that the other doesn’t care. A child may laugh and play the day after a funeral and then cry at bedtime, and both belong to grief. A friend who stops calling after your diagnosis is often stuck for words more than cold, and colleagues who avoid the subject when someone returns after a death can leave that person feeling as if the loss has been erased. A whole community can grieve together too, when a town loses its library or its factory.

On your own: carrying it gently

Grief can be lonely even with people around you. When you are carrying it alone, it helps to give the day a small shape, with one meal, one walk and one person you message. Expect harder days around birthdays and anniversaries, and plan something gentle for them. Writing to the person you lost, or about what you lost, can help too, and nobody else ever needs to read it. Some days the only goal is to get to tonight, and that is allowed.

If someone close to you has died. Grief and later life (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief) goes further, with family after a loss, coming back to people, and a new chapter on your own. On a heavy night, the page called For a hard evening (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grief#hard-evening) may help.

If you want to help someone else with this

  • Show up, and keep showing up. Support often floods in for two weeks and then stops, so a text at three months, or on a birthday, can mean a great deal.
  • Offer something specific. “Can I drop off dinner on Thursday?” is easier to say yes to than “Let me know if you need anything.”
  • Say the name. Many grieving people find it a comfort to hear the name of the person they lost, and to hear a memory of them. If you are unsure, ask.
  • Leave out the explanations. “Everything happens for a reason” and “At least…” tend to hurt, while “I’m so sorry. I’m here” rarely does.
  • Comfort in, vent out. If you are upset too, lean on people further from the loss rather than on those closest to it.

You could say “I don’t know what to say, but I’m here.” “I was thinking about your mum today. I remember her laugh.” “I’m going to the shop. What can I bring you?”

When to get more help

Grief is not an illness. But it’s worth talking to a doctor or a grief counsellor if, after many months, the pain isn’t easing at all, you can’t manage daily life, you feel life has no meaning without the person, or you are drinking or using other things to get through. Many hospices, faith communities and charities offer free bereavement support, including for children.

If you are having thoughts of not wanting to be here, please tell someone today. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.

If a loss involved violence, or you are grieving a relationship you left because you weren’t safe, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has free, private help, including after you separate (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#after-separation).

Part Three · Chapter 9

Minds that work differently

How autistic, ADHD, sensory and learning differences work, why none of them is a character flaw, and how people with different minds can meet in the middle.

In this chapter

  1. Brains vary, like bodies do
  2. Autism is a different way of sensing and connecting
  3. ADHD is about steering attention, not lacking it
  4. Everyone has a sensory profile
  5. Learning differences aren’t about intelligence
  6. Masking costs energy
  7. Autistic burnout is more than being tired
  8. Meltdowns and shutdowns aren’t choices
  9. Stimming helps, so let it be
  10. Deep focus makes switching hard
  11. Deep interests are a source of joy and rest
  12. Meet in the middle, out loud
  13. Labels are tools, and they belong to the person
  14. Finding out later in life
  15. Getting things started and finished is a skill of its own
  16. When demands feel like a threat
  17. Not recognising faces isn’t rudeness
  18. Not speaking isn’t the same as having nothing to say
  19. Telling friends and dates is your choice
  20. Finding your people
  21. In everyday life
  22. Common mix-ups
  23. If you want to help someone else with this
  24. When to get more help
  25. Tools and reading on this site
  26. More for your situation

In short

  • Brains vary, like bodies do. A different mind is not a broken one, though differences can still be disabling in a world built for one kind of mind.
  • Nobody chooses overload. Meltdowns, shutdowns and burnout are what happens when a nervous system has had too much.
  • Less masking, room to stim, time for deep interests and real rest help a great deal.
  • Meet in the middle, out loud. Ask what helps, say what helps you, and use the words each person chooses.

Why the tools work. Two tools in other chapters rest on what this one explains.

  • The “How to talk to me” card (Part One, Now, page 35) works because different minds need different input, and saying things plainly is an adjustment that helps almost everyone.
  • One owner per job and the written job list (Part Two, Chapter II, page 91) move memory out of anyone’s head and onto paper, which helps ADHD and autistic minds most and everyone a little.

Monday, 8:15am

You ask him for the third time to just put his shoes on. Your son is lying on the hall floor with his hands over his ears, because the new socks feel wrong, and you are already late. To him the seam across his toes feels like sandpaper, and the alarm clock from the bedroom is still ringing in his head.

This chapter is for neurodivergent people, diagnosed or not, and for the people who live, work and learn with them. It explains how these minds work and then what helps. It can’t diagnose anyone, and only you get to choose the labels you use for yourself.

  1. Brains vary, like bodies do.

    People’s brains differ in how they take in the world, focus, move, read, remember and connect with others. “Neurodiversity” is the idea that this variety is natural. “Neurodivergent” describes people whose minds work differently from what is treated as typical. A different mind is not a broken one, and at the same time differences can be disabling, especially when the world is built for one kind of mind.

    For example, a man who struggled all through school finds out at forty that he is dyslexic. Mostly he feels relief, because for thirty years he had half believed the teachers who called him lazy.

    Thoughts you could try “Maybe this isn’t a flaw. Maybe it’s a difference that needs a different setup.”

    Try this. Think of one thing that is hard for you and easy for others, and ask whether the difference is effort or a different kind of brain.

    Dig deeper: neurodiversity and disability

  2. Autism is a different way of sensing and connecting.

    Autistic people often communicate more directly and literally, have deep and focused interests, feel senses more (or less) intensely, and find predictability calming. Autism doesn’t run along a single line from “mild” to “severe”, because each autistic person has their own mix of strengths and needs, which can change from day to day. Misunderstandings between autistic and non-autistic people usually run both ways.

    An autistic coworker mentions that her colleague’s slides have three typos. She means it as help, and he hears criticism, because they are using different rules for what kindness sounds like.

    You could say “I like it when people say exactly what they mean. You can be direct with me.” “Do you want my honest view, or just support right now?”

    This week. In one conversation today, say exactly what you mean without hints, and notice whether it makes things easier.

    Dig deeper: autism and the double empathy problem

  3. ADHD is about steering attention, not lacking it.

    People with ADHD often have plenty of attention but find it hard to point it where they choose. Boring tasks can feel impossible while interesting ones swallow hours, time can feel slippery, divided into “now” and “not now”, and feelings can come fast and big. It is a real difference in how the brain manages itself, and it has nothing to do with effort or care.

    For example, a woman with ADHD forgets her friend’s birthday and then spends six hours making her a handmade card with pressed flowers, because the forgetting and the focus come from the same brain.

    Words you could use “I care about this. My brain drops things. A reminder really helps, and it doesn’t annoy me.”

    One small step. Move one thing you keep forgetting out of your head and into the world, with an alarm, a note on the door or a basket by the exit.

    Dig deeper: ADHD, time and motivation

  4. Everyone has a sensory profile.

    We all take in sound, light, touch, smell, taste, movement and signals from inside the body. Some people feel these strongly and get overloaded by noise or scratchy clothes. Others need more input, such as movement, strong flavours or pressure. Overload is a body at its limit, which is very different from being fussy.

    Two housemates argue about the kitchen radio, because one finds silence eerie and the other finds the radio painful. They settle on the radio in the mornings and headphones in the evenings.

    Ways to say it “The noise in here is too much for me right now. Can we move somewhere quieter?”

    Something to try. Notice one sound, light or texture that drains you and one that calms you, and make one small change today.

    Dig deeper: senses, overload and needs

    Professor Puddles

    Knowing your own sensory profile is useful information, not a complaint. A one-page card lets you share what helps, in your own words.

    Tool: How you connect: how I like to be spoken to spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card

  5. Learning differences aren’t about intelligence.

    Dyslexia (reading and spelling), dyscalculia (numbers), dyspraxia (coordination and planning movement) and language disorders are specific differences, and none of them measures how clever someone is. Many people have a “spiky” profile, very strong in some areas and struggling in others, and the right tools, like audiobooks, spoken notes or extra time, can level the ground.

    For example, a teenager with dyspraxia is called clumsy on the football pitch, and in the same term he writes and directs the school play.

    Words to try “I learn better when I can listen than when I read. Could you send a voice note instead?”

    Try this. Ask someone you live or work with what the easiest way is for them to take in information, and then use it.

    Dig deeper: spiky profiles and learning tools

  6. Masking costs energy.

    Many neurodivergent people learn to hide their differences by copying others, forcing eye contact, holding back movements and rehearsing small talk. This is called masking. It can help someone get through a day, but it uses a lot of energy, and over years it can lead to exhaustion, anxiety and burnout.

    A student seems fine all day at college, then comes home and can’t speak for an hour while she recovers from a day of performing.

    You could say “I need some quiet time after work. It’s how I recharge, and I’m not upset with you.”

    This week. Notice one place where you can drop the mask a little, and one person you can be fully yourself with. Spend a bit more time there.

    Dig deeper: masking, energy and burnout

  7. Autistic burnout is more than being tired.

    Autistic burnout is a deep, long-lasting exhaustion. Working with autistic adults, Raymaker and colleagues (2020) described it as long-term exhaustion, loss of skills (like speech, planning or self-care) and lower tolerance of noise, light and other input. It comes from long stress without enough support, and often lasts months. Rest, fewer demands and less masking help. Pushing harder usually makes it worse.

    Words you could use “I’m in burnout. What I need for a while is fewer demands.” “I can’t do phone calls at the moment. Can we message instead?”

    One small step. If you think you might be in burnout, list three demands you could drop, delay or share for a month. If it goes on, or you feel hopeless, talk to a doctor.

    Dig deeper: burnout, rest and recovery

  8. Meltdowns and shutdowns aren’t choices.

    A meltdown is an involuntary loss of control when overwhelm gets too much, which can look like crying, shouting, running off or lashing out. A shutdown is the quiet version, going still, losing speech and not being able to respond. Neither is a tantrum. In interviews by Phung and colleagues (2021), autistic young people described meltdowns and shutdowns as separate experiences, both linked to overload. What helps is less of everything, so less noise, fewer words and fewer questions, with more space and safety. Talking can wait.

    Ways to say it (to someone else) “You’re safe. I’m right here. No need to talk.” (for yourself) “I’m overloaded. I need quiet for twenty minutes.”

    Something to try. On a calm day, agree a simple signal for “I’m overloaded” and a quiet place to go.

    Dig deeper: meltdowns and shutdowns

  9. Stimming helps, so let it be.

    Stimming means repeated movements or sounds, like rocking, flapping, tapping, humming, pacing or fiddling with something. Most people stim a little (think of a jiggling foot). For many autistic people it matters a lot. In interviews by Kapp and colleagues (2019), autistic adults described stimming as a way to cope with overwhelming emotions and sensations, and objected to efforts to stop harmless stimming. If it isn’t hurting anyone, it doesn’t need stopping.

    Words to try “Rocking helps me think. It doesn’t mean anything’s wrong.” “You don’t need to stop. It’s fine with me.”

    Try this. Notice what your own hands or body do when you’re stressed, focused or happy. That’s your stim.

    Dig deeper: stimming

  10. Deep focus makes switching hard.

    Some minds, often autistic and ADHD ones, focus deeply on one thing at a time. That focus can be a gift, bringing real expertise, flow and joy. It also makes switching tasks hard, so being interrupted can feel like being pulled out of water, and warnings before a change help a lot.

    For example, a dad calls his daughter to dinner three times and gets more frustrated each time. The next evening he gives her a ten-minute warning and then a five-minute one, and she comes to the table still talking about the castle she has been building.

    You could say “Dinner is in ten minutes. I’ll come and get you at five to.” “Can you give me a warning before we switch?”

    This week. Before you interrupt someone who is focused, give them a heads-up and a time, and see whether it goes more smoothly.

    Dig deeper: monotropism, flow and transitions

  11. Deep interests are a source of joy and rest.

    Many autistic people have deep, intense interests, often called special interests. The theory of monotropism (Murray, Lesser and Lawson, 2005) describes autistic attention as pulled strongly into a few things at a time. In a survey of autistic adults by Grove and colleagues (2018), people who were more motivated by and engaged with their special interests reported higher wellbeing, though very intense engagement went with lower wellbeing.

    Words you could use “Can I tell you about this for five minutes? It’s how I unwind.” “Tell me more. What’s the best bit?”

    One small step. Ask someone about their favourite subject, and let them talk for five minutes without steering.

    Dig deeper: special interests and wellbeing

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: this site can change to fit your mind too, with bigger text, calmer pages and fewer surprises. Ooh, try it!

    Tool: Read your way spreadloveandacceptance.com/how-you-take-things-in

  12. Meet in the middle, out loud.

    When two kinds of mind live or work together, neither should have to do all the adjusting. Clear, explicit words help everyone, so say what you mean, give times, write things down and ask what helps. Changes made for one person, like quiet spaces, written agendas or flexible hours, often help many others too.

    A team starts sending meeting agendas a day early for one autistic colleague, and within a month most of the team are saying the meetings have become shorter.

    Ways to say it “What would make this easier for you?” “Here’s what helps me. What helps you?”

    Something to try. Swap one “how I work best” fact with someone today, telling them one thing that helps you and asking for one that helps them.

    Dig deeper: adjustments that help everyone

  13. Labels are tools, and they belong to the person.

    A diagnosis can bring understanding, support and community. Some people find their way to a label through self-discovery first. Many autistic adults prefer “autistic person”; others prefer “person with autism.” The kindest rule is to ask and to use the words the person chooses, and never to try to diagnose someone else, especially in an argument.

    For example, during a row, a man tells his partner, “You’re so autistic.” It lands as an insult and ends the conversation. The next morning he apologises and asks what his partner actually needs from him.

    Words to try “How do you like to describe yourself?” “I’m wondering if I might be neurodivergent. I’d like to find out more.”

    Try this. If you have wondered about yourself, write down what you have noticed and decide one small next step, such as reading, talking to someone or asking a doctor.

    Dig deeper: diagnosis, identity and words

  14. Finding out later in life.

    More and more adults are finding out they are autistic, or have ADHD, in their thirties, fifties or seventies. Many were missed as children, especially women. In interviews by Leedham and colleagues (2020), women diagnosed at forty or older described how exhausting it had been to go so long without an explanation, and how much the diagnosis changed how they understood their lives. Relief, grief and joy can all come together.

    You could say “I’ve just found out I’m autistic. I’m still working out what it means.” “That explains so much about my life.”

    This week. If you’ve found out later in life, look for one autistic-led group, book or online space, and give yourself time to make sense of it.

    Dig deeper: diagnosis later in life

  15. Getting things started and finished is a skill of its own.

    Planning, starting, switching, remembering what you were doing and keeping track of time are called executive function. Many autistic and ADHD people find some of these harder, on some days more than others. A review of 235 studies by Demetriou and colleagues (2018) found differences in executive function in autism on average, with a lot of variation between people. The brain’s self-management system is working differently, and laziness has nothing to do with it, so it often helps to move the managing out of your head and into the world.

    A woman can write a brilliant report but can’t get herself to post a parcel. Once the parcel sits by the front door with a sticky note and a phone alarm, it goes on Tuesday.

    Words you could use “Could you send me that as a list? Spoken steps fall out of my head.” “I’m not ignoring it. Starting is the hard bit for me.”

    One small step. Pick one task that keeps not happening and make the first step tiny and visible, with a note, an alarm or the thing left where you will trip over it. See routines that help (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids) and Wired differently (spreadloveandacceptance.com/wired-differently).

    Dig deeper: executive function in daily life

  16. When demands feel like a threat.

    Some people, often autistic, feel strong anxiety when asked or expected to do things, even things they want to do. Avoiding the demand can look like refusing, joking, distracting or a meltdown. The profile was first described as “pathological demand avoidance,” or PDA, by Newson and colleagues (2003).

    It is not in the main diagnostic manuals, and researchers disagree about it. A review by Kildahl and colleagues (2021) found the evidence limited and mostly based on parent reports. Many people who identify with it prefer the phrase “persistent drive for autonomy.” Whatever it is called, what helps tends to be the same, which is less pressure, more choice and requests that feel like invitations.

    For example, a boy who refuses “Put your coat on now” happily puts it on when his dad says, “It’s cold out. Coat or jumper, your choice.”

    Ways to say it “I wonder if we could…” “No rush. Which would you rather?” (for yourself) “Being told makes it harder. Can I choose when?”

    Something to try. Turn one daily instruction into a choice or an invitation this week, and see what changes.

    Dig deeper: demand avoidance, carefully

  17. Not recognising faces isn’t rudeness.

    Prosopagnosia, or face blindness, means finding it hard to recognise people’s faces, sometimes even close friends out of context. It can be something you’re born with, and it often runs in families (NHS). Many autistic people also find remembering faces harder, as a review by Weigelt and colleagues (2012) found. People who don’t recognise you may be relying on voices, hair, clothes or where they usually see you.

    A man walks past his neighbour in the supermarket without a word, and she feels snubbed. When he explains later that he didn’t recognise her without her dog, she starts saying hello first, with her name.

    Words to try “I’m bad with faces, so please say who you are when you say hi.” (to someone else) “Hi, it’s Jo from next door.”

    Try this. If faces are hard for you, tell one or two people you see often. If not, try saying your name when you greet someone out of context.

    Dig deeper: face blindness

  18. Not speaking isn’t the same as having nothing to say.

    Some autistic people speak rarely, sometimes, or not at all, and some lose speech when stressed. Many communicate through AAC (augmentative and alternative communication), which can mean typing, letter boards, picture cards, apps or sign. Using AAC doesn’t stop speech developing, and a review by Millar, Light and Schlosser (2006) found it did not hold speech back, and may help it. The safest starting point is to presume competence, which means assuming the person understands and has something to say, and giving them the time and tools to say it.

    For example, at a family meal, a non-speaking teenager types on her tablet. Her uncle used to talk about her in front of her, and now he waits, reads her reply and answers her directly.

    You could say “Take your time. I’ll wait.” “Would you rather type or point?” (for yourself) “I can’t talk right now. I can type.”

    This week. Talk to the person directly, and wait longer than feels natural for an answer.

    Dig deeper: non-speaking people and AAC

  19. Telling friends and dates is your choice.

    Whether to tell someone you’re autistic or ADHD, and when, is up to you. Telling can bring understanding. In a study by Sasson and Morrison (2019), people formed better first impressions of autistic adults when they knew they were autistic, especially if they knew more about autism.

    But people don’t always respond well, and interviews by Au-Yeung and colleagues (2025) describe autistic adults weighing hope for support against fear of not being believed. Many people share a little at a time, starting with what helps before any label.

    On a second date, a woman says, “I’m autistic, so I’m pretty direct, and I’d rather walk than sit in a loud bar.” Her date admits that he hates loud bars too, and they walk along the canal instead.

    Words you could use “I’m autistic. For me that means…” “I won’t always pick up hints, so please just tell me.” (if someone shares with you) “Thanks for telling me. What helps?”

    One small step. Write one sentence about what helps you, without a label, and practise it. You can add the label later if and when you want to.

    Dig deeper: disclosure in friendships and dating

  20. Finding your people.

    Many autistic people describe finding other autistic people as a turning point, because at last they don’t have to translate, explain or mask. Research backs this up. Cooper, Smith and Russell (2017) found that autistic people who felt more connected to other autistic people had higher self-esteem, and through that, less anxiety and depression. Being autistic can be an identity and a community as well as a diagnosis.

    For example, after a late diagnosis, a man joins an online group for autistic adults who love old maps, and for the first time in years a long conversation leaves him with energy to spare.

    Things to tell yourself “There are people who work like me.” “I can belong somewhere without masking.”

    Something to try. Look for one autistic-led group, book, podcast or online space about something you love.

    Dig deeper: autistic community and identity

Your part, and only your part. You can’t change how your brain, or anyone else’s, is wired. You can learn how yours works, say what helps, and ask others what helps them. Meeting in the middle means both people move a little. If you’re always the one adjusting, it’s fair to say so. More in Part One: who you are today (page 35)

Monday, 8:30am

You stop asking and sit on the hall floor next to him. “Socks feel wrong?” He nods. You switch off the alarm clock still beeping in the bedroom and fetch the old seamless pair, and two minutes later his shoes are on. You are ten minutes late, nobody has shouted, and that evening you order three more pairs of seamless socks and let him choose the colours.

In everyday life

On your own

Knowing how your mind works helps you build a life that fits it and spot burnout early (see Get to know your wiring, spreadloveandacceptance.com/self-path). Partners can swap “how I work best” notes about plans, messages, touch and time alone. With children, behaviour often has a sensory or overload reason, so “What’s too much right now?” is worth asking before “Why are you doing this?” A friend who cancels at the last minute may simply be out of energy, and offering an easier option, like a walk or a message, keeps the door open. At work, written agendas, clear deadlines and quiet spaces help many people beyond the neurodivergent ones.

  • If you have ADHD and share a home. Make the chore tools lighter. Log three days, not seven, with a tally on the fridge. Own a few jobs completely, each with a labelled alarm, instead of helping a bit with everything. Forgetting is a setup problem to fix together. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-9-minds-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

  • “Everyone’s a bit autistic.” Everyone shares some traits, but autism is a whole pattern, present across life, and the phrase can make real needs sound small.
  • “ADHD just means you can’t sit still.” Many people with ADHD, especially girls and women, are mostly inattentive or restless on the inside.
  • “They seem fine to me.” Masking can hide a lot, and seeming fine can cost someone the rest of their evening.
  • “Adjustments are special treatment.” They remove barriers so people can do what is expected, in the way glasses do.
  • “Autistic people lack empathy.” Many feel others’ feelings strongly, and differences in how empathy is shown run both ways.

If you want to help someone else with this

  • Believe them about what’s hard, what hurts and what helps, even if it’s different for you.
  • Be clear. Say what you mean, give times, and write down anything important.
  • Ask what helps. Every neurodivergent person is different, and their answer will be better than any list.
  • Protect their energy. Quiet time, warnings before changes and a way out of loud places matter more than they look.
  • Enjoy their interests. Listening to someone talk about what they love is one of the warmest things you can do.

Ways to say it “Is there anything about this place, or this plan, that would make it hard for you?” “You don’t have to explain. Just tell me what you need.”

When to get more help

If you wonder whether a difference is part of ongoing difficulties at school, work or home, for you or someone you care for, a doctor, school support staff or a psychologist can talk you through an assessment. Waiting lists can be long, so start early and write down what you notice.

Burnout, depression and anxiety are more common among neurodivergent people, often because of the stress of living in a world that doesn’t fit. If you’re exhausted most days, losing skills you used to have, or feeling hopeless, please talk to a doctor. If you are having thoughts of hurting yourself, please tell someone today.

In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines.

A difference never excuses harm, and it never makes someone deserve harm. If someone uses your differences to control or belittle you, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) has free, private help.

10

Part Three · Chapter 10

Values, meaning and a good life: what philosophy offers everyday life

What matters to you, how to find it, what to do when two good things pull against each other, and what a few very old ideas can offer an ordinary, busy week.

In this chapter

  1. Values are directions, not finish lines
  2. Your strong feelings point to what you value
  3. Two good things can pull in different directions
  4. Put your effort where it can land
  5. A good life is more than a good mood
  6. Meaning comes from ordinary places
  7. Different values aren’t wrong values
  8. Values live in small, everyday acts
  9. In everyday life
  10. If you want to help someone else with this
  11. When to get more help
  12. Tools and reading on this site
  13. More for your situation

In short

  • Values are directions you keep turning towards. You never finish being kind, and that is why values still work on days when goals fall apart.
  • Strong feelings point to what you value. Anger often guards fairness, and hurt often guards closeness.
  • Meaning comes from ordinary places. People, care and everyday work give most of us most of our meaning.
  • Values live in small acts. One small thing this week, done because it matters, counts.

Sunday, 9pm

The week ahead is full, and none of it feels like yours. You aren’t sad exactly. You just can’t remember the last time you did something because it mattered to you, rather than because it was next on the list.

This chapter is about values, the things you care about and the direction you want your life to face, and about what makes a life feel worth living. It borrows from psychology and from philosophy, which has been asking how we should live for more than two thousand years. You don’t need to have read any of it, and everything here is in plain words.

  1. Values are directions, not finish lines.

    A goal is something you can tick off, such as running a 5k, painting the hall or passing a test. A value is a direction you keep walking in, such as looking after your health, making your home feel cared for or being a fair friend. Nobody ever finishes being kind, which is exactly why a value still works on a day when a goal falls apart.

    Bethan planned to go to the gym three times this week and went once, and on Thursday evening she felt like a failure. When she asked herself what the gym was for, the answer was looking after her body so that she had energy for her children. On Friday she walked for twenty minutes at lunchtime, round the park behind the office, and it counted. If you have a goal that has stalled, try asking “what is this for?” three times in a row, and write down where you end up.

    Dig deeper: goals and values

  2. Your strong feelings point to what you value.

    You don’t have to invent your values from nothing, because they show up in your strongest reactions. Anger often means that something you care about has been stepped on, envy can point to something you want for yourself, and sadness often shows what you love. Sacha is furious when a colleague takes credit for the team’s work. Under the anger is a value, which is fairness and seeing people’s effort, and once he names it he can raise fairness at the next team meeting instead of seething at one person for a week. He might say, “I think I’m upset because fairness really matters to me, more than winning this one.”

    Think of the last time you felt strongly, in a good way or a bad one, and finish the sentence “That mattered to me because I care about…”

    Dig deeper: finding your values

  3. Two good things can pull in different directions.

    Most hard choices are between two good things, such as honesty and kindness, freedom and safety, or family and rest. Feeling torn usually means you care about more than one thing, and even when you choose well it is normal to feel a little sad about the side you didn’t choose. A mum cares about being honest and about protecting her eight-year-old. When the family dog is very ill, she finds a way to honour both and tells the truth gently, in words a child can hold. “Biscuit is very poorly. The vet is helping, and we’ll look after him together.”

    If you feel stuck on a choice, write down the good thing on each side. It often helps to ask whether you can honour some of both, even if you can’t have all of either.

    Dig deeper: when values clash

  4. Put your effort where it can land.

    About two thousand years ago, a teacher called Epictetus, who had been born into slavery, taught that some things are up to us and some aren’t. Your own choices, effort and treatment of other people are up to you, while other people’s choices, the weather and the past are not. Worry tends to collect in the second pile, and values do their work in the first. Ingrid wants her partner to enjoy Christmas with her family, and she can’t make him enjoy it. She can plan a shorter visit, include a walk on Boxing Day that he will like and be warm herself, and that is her part.

    One way to try this is to write a worry in two columns, the parts that are up to you and the parts that aren’t, then pick one small thing from the first column and do it.

    Dig deeper: what is up to us

  5. A good life is more than a good mood.

    Feeling good matters. Many thinkers, from the Greek philosopher Aristotle to psychologists today, also describe a second kind of wellbeing, which comes from growing, using your strengths, being a good friend and doing things that matter even when they are hard. Aristotle called it flourishing, and he thought we build it the way we build any skill, by practice, a little at a time. Jade spent a month helping a friend move out of a damp, unhappy flat. It was tiring and not much fun, and when she looks back on her year she counts it among the best months of it.

    Tonight you might write down one thing that felt good today and one that felt worthwhile, and notice whether they turn out to be the same thing.

    Dig deeper: happiness and flourishing

    Professor Puddles

    If you enjoy big questions, try putting philosophy next to psychology and see what they share. It’s one of my favourite rainy-day games.

    Tool: Learn by doing: connect two fields of study spreadloveandacceptance.com/polymath

  6. Meaning comes from ordinary places.

    Researchers who study meaning often describe three parts to it. Your life makes some sense to you, you are heading somewhere, and your life matters to someone. Most meaning comes from people, from work done with care and from small roles that others count on, far more than from big moments. Walter has lived alone since his wife died, and for a long time his days went quiet. Now he reads to children at the library one morning a week, which gives him a reason to iron a shirt on Tuesday nights and a small group of people who notice when he isn’t there.

    Try listing three roles you play, big or small, such as neighbour, sister or the one who waters the office plants, and next to each one write who it matters to.

    Dig deeper: where meaning comes from

  7. Different values aren’t wrong values.

    Two people can share a home, a family or a team and still put the same good things in a different order, with one putting safety first and another adventure. The philosopher Isaiah Berlin argued that there are many real goods in life and that they can’t all be ranked on one scale, which leaves room to disagree without either person being bad. Jasper values a calm, tidy home, and his housemate Darnell values an open door and friends dropping by. For months each privately thought of the other as messy or uptight. Once they named what each of them cared about, they could make a plan, and Friday nights became open house while Sundays stayed quiet.

    In your next disagreement, it may help to ask, “What matters to you about this?”, and to listen for the value underneath the position.

    Dig deeper: living with different values

  8. Values live in small, everyday acts.

    A good life is built mostly from small things done again and again, such as how you greet people, whether you keep small promises and how you talk about someone who isn’t in the room. The Chinese teacher Confucius taught that small, everyday courtesies shape who we become, and later thinkers who wrote about care said that being good starts with paying attention to the person in front of you. At the supermarket an older man is struggling with the card machine, and the queue behind him is growing. You wait without sighing and tell him there’s no rush, which costs you forty seconds.

    Pick one value, choose one tiny act that shows it, and do it each day this week. When you drift, you can simply turn back without punishing yourself.

    Dig deeper: everyday ethics

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: a value can be as small as a cup of tea made just the way someone likes it. A “What feels like care” card helps you learn what feels like care to each of you.

    Tool: How you connect: what feels like care spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages

Your part, and only your part. You can choose your direction, notice when you drift, and turn back without shame. You can’t choose other people’s values for them, and you don’t have to adopt theirs to love them. You can share what matters to you, listen to what matters to them, and look for the places where your directions overlap.

Sunday, 9:20pm

You write three words on the back of an envelope, people, health and making things, and under each one a small thing for this week. Call Gran, walk on Wednesday, finish the shelf. The week is still full, and you prop the envelope against the kettle where you will see it in the morning.

In everyday life

Partners may rank the same values differently, such as security and adventure, and it helps to say what each of you is protecting before you argue about the plan. Two generations of a family can both value family and mean quite different things by it, from living close by to being free to go, so it is worth asking what the word means to each of you. When a job keeps asking you to act against a value, the strain often shows up as tiredness or cynicism, and naming the clash is a first step. A club, a faith group or volunteering can give you a place to act on a value alongside other people.

If you want to help someone else with this

Asking “What matters most to you about this?” helps more than telling someone what they ought to care about. People often see their values for the first time in someone else’s words, so it can help to notice them out loud, as in “You stayed late to help your friend. Loyalty really matters to you, doesn’t it?” With children, naming the value when you see it teaches more than a lecture. Try not to use values as a weapon, because “I thought you valued family” lands as a guilt trip. You can disagree with someone’s choice and still see the good thing they were reaching for.

You could say “What would a good outcome look like to you?” “What do you want to be able to say about how you handled this, a year from now?”

When to get more help

Feeling a bit lost or flat for a while is part of being human. But some signs mean it’s worth talking to someone trained:

  • Life has felt empty or pointless for more than two weeks, and things you used to enjoy don’t reach you. That can be depression, which is common and treatable. A doctor or counsellor is a good first step.
  • You have thoughts of not wanting to be alive. Please talk to someone today. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines. If you are in danger now, call your local emergency number.
  • Someone in your life is pushing you to give up what matters to you, cutting you off from friends, or making you afraid to disagree. That’s about control, not values. The page When it’s more than a rough patch (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) can help you think it through.

Some therapies, such as acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), work directly with values. A counsellor can help you find yours when everything feels foggy.

A limit to keep in mind: This chapter shares ideas to think with, not answers to follow. Your values are yours to find, and it’s fine if they change as your life does.
