Part Three · Chapter 11

Healing after hurt: repair, forgiveness, and when to get help

How hurt heals, why it lingers, how small breaks get mended, what a real apology sounds like, what forgiveness is and isn’t, and when it’s time to get more help.

In this chapter

  1. Hurt is real, and healing takes time
  2. Every close relationship has breaks. Repair is what counts
  3. Telling someone they hurt you
  4. A real apology names it, owns it, and mends it
  5. Forgiveness isn’t forgetting, excusing or going back
  6. You can heal even if they never say sorry
  7. Trust comes back in small, kept promises
  8. Going back is a choice. Safety comes first
  9. Look after the hurt part of you
  10. In everyday life
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Hurt is real, and healing takes time. Replaying a hurt says more about how much it mattered than about any weakness in you.
  • Repair is what counts. Every close relationship has breaks, and a real apology names what happened, owns it and offers to mend it.
  • Forgiving and going back are separate choices. You can forgive without forgetting, excusing or letting someone back in.
  • Safety comes first. You can heal even if they never say sorry, and you never owe anyone a risk to your safety.

Thursday, 2am

It was one sentence, three weeks ago, and they have probably forgotten it. You haven’t. It plays again word for word, along with all the things you could have said back, and you are tired of carrying it without knowing how to put it down.

Everyone gets hurt, and everyone hurts other people, mostly without meaning to. This chapter looks at how hurt works, how relationships mend and how you can heal, with or without the other person, for small hurts and bigger ones. If someone is hurting you on purpose, or you feel afraid, start with safety first: Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety)

  1. Hurt is real, and healing takes time.

    Being hurt by someone shows that something mattered, whether the person, your trust or your sense of being respected. The mind replays hurts because it is trying to understand them and keep you safe. Healing rarely runs in a straight line, and the feeling can come back on an anniversary or when something reminds you, without meaning you have failed.

    Months after a friend said something cruel at a party, Kwesi feels a jolt when the song that was playing comes on the radio. He tells himself it is an old bruise being pressed, and turns the volume down.

    Thoughts you could try “This hurts because it mattered.” “A feeling coming back doesn’t mean I’m back at the start.”

    Try this. When a hurt replays, notice it, name it (“there’s that memory again”), and gently bring your attention to something in the room you can see or touch.

    Dig deeper: why hurt lingers

  2. Every close relationship has breaks. Repair is what counts.

    No relationship is smooth all the time, and people snap, forget, misread and let each other down. Research on parents and babies, on couples and on therapy points the same way. Breaks are normal, and what matters most is whether they get mended. A small repair, made soon, often leaves a relationship feeling safer than before.

    For example, a dad snaps at his son for spilling juice. Twenty minutes later he sits down next to him and says, “I was grumpy and I shouted. That wasn’t fair. Spills happen. Want to help me make a new one?”

    You could say “Can I have a do-over? That came out badly.” “I didn’t like how I spoke to you earlier. I’m sorry.”

    This week. Think of a small break this week, with anyone. Go back and repair it with one sentence.

    Dig deeper: breaks and repair

  3. Telling someone they hurt you.

    People can’t mend what they don’t know about. Saying “that hurt” is a risk, but it gives the relationship a chance, and it works best when you describe what happened and how it felt, leaving out what kind of person they are. Pick a calm moment, well away from the middle of an argument.

    Amara says to her friend, “When you told the group about my breakup before I was ready, I felt exposed. I’d like to be the one who shares my news.” She leaves the word “gossip” out of it entirely and sticks to what happened and what she needs.

    Words you could use “When… happened, I felt… What I’d like is…” “I’m telling you because I want us to be okay.”

    One small step. Before you say it, write it in three short lines, covering what happened, how you felt and what you would like.

    Dig deeper: saying “that hurt”

  4. A real apology names it, owns it, and mends it.

    “Sorry if you were upset” doesn’t heal much. A real apology says what you did, takes responsibility without excuses, shows you understand how it affected the other person, and offers to put it right or do things differently. Research, such as a study led by Roy Lewicki (2016), suggests owning it and offering repair are the parts that matter most.

    For example, Leila presented a shared idea in a meeting as if it were hers. The next day she tells her colleague, “I presented our idea as mine. That wasn’t fair to you. I’ll email the team today and say it was joint work.”

    Ways to say it “I did… That was my doing. I can see it left you feeling… Here’s what I’ll do.”

    Something to try. Next time you say sorry, check it covers what you did, that it was yours, how it affected them and what you will do now. Apology languages (spreadloveandacceptance.com/apology-languages) has more.

    Dig deeper: what makes an apology work

    Professor Puddles

    An apology lands best when it’s plain: what happened, that it was yours, and what you’ll do now. Rewind the talk can help you find those words.

    Tool: Rewind the talk spreadloveandacceptance.com/carrier-wave-decoder

  5. Forgiveness isn’t forgetting, excusing or going back.

    Forgiveness is usually described as letting go of resentment and the wish to get even, and it happens inside you. Forgiving someone doesn’t mean saying that what happened was okay, or forgetting it, or trusting the person again, or keeping them in your life. It is a choice, often a slow one, and you never owe it on someone else’s timetable.

    Danielle forgave her father for missing much of her childhood. She still keeps his visits short, and she still won’t leave her children alone with him when he has been drinking, and for her the forgiving and the protecting sit together without strain.

    Things to tell yourself “I can let go of wanting to get even, and still keep my limits.” “I don’t have to forgive today. I can just stop feeding the anger today.”

    Try this. Write down what forgiving someone would mean to you, and what it would not mean. Seeing the difference can make it feel possible, or show you that you aren’t ready, which is fine too.

    Dig deeper: what forgiveness is

  6. You can heal even if they never say sorry.

    Waiting for an apology that never comes can keep you stuck, because the person may be gone, unwilling or unable to understand. Your healing doesn’t have to depend on them. You can make sense of what happened, tell your story to someone safe and decide what it means for you now.

    After a hard breakup, Martha writes a letter she never sends, covering what hurt, what she had hoped for and what she is taking with her. She folds it into the back of a notebook, and over the following weeks she finds she reaches for it less often.

    Things to tell yourself “I don’t need them to understand for my healing to count.”

    This week. Write about the hurt for fifteen minutes, three or four days in a row. Write about the facts and your feelings. If it ever makes you feel much worse, stop, and talk to someone instead.

    Dig deeper: healing on your own

  7. Trust comes back in small, kept promises.

    After trust is broken, one big apology rarely rebuilds it. Trust grows back slowly, in many small moments where someone does what they said they would do. If you broke trust, being patient and consistent matters more than a grand gesture, and if you were let down, it is fair to watch what someone does as well as what they say.

    For example, Declan hid a credit card debt from his partner. After it came out, he offered to share his bank statements each month, without being asked. After a year of small, steady openness, his partner says she can breathe again.

    Words to try “I know my words aren’t enough. I want to show you, over time.” “I need to see it for a while before I can feel it.”

    One small step. If you’re rebuilding trust, choose one small promise you can keep every week, and keep it.

    Dig deeper: how trust is rebuilt

  8. Going back is a choice. Safety comes first.

    After a hurt, you can mend the relationship, change its shape, or step away. All three can be healthy. If someone keeps hurting you after you’ve told them, if you feel afraid of them, or if they control, threaten or put you down, the work is to protect yourself, not to repair. Counselling together isn’t advised when someone is afraid of their partner.

    Ellie’s housemate borrowed money twice and didn’t pay it back. Ellie let the first time go. The second time she said, “I won’t lend money again. I still want us to get on in the house,” and they still share the Sunday roast most weeks.

    You could say “I’m not angry any more, and I’m not going back to how it was.” “I need some distance while I work out what I want.”

    Something to try. Ask yourself whether it is safe, whether the hurt has stopped and whether you want this relationship in your life, and let the answers guide what comes next. If you feel unsafe, see signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#signs).

    Dig deeper: limits, distance and safety

  9. Look after the hurt part of you.

    Hurt lives in the body as well as the mind, as poor sleep, a tight chest or a jumpy feeling. Healing goes better with basic care, which means rest, food, movement, people who are kind to you, and talking to yourself the way you would talk to a hurting friend. Some people find they grow after something painful, and some don’t, and neither is a test.

    A man shouted at Idris on the bus and called him names. For days afterwards he felt shaky. He told a friend, went for long walks and kept reminding himself that it was about the man on the bus and that he was safe now, and over a couple of weeks the shakiness faded.

    Things to tell yourself “This was hard. Anyone would be shaken. What do I need right now?”

    Try this. Pick one small act of care for today, perhaps an early night or a call to someone kind. Calm tools are in Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now)

    Dig deeper: healing in body and mind

Your part, and only your part. You can say what hurt, apologise for what you did, and look after your own healing. You can’t make someone apologise, understand or change, and you don’t have to wait for them to start feeling better. Forgiveness, trust and going back are all yours to choose, in your own time.

Saturday, 11am

You have written it all down, every word of it, and then a smaller version. “When you said that, I felt small. I’d like you to know.” You still haven’t decided whether to send it, and it sits in your drafts. The two o’clock replays have gone a little quieter since it went onto paper.

In everyday life

Between partners, small breaks happen most days, and a quick “That came out wrong. Can I try again?” mends most of them (see How to apologise so it counts). Old family hurts often need a different kind of talk from new ones, and sometimes more time apart. A friend may not know they hurt you, and “Can I tell you something that stung? I’d rather say it than drift” keeps the door open. You can even heal a hurt with someone who has died, by writing to them or talking it through with someone you trust.

  • After an affair. The shock is real for both people. Couples can recover, and some decide to part; both can be done with care. Trust returns through kept promises over months, and a couples therapist can help. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-11-healing-in-depth).
  • If you decide to separate. Part as kindly as you can. Tell children together, without blame, and never ask them to choose. Write decisions down, and consider family mediation where it’s safe. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-11-healing-in-depth#separating).

If you want to help someone else with this

  • Listen before you advise. “That sounds really painful” helps more than “You should just let it go.”
  • Don’t rush forgiveness. Pushing someone to forgive can feel like being told their hurt doesn’t matter.
  • Don’t push them to cut someone off, either. It’s their relationship and their choice, unless they’re in danger.
  • If you caused the hurt, give a real apology and then give them time. Don’t ask them to make you feel better about it.
  • If they mention fear, threats or control, take it seriously and share Not safe at home?

Words you could use “Do you want to talk it through, or would it help more to take your mind off it?” “Whatever you decide about them, I’m on your side.”

When to get more help

Some hurts are too heavy to carry alone, and getting help is a sign of strength, not weakness. Think about talking to a doctor, counsellor or therapist if:

  • More than a month after something frightening, you still have flashbacks, nightmares, feel constantly on edge, or avoid places and people that remind you of it. These can be signs of trauma, and there are well-tested treatments for it, such as trauma-focused talking therapies.
  • The hurt is taking over: you can’t sleep, work or enjoy anything, or you’re drinking or using more to cope.
  • The hurt came from abuse or violence, now or in the past. The page Free, private people to talk to (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#talk) includes specialist lines.
  • You’re having thoughts of hurting yourself or someone else. Please reach out today. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number.

If you and someone else both want to mend things, a couples or family counsellor can help, as long as nobody is afraid of the other.

Tools and reading on the website

Tools helpers you use on the website

  • Upset right now? for calming down in the moment, and the Nervous System Ladder (spreadloveandacceptance.com/quick-checks) for checking your state.

Reading pages to read on the website

  • Apology languages: how to say sorry so it lands, and asking for forgiveness (spreadloveandacceptance.com/apology-languages#forgive).
  • Library: forgiveness (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/conflict), what research says about apologies (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/conflict#apology-research) and repair attempts (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/relationships).
  • Library: rumination (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions), expressive writing (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/emotions#expressive-writing) and self-compassion (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection).
  • Stories from philosophy: the Second Arrow (spreadloveandacceptance.com/learn/index-in-depth).

Part Three · Chapter 12

Helping others well: support without fixing, boundaries, and not burning out

How to help someone without taking over, by asking what they need, listening first, caring without drowning and keeping kind limits, with what to do in a crisis and how to keep going without burning out.

In this chapter

  1. Ask what kind of help they want
  2. Listening is a kind of help
  3. Fixing it for them can take away their power
  4. Care without drowning in their feelings
  5. Your limits make your help last
  6. Notice when you’re running on empty
  7. In a crisis, stay with them and bring in help
  8. Don’t wait for someone else to step in
  9. Let other people help you too
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Tools and reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

In short

  • Ask what kind of help they want. “Ideas, or just someone to listen?” saves a lot of misfires.
  • Listening is help. Fixing a problem for someone can take away their power.
  • Your limits make your help last, and caring from a steady place helps more than drowning in their feelings.
  • In a crisis, stay and bring in help. It’s okay to ask directly about suicide, and to call for help.

Why the tools work. Two tools in other chapters rest on what this one explains.

  • One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, page 91) works for families sharing care because help lasts when it is shared and named, and carers burn out when everything counts as “just helping” and nobody else owns a job.
  • How much are you carrying? (Part Two, Chapter III, page 107) helps you notice when you are running on empty before you snap or stop.

Wednesday, 7:15pm

Your friend is telling you about her awful week, and you have five good ideas before she has finished her first sentence. You share all of them. She goes quiet and says, “Yeah, maybe,” and you both hang up feeling a little worse without quite knowing why.

Most of us want to help the people around us, and helping well is a skill, because good intentions don’t always land. This chapter looks at how support works, why fixing can backfire and how to care for others in a way you can keep up, whether you are a friend, partner, parent, coworker, carer or neighbour.

  1. Ask what kind of help they want.

    Help comes in different kinds. Some people want ideas, some want someone to listen, some want a practical hand such as a meal or a lift, and some just want company. Giving the wrong kind, however kindly, can leave someone feeling unheard, and the simplest fix is to ask.

    For example, in the phone call above, a better start might have been, “That sounds like a rotten week. Do you want ideas, or do you just want to vent?”

    You could say “Would ideas help, or would you rather I just listened?” “What would help most right now?”

    Try this. Next time someone tells you about a problem, ask what kind of help they want before you give any.

    Dig deeper: kinds of support

  2. Listening is a kind of help.

    Being truly heard helps people calm down, think more clearly and often find their own answers. Good listening means paying attention, letting them finish, checking you understood and showing that their feelings make sense, even if you would feel differently.

    Ravi comes home upset about his boss. His partner resists saying “Just quit” and says, “So he criticised you in front of everyone, after you stayed late all week. No wonder you’re furious.” Ravi’s shoulders drop, and ten minutes later he is sketching out his own plan on the back of an envelope.

    Words you could use “So what happened was… Have I got that right?” “That makes sense. Anyone would feel that way.”

    This week. In one conversation today, listen for two whole minutes without giving advice, then sum up what you heard.

    Dig deeper: how listening helps

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: sometimes the best help is sitting close and listening, no fixing needed. Listening takes energy too, so check your own tank now and then.

    Workpaper WP-02: How much are you carrying? spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-02

  3. Fixing it for them can take away their power.

    When we love someone, we want to make the problem go away. Doing things for people that they could do themselves can leave them feeling less capable, though, so helping well often means helping someone do it themselves, which respects that it is their life and their choice.

    For example, Rosalind’s twenty-four-year-old son is struggling with a job application, and she itches to rewrite it. She asks instead whether he would like her to read it and say what stands out, and he makes the changes himself and is quietly proud when he gets the interview.

    Things to tell yourself “Is this mine to fix, or theirs to solve with my support?” “What do they want to do here?”

    One small step. Notice the urge to fix, and before acting ask, “Would you like me to do that, or help you do it?”

    Dig deeper: support without taking over

  4. Care without drowning in their feelings.

    Feeling someone’s pain as if it were your own can wear you out fast. Researchers separate this “empathic distress” from compassion, which is warm concern from a steadier place, still caring deeply without sinking alongside the other person. A steady helper is more use than a second person drowning.

    When Abi’s housemate went through a breakup, Abi cried with her every night and stopped sleeping, and after a week she was exhausted. She stayed kind and present after that while taking breaks, and reminded herself that this was her housemate’s pain to feel and hers to accompany.

    Things to tell yourself “I can be with them in this without making it mine.” “I care, and I’m steady.”

    Something to try. After a heavy conversation, do something that brings you back to yourself, such as a walk, a shower or five slow breaths.

    Dig deeper: empathy and compassion

  5. Your limits make your help last.

    Saying yes to everything leads in the long run to resentment, exhaustion and eventually to not being able to help at all. Limits tell people what you can give, so your yes means something, and a kind no that comes with an offer of what you can do is still help.

    For example, Kojo’s sister keeps asking to borrow money. He loves her and he is running out, so he tells her, “I can’t lend money any more. I can help you go through your bills on Sunday, if you’d like.”

    Ways to say it “I can’t do that, but I can do this.” “I want to help, and I need to stop at nine tonight.”

    Try this. Write down one thing you are giving that you can’t keep giving, and plan a smaller version you could offer instead.

    Dig deeper: boundaries in helping

    Professor Puddles

    Your limits keep your help going for longer. When you need to say “not this time”, Say no kindly helps you find the words, with something to offer instead.

    Tool: Say no kindly: make your scripts spreadloveandacceptance.com/refusals

  6. Notice when you’re running on empty.

    People who help a lot, such as carers, parents, nurses, teachers and the friend everyone calls, can burn out. The signs include feeling exhausted most of the time, feeling numb or cynical about the people you help, getting ill more often and dreading the next call, and they mean that you need help too.

    Helen has looked after her husband since his stroke. She snaps at him and then feels terrible, and her doctor says it sounds like carer strain. A local carers’ group and a few hours of respite each week give her back a little of herself.

    Thoughts you could try “Looking after myself is part of looking after them.”

    This week. Rate your energy from 1 to 10 each evening for a week. If it’s often 3 or lower, ask someone for one specific kind of help. See Caring for someone you love (spreadloveandacceptance.com/caregivers).

    Dig deeper: burnout and refilling

  7. In a crisis, stay with them and bring in help.

    If someone tells you they’re thinking of ending their life, or you’re worried they might be, it’s okay to ask them directly. Research, such as a review led by Dazzi and colleagues (2014), suggests asking about suicide doesn’t put the idea in someone’s head; it can bring relief. You don’t have to be their therapist. Your job is to listen, stay with them, and help them reach trained support.

    For example (a coworker): A colleague says, “Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me.” Kirsty says gently: “I’m really glad you told me. Are you thinking about ending your life?” She says she’s had thoughts. Kirsty stays with her and they call a crisis line together.

    Words to try “Are you thinking about suicide?” “I’m glad you told me. You don’t have to go through this alone. Let’s call someone together.”

    One small step. Save a crisis number in your phone now, so you have it if you ever need it. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines. If someone is in immediate danger, call your local emergency number.

    Dig deeper: helping in a crisis

  8. Don’t wait for someone else to step in.

    When lots of people see something go wrong, each person can assume someone else will act. Psychologists call this the bystander effect, and knowing about it helps you break it. Small, safe actions count, such as asking “Are you okay?”, getting staff or calling for help.

    For example (a stranger): On a train, a man is making a young woman uncomfortable. Yvonne doesn’t confront him. She sits next to the woman and asks loudly, “Hi! Is this the train to Leeds?” The woman joins in the chat, and the man moves away.

    You could say “Are you okay? Do you need anything?” To someone else nearby: “Can you get the driver? I’ll stay here.”

    Something to try. Think of one safe thing you could do if you saw someone in trouble in a public place, such as distracting, getting help or checking in afterwards, because having a plan makes it easier to act.

    Dig deeper: helping strangers and community

  9. Let other people help you too.

    Helping goes both ways, and people who are good at giving help are often bad at receiving it. Letting others help is a gift to them too, because most people like being useful to someone they care about, and relationships where only one person ever helps tend to feel uneven over time.

    For example, Nkechi said “We’re fine, thanks” to every offer after the baby came. When she finally said yes to a neighbour’s offer of a lasagne, the neighbour was delighted, and these days they walk their buggies round the park together.

    Words you could use “Yes, thank you. That would really help.” “Could you do one thing for me this week?”

    Try this. Say yes to the next small offer of help you get, even if you could manage without it.

    Dig deeper: receiving help

Your part, and only your part. You can offer help, listen well, and be honest about your limits. You can’t make someone accept help, take your advice or get better on your timetable. Their life and their choices are theirs. If someone is in danger, your part is to bring in help, not to carry it alone.

The next Wednesday, 7:15pm

Your friend calls again, and this time you ask whether she wants ideas or just to talk it out. She laughs and says just talk, so you listen, through her manager, her landlord and the cat’s vet bill. At the end she says she thinks she knows what she is going to do, and you realise you haven’t offered a single idea.

In everyday life

Helping yourself counts too, and you can ask yourself the same question, whether you need ideas right now or just some rest. Caring for a parent or a child with extra needs is long-haul help, so share the load early (see Caring for someone you love). The friend everyone calls needs someone to call too. Covering for a struggling coworker is kind for a week, and after that it needs a real conversation with the team. In an emergency, point to one person, as in “You in the blue coat, please call for help,” because a crowd often waits for someone else. If you have ADHD, helping can feel interesting and urgent, so a fast yes comes easily, and “I’d like to help. Let me check my week and come back to you tonight” gives you time. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-12-helping-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

  • “Helping means solving the problem.” Often, helping means listening, being there or helping someone find their own answer.
  • “Good helpers never say no.” Good helpers last because they know their limits.
  • “Asking about suicide might give them the idea.” Research suggests it doesn’t, and asking can help someone open up.
  • “I’ll make it worse if I step in.” There are small, safe ways to help. Doing nothing often feels worse for the person in trouble.

If you want to help someone else with this

The helpers around you need looking after too.

  • Notice the helpers, such as the carer, the friend everyone calls and the coworker who always covers, and ask them how they are as if you mean it.
  • Offer specific help. “Can I take the kids on Saturday morning?” is easier to accept than “Let me know if you need anything.”
  • Give them permission to rest. “You’re allowed a night off. I’ve got this.”
  • If a helper seems burned out, share Caring for someone you love or suggest they talk to a doctor.

Ways to say it “You look after everyone. Who looks after you?” “I’d love to do something for you this week. What would help?”

When to get more help

  • If someone is in danger now, call your local emergency number.
  • If someone talks about suicide, stay with them and contact a crisis line together. In the US and Canada, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans free on 116 123. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. In New Zealand, call or text 1737. Anywhere else, findahelpline.com lists free helplines.
  • If someone tells you they’re being hurt or controlled at home, believe them, don’t confront the other person yourself, and share Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety)
  • If you’re burned out as a helper or carer, talk to your doctor, a carers’ organisation or a counsellor. Respite and support are not luxuries.
  • If helping someone is becoming unsafe for you, step back and bring in professionals. You can still care from a safer distance.

Tools and reading on the website

Tools helpers you use on the website

  • Check-ins (spreadloveandacceptance.com/check-ins), for tender conversations, and Professor Puddles (spreadloveandacceptance.com/ask) if you want help finding words.

Reading pages to read on the website

  • Library: active listening (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication), advice or support? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication#advice-vs-support) and validation (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication#validation-in-conversation).
  • Library: empathic distress and compassion (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection) and social support (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/connection#social-support).
  • Library: burnout (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress) and caregiver strain (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/stress#caregiver-strain).
  • Library: saying no (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication#saying-no) and boundaries (spreadloveandacceptance.com/library/communication#boundaries).
  • Stories from philosophy: the circles of Hierocles (spreadloveandacceptance.com/learn/index-in-depth).

More for your situation

  • Carers: Caring for someone you love · When one of you is ill (spreadloveandacceptance.com/when-one-is-ill)
  • Friends: Friends (spreadloveandacceptance.com/friends)
  • Parents and grandparents: For parents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/parents) · For grandparents (spreadloveandacceptance.com/grandparents) · When a child has ADHD (spreadloveandacceptance.com/adhd-kids)
  • At work: At work (spreadloveandacceptance.com/work) · For counsellors, coaches and group leaders (spreadloveandacceptance.com/for-counselors)

A limit to keep in mind: This chapter is about everyday helping. It isn’t training in crisis care or therapy. When someone’s safety is at risk, the most helpful thing you can do is bring in people trained to help.

Part Three · Chapter 13

Anger: what it’s for and what to do with it

What anger is for, what to do in the hot minutes, how to repair afterwards, and how to tell when anger has turned into harm. For anyone, in any kind of relationship, or on your own.

In this chapter

  1. Anger is a signal about something that matters
  2. Anger often guards a softer feeling
  3. Anger rises in the body fast
  4. In the hot minutes: slow the body first
  5. Letting rip doesn’t empty it
  6. Step back and look from the outside
  7. Say it, don’t throw it
  8. After anger, repair
  9. When anger becomes harm
  10. If you’re a teenager
  11. In everyday life
  12. Common mix-ups
  13. If you want to help someone else with this
  14. When to get more help
  15. Workpapers, tools and reading on this site
  16. More for your situation

In short

  • Anger is a signal that something seems unfair, blocked or threatening. The feeling is allowed, and what you do with it is the part you choose.
  • The first minutes are about the body. Slow down, breathe out long, and step away with a time to come back.
  • Letting rip doesn’t empty anger. Shouting tends to feed it, while calming the body, putting it into words and repairing any sharp moments help more.
  • Anger that frightens, controls or hurts someone has become harm. That needs more help, and safety comes first.

Why the tools work. Two tools in other chapters rest on what this one explains.

  • The Calm-Down Kit (Part One, Now, page 35) works because anger rises in the body first, and slowing the body is what makes words possible.
  • Letting a comment land before you react (Part Two, Chapter IV, page 122) is the step back this chapter describes, where you look at the moment from the outside and then choose.

Tuesday, 6:10pm

Your brother texts to say he can’t take Mum to the hospital on Thursday after all, with two exclamation marks after the sorry. It’s the third time this month. Your jaw sets, your face goes hot and your thumbs are already typing “TYPICAL. You never…” with the message one tap from sent.

Many of us were taught that anger was rude or dangerous, or grew up around anger that was frightening. Anger itself is a normal human feeling, though, and it often points at something real. This chapter looks first at how anger works and then at what to do with it.

  1. Anger is a signal about something that matters.

    Anger usually says that something is unfair, that someone is in your way or that a line has been crossed. It pushes us towards a problem so that we change it. It can also land on the wrong person, or be far bigger than the problem in front of it.

    For example, a woman keeps finding her lunch gone from the office fridge. By the third week her anger has told her that a line has been crossed, and it is the anger that finally gets her to raise it at the Monday meeting.

    Thoughts you could try “What is this anger trying to protect?” “Is this about fairness, a blocked plan or feeling unsafe?”

    Try this. Next time you feel angry, finish this sentence privately. “I’m angry because something I care about, which is ___, seems ___.”

    Dig deeper: what anger is for

  2. Anger often guards a softer feeling.

    Anger can arrive first because it feels stronger and safer than what sits under it, which might be hurt, fear, shame, worry or plain tiredness. Chapter 1 (page 154) calls this layers. Finding the layer underneath often shows what you actually need.

    A man snaps at his teenage daughter for coming home an hour late. Under the anger is an hour of fear spent imagining the worst. When he tells her about that hour instead of the curfew, she hears it and says sorry.

    You could say “I’m angry, and I think underneath I was really scared.” “I came across cross, but I think I’m actually hurt.”

    This week. After the next angry moment, once you are calm, ask whether there was hurt, fear or tiredness under it.

    Dig deeper: what anger can cover

  3. Anger rises in the body fast.

    A hot face, a tight jaw, a pounding heart and a louder voice are the body getting ready for a fight, and they can arrive in seconds. When anger is high, careful thinking and listening get much harder. Chapter 2 (page 169) calls this being flooded, when you are so stirred up that the thinking part of you goes quiet for a while.

    For example, arguing about the bins, a woman notices her hands shaking and realises she hasn’t heard a word her housemate has said for a minute or more, which is her sign to stop.

    Things to tell yourself “My body is ready for a fight, but I don’t have to have one.” “Where is this in my body?”

    One small step. Learn your own early signs and write down two or three of them, such as a tight jaw or talking faster. They are your cue to slow down.

    Dig deeper: anger in the body

    Professor Puddles

    Anger moves faster than words. The Calm-Down Kit is a plan you make on a calm day, for the hot minutes.

    Workpaper WP-11: The Calm-Down Kit spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-11

  4. In the hot minutes: slow the body first.

    When anger is high, settle your body before you try to sort anything out. Stop talking or typing, breathe out slowly so the out-breath is longer than the in-breath, unclench your hands and, if you can, move away for a while. A large review of 154 studies by Kjærvik and Bushman (2024) found that activities which calm the body, like slow breathing, relaxation and mindfulness, reduced anger, while ones that rev you up showed little or no benefit.

    A dad feels his temper rising while he helps with fractions homework. He says, “I’m getting frustrated, and that’s not your fault. I’m going to get a glass of water and come back in five minutes.” He comes back in five, and they finish the sheet together.

    You could say “I’m too angry to talk well right now. I’ll come back at eight.” “I need ten minutes. I’m coming back to this conversation.”

    Something to try. On a calm day, make a three-step plan with your early sign, the words you’ll say and where you’ll go for ten minutes. Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now) has steps for the hottest moments.

    Dig deeper: what to do in the moment

  5. Letting rip doesn’t empty it.

    Many people believe anger works like steam, so that shouting, slamming a door or hitting a pillow lets it out and leaves you calmer. Research doesn’t support this. In a well-known study by Bushman (2002), angry people who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who annoyed them ended up angrier than before.

    Going over what happened again and again in your head has a similar effect. In studies by Bushman and colleagues (2005), people who dwelt on a provocation were later more aggressive, even towards someone who only mildly annoyed them. Anger tends to fade faster when the body is calmed and the mind has something else to do for a while.

    For example, after a row with a coworker, a man spends his lunch break telling three people how awful she is, and by the afternoon he is angrier than he was at noon. The next time it happens he takes a walk instead, and by two o’clock he can think about the problem clearly.

    Thoughts you could try “Going over this again is feeding it.” “I can come back to this later, when I’m calmer.”

    Try this. If you catch yourself replaying an argument, set a timer for twenty minutes and do something absorbing, then come back to the problem.

    Dig deeper: venting and going over it

  6. Step back and look from the outside.

    Once the body has settled a little, it helps to look at the moment as if you were watching from across the room. What happened, and what might the other person have been dealing with? In experiments by Mischkowski, Kross and Bushman (2012), people who looked back on an annoying moment “like a fly on the wall”, instead of reliving it, felt less angry and acted less aggressively. Rethinking what happened, which psychologists call reappraisal (Gross, 1998), helps too.

    Furious that a friend has cancelled again, a woman imagines telling the story to a kind stranger on a train. Telling it that way, she remembers that her friend is caring for a sick parent, and the anger turns slowly into worry for her.

    Things to tell yourself “If I were watching this from the side, what would I see?” “What else might be going on for them?”

    This week. Write two lines about the moment that start with your own name in place of “I”, as in “Wes got angry because…”

    Dig deeper: stepping back

  7. Say it, don’t throw it.

    Anger is often a fair message sent in a hurtful way. Once you are calmer, you can still say that you were angry, and why, without attacking anyone. A simple shape helps. Say what happened, how you felt and what you are asking for.

    For example, in place of “You always let me down,” a woman says to her sister, “When you cancelled Mum’s appointment again, I felt really angry and alone with it. Can we make a plan for who takes her over the next three months?”

    You could say “I was angry about what happened on Monday. Can I tell you why?” “When ___ happened, I felt ___, and what I’m asking for is ___.”

    One small step. Write your angry message, then rewrite it in that shape before you send anything. Chapter 4 (page 198) has more on saying hard things.

    Dig deeper: saying anger in words

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: say it slowly, in one plain sentence. A soft start makes it easier for the other person to hear you.

    Tool: Cool-down corner: soften a tense moment spreadloveandacceptance.com/tools/soften-a-tense-moment

  8. After anger, repair.

    Everyone gets angry, and most of us say something sharp now and then. What happens next matters a great deal. A short, real repair helps rebuild trust, which means naming what you did without a “but” and saying what you will do differently.

    A grandmother shouts at her grandson for breaking a vase, and he cries. An hour later she sits beside him on the stairs and says, “I shouted, and that was scary. You matter far more to me than the vase. I’m sorry.” He leans against her shoulder and asks whether they can glue it.

    You could say “I was sharp with you earlier. That wasn’t fair, and I’m sorry.” “I’m still upset about what happened, and I also shouldn’t have spoken to you that way.”

    Something to try. Think of one recent moment when your anger landed on someone. Is there a short repair you could still make? Chapter 11 (page 298) has more on apologies that land.

    Dig deeper: repair after anger

  9. When anger becomes harm.

    Feeling angry is human. But some things done in anger are harm, whatever the feeling behind them: hitting, pushing, throwing things at or near someone, breaking their things, threatening, shouting so someone is scared, or using anger to control what another person does, wears, spends or who they see. People walking on eggshells around you is a sign too. Anger is never a reason someone deserves to be hurt.

    For example, a man realises his partner and children go quiet when he comes home in a bad mood. He doesn’t hit anyone, but they are afraid of him. He talks to his doctor and joins an anger course.

    You could say “I think my anger is scaring people I love. I want help with it.” (If it’s happening to you) “I’m frightened of how they get when they’re angry.”

    Try this. If this sounds like you, see Find a counsellor or therapist (spreadloveandacceptance.com/outside-help) and the Cool-down corner. If you’re afraid of someone else’s anger, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.

    Dig deeper: when anger becomes harm

Your part, and only your part. You can learn your early signs, settle your body, say what made you angry in words, and repair when you get it wrong. You can’t make someone else calm down, and you don’t have to accept being shouted at, threatened or controlled. If someone else’s anger frightens you, getting safe matters more than working it out. Not safe at home?

Tuesday, 6:40pm

You put the phone face down and walk round the block, breathing out long. Somewhere near the postbox you notice what is under the anger. You are tired, and you are frightened about Mum. Back home you delete the capitals and write, “I’m really frustrated. This is the third time and I feel alone with Mum’s care. Can we talk tonight and make a plan?”

He reads it at 6:52. By ten o’clock there is still no reply, and you go to bed not knowing who will drive her on Thursday. You sent the message you can stand behind, and that part is done, even if the rest of it isn’t.

zqaxunderstandingx13xangerxxteensqzIf you’re a teenager

Maisie is sixteen, and her dad takes her phone at ten o’clock in the middle of a chat with her friends. She shouts and slams her bedroom door. The next morning, calmer, she tells him it felt as if he didn’t trust her, says sorry for the door and asks for ten minutes’ warning next time. He agrees, and adds that he would rather hear this over breakfast than through a door.

Being angry with a parent is normal, and arguments often feel most intense in the middle teens. A rule given out of care is not control, even when it feels unfair, and a calm request the next day works more often than a slammed door.

You could say “I’m too angry to talk properly. Can we talk tomorrow?” “I don’t mind the rule so much as how it happened.” “Could we try it for two weeks and then check?”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

In everyday life

Anger at yourself counts too. “I’m so stupid” is anger turned inward, and it helps to speak to yourself as you would to a friend who had made the same mistake (Chapter 7, page 241, goes further). With a partner, agree a pause word on a calm day and a time you will always come back. Children copy what we do with anger far more than what we say about it. At work, anger is common and rarely said out loud, and “I’m frustrated about the deadline change. Can we talk about what’s realistic?” keeps it useful.

If you have ADHD, anger can arrive fast and big and then pass quickly, so plan for the speed with a three-word pause line such as “Back in ten” and a rule to wait before you send anything. If you are managing a clash between two other people, hear each of them alone first and then together, about what happened and never about each other. The fight is often about the setup, such as two people who both believe they own the same job. The full chapter has a worked example (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-13-anger-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

  • “Anger is a bad feeling.” Anger is a normal feeling that carries information. It is some of the things done in anger that cause harm.
  • “Letting it out is healthy.” Shouting or hitting things tends to keep anger going, and calming the body before talking helps more.
  • “They made me angry, so it’s their fault I shouted.” Someone can do something unfair. What you do next is still yours.
  • “Holding it in is the safe option.” Anger swallowed for years tends to come out sideways, as coldness, sarcasm or a sudden explosion. Saying it calmly and early is safer.

If you want to help someone else with this

  • Keep yourself safe first. If someone’s anger scares you, step away. You don’t have to stay and calm them down.
  • Lower, slower, fewer words. Speak quietly and simply, and leave the argument until they have come down.
  • Hear the message under it. There is often something fair under the anger. You can take that part seriously and still say that the way it was said wasn’t okay.

You could say “I want to hear this, and I can’t while we’re both shouting. Can we try again at seven?” “I can tell this really matters to you.”

When to get more help

Everyone gets angry. It may be time to talk to a doctor, a counsellor or an anger management course if:

  • your anger feels out of control, or you often regret what you do or say when angry;
  • people close to you seem nervous or walk on eggshells around you;
  • you have hit, pushed, thrown things, broken things or threatened anyone;
  • anger is hurting your work, your friendships or your health;
  • you are using alcohol or drugs to cope with angry feelings.

Help for anger works for many people: a review of anger treatments by Del Vecchio and O’Leary (2004) found medium to large benefits. It is good for your health too: a review by Chida and Steptoe (2009) linked anger and hostility with a higher risk of heart disease. Asking for help is a responsible thing to do. Find a counsellor or therapist (spreadloveandacceptance.com/outside-help#counsellor) lists places to start, some of them free, and the Cool-down corner helps in the hot minutes.

If you are afraid of someone else’s anger, that fear is an important signal. Not safe at home? lists free, private help. If you or anyone is in danger right now, call your local emergency number.

This chapter is general education, not therapy.

zqunderstandingx14xpersonalityqz

14

Part Three · Chapter 14

Personality, temperament and change across life

What personality is, where temperament comes in, how people change across their lives, and how to live and work with people who are made differently from you, without putting anyone in a box.

In this chapter

  1. Traits are dials, not boxes
  2. Temperament is the starting point
  3. Situations matter too
  4. Introvert and extravert is about energy, not liking people
  5. People change across life
  6. You can change on purpose, a little at a time
  7. Every trait has gifts and costs
  8. Differences are about fit, not fault
  9. In everyday life
  10. Common mix-ups
  11. If you want to help someone else with this
  12. When to get more help
  13. Tools and reading on this site
  14. More for your situation

In short

  • Traits work like dials. Everyone sits somewhere along each one, and most people are near the middle.
  • Temperament is a starting point. Babies already differ in how active, cautious or easily upset they are, and what happens next matters too.
  • People keep changing. On average people grow steadier and more organised as they get older, and you can change on purpose, slowly.
  • Most clashes between personalities are about fit, and nobody has to be at fault.

Why the tools work. Two tools in other chapters rest on what this one explains.

  • The “How to talk to me” card and the style quiz (Part One, Now, page 35) describe how you lean on a few dials, which is more useful than knowing which box someone put you in.
  • One owner per job (Part Two, Chapter II, page 91) lets people with different temperaments share a home or a team without changing who they are, because the jobs are arranged around the differences.

Saturday, 3:00pm

It is your aunt’s seventieth birthday, and you are standing quietly by the cake when she announces, loud enough for the whole room, that you were always the shy one. Everyone laughs, and you smile along while something stings. You are forty-two and you stand in front of thirty children every weekday morning, so are you still the shy one, and were you ever?

We all describe people by their personality, as laid-back, a worrier or the organised one, and descriptions like these can harden into boxes. This chapter looks at how personality actually works, what stays the same and what changes.

  1. Traits are dials, not boxes.

    Personality is your usual pattern of thinking, feeling and acting. Many psychologists describe it with five broad traits, often called the “Big Five”. They are openness (curious about new ideas and experiences), conscientiousness (organised and careful), extraversion (drawn to people and busy places), agreeableness (warm and cooperative) and emotional stability (how steady your moods are).

    The same five turned up in work such as McCrae and Costa (1987), whether people rated themselves or were rated by people who knew them. Each one works like a dial, and most people sit somewhere near the middle of most dials.

    For example, two friends take an online quiz, and one is told she is an introvert while the other is told he is an extravert. When they look at their actual scores, they are only a few points apart, both close to the middle.

    Things to tell yourself “I’m more of this than that, some of the time.” “A label is only a summary.”

    Try this. For each of the five dials, mark where you think you sit from one to ten, and then ask yourself where a close friend would put you.

    Dig deeper: the five dials

  2. Temperament is the starting point.

    Temperament is the part of personality we can see from very early on. Some babies are very active and some calm, some settle easily into new routines while others take time, and some react strongly to noise or change. In their long-running study, Thomas and Chess (1977) described these early differences and the idea of “goodness of fit”, meaning how well a child’s temperament fits what the people and places around them expect.

    A toddler who is slow to warm up cries at every new playgroup. Her mum stops pushing her to join in and lets her watch from her lap for ten minutes first, and by the third week she climbs down and joins the sand table on her own.

    You could say “You like to watch first. That’s fine. Join in when you’re ready.” (to yourself) “I need time to warm up. That’s how I’m made.”

    This week. Think about what you were like as a small child, from what your family say or what you remember, and notice what seems the same now and what seems different.

    Dig deeper: temperament and fit

  3. Situations matter too.

    Personality describes a pattern. The same person can be loud with family and quiet at work, organised in their job and messy at home, patient with children and short with call centres. A trait tells you what someone tends to do across many situations, and much less about what they will do in this one.

    For example, a manager decides that a new colleague is cold. At the team’s charity football match, the same colleague turns out to be chatty, funny and warm, and the manager starts to wonder how much the open-plan office was shaping what she saw.

    Things to tell yourself “I’ve only seen them in one setting.” “Where am I most myself, and where am I least?”

    One small step. Before deciding what someone is “like,” try to see them in one different setting, or ask them about one.

    Dig deeper: person and situation

  4. Introvert and extravert is about energy, not liking people.

    People who are more introverted often enjoy people very much, but find that busy, noisy social time uses up energy and that they need quiet to recover. People who are more extraverted often feel energised by company and busy places. Most of us are a mix, sometimes called an ambivert, and each kind of person simply needs different things to feel at their best.

    After a wedding, one partner wants to go on to the after-party and the other wants bed and silence. One goes for an hour, the other goes back to the hotel, and they meet for a late breakfast.

    Words you could use “I loved tonight, and I’m out of social energy.” “Shall we go together, and I’ll head home at ten?”

    Something to try. Notice whether company, quiet or a bit of both refills you after a busy week, and plan some of it for this weekend.

    Dig deeper: introversion and extraversion

    Tidbit

    Tidbit wants you to know: some of us recharge at the park with everyone, and some under a quiet blanket. Both are great! A quiz can show you your own style.

    Tool: How you connect: the 2-minute style quiz spreadloveandacceptance.com/wavelength

  5. People change across life.

    Personality is fairly stable, but it can move. A large review by Roberts, Walton and Viechtbauer (2006) found that, on average, people become more organised, more emotionally steady and more confident with others as they move through adult life, with much of the change between 20 and 40. A later review by Bleidorn and colleagues (2022) found that emotional steadiness kept growing right across the lifespan. Big life events, roles and relationships all play a part.

    For example, a man who was a nervous, disorganised student becomes a calm, steady nurse in his forties, and his old school friends barely recognise him. When they ask, he says that life kept asking him to cope and he slowly learned how.

    Thoughts you could try “Who I was at fifteen isn’t who I have to be now.” “People I knew years ago may have changed too.”

    Try this. Write down one way you have changed in the last ten years, and what helped it happen.

    Dig deeper: how personality changes with age

  6. You can change on purpose, a little at a time.

    People who want to change a trait can, slowly, mostly by acting differently in small ways, again and again. In a study by Hudson and Fraley (2015), people who set goals to change one of their traits tended, over sixteen weeks, to change in the direction they wanted. A review by Roberts and colleagues (2017) found that therapy was often linked to lasting change too, especially towards more emotional steadiness.

    A woman who wants to be less shy at work makes one small plan, to say one thing in each team meeting, and after two months speaking up has started to feel ordinary.

    Things to tell yourself “I don’t have to become a different person. I can practise one different thing.”

    This week. Pick one small action that fits who you would like to be more of, such as replying to messages the same day or saying hello first, and do it three times this week. Chapter 6 (page 228) has more on habits.

    Dig deeper: changing on purpose

  7. Every trait has gifts and costs.

    No personality is the good one. Each trait helps in some places and gets in the way in others. Very agreeable people are kind and easy to be with, and may find it hard to say no. Very conscientious people are reliable, and may struggle to rest. People high in openness love new things, and may get bored with routine. Knowing your mix helps you use the gifts and plan for the costs.

    For example, a highly organised woman is often irritated by her relaxed housemate. Then the boiler breaks on a freezing night, and he is the one who stays calm and finds a plumber at ten o’clock.

    Things to tell yourself “What is the gift in this trait, and what is the cost?” “What they do that annoys me might be the flip side of something I value.”

    One small step. Pick one trait of yours that people sometimes complain about. Write down one time it helped.

    Dig deeper: gifts and costs

    Professor Puddles

    Every trait has gifts and costs. Writing down what helps you on a one-page card turns a “flaw” into useful information.

    Tool: How you connect: how I like to be spoken to spreadloveandacceptance.com/wiring-card

  8. Differences are about fit, not fault.

    When two people with different personalities share a home, a family or a job, friction is normal. A tidy person and a relaxed one, a planner and someone spontaneous, a talker and someone who needs quiet can each be right in their own way, and what helps is naming the difference and agreeing how to live with it. Personality is also different from neurodivergence and from mental health conditions, and if something feels bigger than personality, Chapter 9 (page 265) may help.

    A couple argue about every holiday, because one wants every hour planned and the other wants to wander. This year they plan the mornings and leave the afternoons free, and they still argue about the mornings.

    Ways to say it “I think we’re just made differently here. What would work for both of us?” “I’m a planner and you’re not. Can we plan half and leave half?”

    Something to try. Think of one person you clash with and name the difference without blame, as in “I like ___ and they like ___.” Then think of one small arrangement that would suit you both.

    Dig deeper: fit, not fault

Your part, and only your part. You can get to know your own mix, look after what you need, and practise one small change if you want to. You can’t change someone else’s personality, and you don’t have to change yours to be loved. If you’re always the one bending to fit, it’s fair to say so. Know your own wiring (spreadloveandacceptance.com/know-yourself)

Saturday, 5:30pm

As people start to leave, you think about sitting down next to your aunt and telling her about the thirty children. In the end you help clear the plates and say nothing. On the drive home you are still turning it over, half annoyed with her and half with yourself, and you wonder whether she will say it again at Christmas, and what you would like to say back if she does.

In everyday life

On your own

Knowing your own mix helps you plan a life that suits you, with the right amount of company, quiet, routine and novelty. “I’m just not a people person” might be true, or it might be an old label worth testing. With a partner, a shared plan such as one of you handling the bills and the other the holidays often works better than trying to change each other. A quiet friend who doesn’t text much may still care a great deal, so it is worth asking what kind of contact suits them. A child’s temperament says nothing about good or bad parenting, and adjusting to fit them is a skill. Family roles like “the clever one” or “the difficult one” can stick long after they stop fitting, and you are allowed to grow out of them.

Common mix-ups

  • “You’re either an introvert or an extravert.” Most people are somewhere in the middle, and it can shift with setting and mood.
  • “Personality is set by adulthood.” It keeps changing, slowly, across the whole of life.
  • “Online type quizzes tell you who you are.” Many popular quizzes sort people into a handful of types, while real people are spread along each dial. Quizzes are good for fun and conversation, and that includes the website’s own Wave Code, which shows four leanings on four dials.
  • “They’re just difficult.” “Difficult” often means “different from me”, and it can also hide stress, illness or a need nobody has asked about.
  • “Changing would mean being fake.” Practising something new feels unnatural at first and becomes part of you over time.

If you want to help someone else with this

  • Drop the old labels. Notice if you still describe someone the way they were years ago, and look for who they are now.
  • Ask instead of guessing. “What helps you recharge?” or “How do you like to plan things?” tells you more than any guess from their personality.
  • Notice growth out loud. “You handled that so calmly” can help someone see a change they hadn’t noticed.
  • Describe the action. “You’re so uptight” or “You’re just lazy” closes doors, while a description of what happened leaves them open.

Words to try “I used to think of you as the shy one. I don’t think that fits any more.” “What do you need to be at your best this week?”

When to get more help

Personality differences are normal and don’t need fixing. It may be worth talking to a doctor, counsellor or psychologist if:

  • a pattern in how you feel, think or relate to people keeps causing you or others real distress, across many parts of life;
  • you feel very unsure who you are, or your moods swing so much it’s hard to cope;
  • worry, low mood or fear of people is stopping you from living the life you want.

Please don’t diagnose yourself or anyone else with a “personality disorder” from what you read online. Those are clinical terms that only a qualified professional can use, after a proper assessment.

A personality trait never excuses controlling, frightening or hurtful behaviour. If you’re afraid of someone close to you, Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety) lists free, private help.

This chapter is general education, not a diagnosis or therapy.

15

Part Three · Chapter 15

Closeness and love: being known, at every age

How closeness grows, what it means to feel truly known, how love changes over the years, and how it looks in every kind of relationship, at every age, including for people on their own.

In this chapter

  1. Love comes in many forms
  2. Closeness grows from being known
  3. Closeness is built a step at a time
  4. Feeling understood matters most
  5. Old maps show up in love
  6. Love changes over time
  7. Love at every age
  8. Love is something you do
  9. If you’re a teenager
  10. In everyday life
  11. Common mix-ups
  12. If you want to help someone else with this
  13. When to get more help
  14. Reading on this site
  15. More for your situation

Friday, 10:30pm

You and Charlie have shared a home for eleven years. Tonight you are both on the sofa and both on your phones, and you realise you can’t remember the last time you talked about anything except bills, the boiler and whose turn it is to cook. You love Charlie, and you feel oddly alone in the same room.

This chapter is about closeness in all its forms, far beyond romance. It looks at what helps people feel near to each other, why closeness can fade and how it can grow again, and it builds on Chapter 5 (page 214), on attachment and trust.

  1. Love comes in many forms.

    The ancient Greeks had several words for love, for friends, for family, for romantic partners and for strangers. People love in many ways today too. There are lifelong friendships, partners of any gender, people with more than one partner, chosen family, people who are asexual or aromantic and build deep closeness without romance or sex, and people on their own who pour love into friends, family, pets, work and community. A life can be full of love without a partner in it. A woman in her fifties who has never wanted a partner describes her best friend of thirty years as her great love story. They have been through two house moves, one cancer scare and more Sunday phone calls than either could count.

    It can help to write down three or more people you love, of any kind, and next to each one way you show it.

    Dig deeper: the many forms of love

  2. Closeness grows from being known.

    Intimacy is about much more than touch or romance, and at its heart is being known. The psychologists Reis and Shaver described it as a back-and-forth, in which one person shares something real about themselves and the other responds in a way that leaves them feeling understood, accepted and cared for. In a diary study by Laurenceau, Barrett and Pietromonaco (1998), feeling that the other person really responded was a big part of what made everyday conversations feel intimate.

    Two brothers who mostly talk about football are driving to their dad’s care home when one admits that he finds the visits really hard. The other says he does too, and that he always feels guilty on the way home. It is the longest conversation they have had in years, and it lasts until the car park. Sharing one small, true thing with someone you care about, a worry, a hope or something that made you happy this week, and noticing how they respond, is the same process on a smaller scale.

    Dig deeper: intimacy as being known

  3. Closeness is built a step at a time.

    People usually get close by sharing a little more, and then a little more, when it feels safe. In a well-known study by Aron and colleagues (1997), pairs of strangers who took turns asking gradually more personal questions, now known as the “36 questions”, felt closer after forty-five minutes than pairs who made small talk. The same idea works in friendships and long relationships, where closeness grows when both people take small, matched steps. Two new neighbours start with the weather and the parking. A few months later one asks how the other’s mum is doing, and some time after that one of them says, “Can I tell you what’s really been going on?”

    Next time you talk to someone you would like to know better, ask one question a little deeper than usual, such as what has been on their mind lately, and if they answer, share something of your own back.

    Dig deeper: building closeness step by step

    Professor Puddles

    Closeness grows when you know what feels like care to the other person, not just to you. A “What feels like care” card is a gentle way to find out.

    Tool: How you connect: what feels like care spreadloveandacceptance.com/love-languages

  4. Feeling understood matters most.

    What makes someone feel loved is often less about grand gestures and more about feeling understood. Researchers call this responsiveness, meaning noticing, understanding and caring about what matters to the other person, and it shows in small moments such as how you react to good news. Gable and colleagues (2004) found that people whose partners usually met their good news with real interest and warmth felt closer and more satisfied together. When a teenager announces that she has been picked for the band, her grandad stops what he is doing, smiles and asks which instrument and when the first concert is, and she talks for twenty minutes.

    The next time someone shares good news with you, put your phone down and ask two follow-up questions.

    Dig deeper: responsiveness

  5. Old maps show up in love.

    The patterns from Chapter 5 (page 214) often come out most strongly with the people we love most. Hazan and Shaver (1987) suggested that adult love uses the same attachment system as childhood bonds. When closeness feels shaky, some people reach harder for reassurance and others pull back to feel safe, and both are ways of protecting something precious. When his partner goes quiet, Leo texts five times in an hour, while his partner, who goes quiet in order to calm down, feels crowded. They agree that his partner will say, “I need an hour, and I’ll message you at eight,” and Leo finds he can wait for a known time.

    Notice what you do when closeness feels shaky, and tell someone you trust what helps you feel safe again.

    Dig deeper: attachment in adult love

  6. Love changes over time.

    Early love is often intense, with racing thoughts and a lot of longing, and over the years it usually settles into something calmer and deeper. A review by Acevedo and Aron (2009) found that some people in long relationships still report strong romantic love, without the anxious, obsessive edge of early love, and that this was linked to being happier together.

    In experiments by Aron and colleagues (2000), couples who tried a new, mildly challenging activity together felt better about their relationship afterwards than couples given a dull task. After twenty-five years, one couple sign up for a pottery class. They are both terrible at it, laugh all evening and bring home a bowl that won’t stand up, and on the way home one of them says it felt like a date. Something new for both of you matters more than something big, whether that is a new walk, a new recipe or a new place.

    Dig deeper: how love changes

    Sugarfoot

    Sugarfoot’s tip: little rituals, like a Sunday walk or a goodnight text, keep love warm through the years. Look after the ones you have.

    Workpaper WP-15: Keep your little rituals alive spreadloveandacceptance.com/wp-15

  7. Love at every age.

    Love looks different across a life. Teenagers’ first loves can be huge and real, and adults juggle love with work, children and caring for parents. Many older people choose to spend their time with fewer, closer people, which Carstensen and colleagues (1999) linked to feeling that time is more limited, so that the most meaningful relationships matter more. People find new love at seventy and eighty, and people lose great loves and carry them always. A widower of seventy-eight meets a woman at his walking group, and when his children are surprised he tells them, “I loved your mother for fifty years. I still do. And I’m allowed to be happy now.”

    If it feels right, ask someone from another generation, an older relative or a younger neighbour, about love in their life.

    Dig deeper: love across the lifespan

  8. Love is something you do.

    Feelings of love come and go, while the actions of love can be steady. They include turning towards someone when they speak, keeping small promises, saying thank you and sorry, and making room for who they are. Physical closeness, like a hug or holding hands, matters a lot to some people and less to others, and sex is part of closeness in some relationships and not in others. What matters is that both people feel comfortable and free to say yes or no. Love never includes fear, threats or control.

    A woman notices that her friend has been quiet since his divorce. She never says she loves him, but every Thursday she texts the single word “Walk?” and turns up at his door. You might ask someone you love what small thing makes them feel cared for, and then do it this week.

    Dig deeper: love as action

Your part, and only your part. You can share a little of yourself, listen well, turn towards the people you love and keep small promises. You can’t make someone love you, or love you in the way you want. If closeness keeps hurting you, or you feel afraid, that is not a failure of love on your part. Not safe at home? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety)

The next Friday, 10:30pm

This time you leave both phones in the kitchen, make two cups of tea and ask Charlie what they have been thinking about lately that they haven’t told you. Charlie is quiet for a moment and then talks about their dad getting older, and how they dread the phone ringing late at night. You listen, and then you talk about the restructure at work. The tea goes cold, and it is midnight before either of you looks at the clock.

If you’re a teenager

First love can be huge and real, and so can a first breakup. Ines is sixteen when she is dumped by message on a Tuesday night, and she cries until two in the morning. Being told by adults that she will get over it doesn’t help. Telling her cousin, who simply listens, does, along with muting the chat instead of rereading it and a rule of no checking his profile after ten. A few weeks later she notices that a whole day has gone by without her thinking about him.

You could say “I don’t need advice, I just need to tell someone.” “Can we reply when we can, rather than all day?” And if you are the one ending it, “I don’t want to go out any more. I’m sorry. It isn’t about something you did wrong.”

Dig deeper: more worked examples

In everyday life

On your own

Being single, widowed, divorced or happily alone doesn’t mean a life without love, because friendships, family, community and the way you treat yourself are all places where love lives. If you want a partner and don’t have one, that longing is real and worth being gentle with (see On my own, spreadloveandacceptance.com/on-my-own). Most partners drift into talking only about jobs and bills, and one real question a week can bring them back. Friendship needs tending like any other love, and families often love each other deeply and say it rarely, so a short “I’m glad you’re my sister” can mean a great deal.

  • Different levels of desire. This is very common in long relationships and is nobody’s fault. Talk at a calm time, keep some affection that doesn’t have to lead anywhere, and remember that a kind “no” is a no to the moment and never a rejection of the person. A qualified sex therapist or couples therapist can help. More in the full chapter (spreadloveandacceptance.com/book/understanding-15-love-in-depth).

Common mix-ups

  • “If the spark fades, love is over.” Early intensity usually settles, and many long relationships stay warm, close and lively.
  • “If they loved me, they’d just know what I need.” Nobody reads minds, and saying what helps is a gift.
  • “Jealousy proves love.” Feeling jealous is human, and asking for something out of care for the relationship is not control. Checking up without agreement, cutting someone off or punishing them is not love. See signs to look out for (spreadloveandacceptance.com/safety#signs).

If you want to help someone else with this

Respect their kind of love, without assuming that everyone wants a partner, children or one kind of relationship. Be a safe person to tell things to, which means listening without judging and keeping what they share private. After a loss or a breakup, keep showing up, because many people get plenty of support for two weeks and very little after that.

  • If you’re worried about someone’s relationship, stay close and kind rather than criticising their partner. If they seem afraid, gently share Not safe at home?

Words you could use “I’m always glad to hear from you.” “You don’t have to explain your relationship to me. I just want you to be happy and safe.”

When to get more help

  • If you feel very lonely or low most days for two weeks or more, talk to a doctor or counsellor.
  • If closeness feels frightening, or you keep ending up in relationships that hurt you, a counsellor or therapist can help you understand why.
  • Couples, family or relationship counselling can help when you feel stuck, distant or keep having the same fight.
  • If someone you love controls you, frightens you, checks your phone, cuts you off from friends or pressures you into anything you don’t want, that isn’t love. Not safe at home? lists free, private help.
  • If you’re in danger now, call your local emergency number. Upset right now? (spreadloveandacceptance.com/upset-right-now) can help you take the first step.

This chapter is general education, not therapy.

What to remember

  • Love comes in many forms.
  • Closeness is built a step at a time.
  • Old maps show up in love.
  • Love changes over time.
  • Love is something you do.
